This company has been formed to acquire and work as :pleasure grounds the whole of the freehold gardens, with buildings and appurtenancet, situate in Rice-lane, Walton-on- 'the Hill, Liverpool. The grounds are very extensive, comprising .20 acres or thereabouts of freehold land, upon which the vendor will erect the additional buildings hereinafter described. To acquire the property when complete, and to Lake over and work the same as pleasure gardens as.a going 'concern is the object of the company. • The grounds are-enclosed by a substantial stone wall and massive iron railings. The main entrance—a handsome stone structure, fitted With gateways and turnstiles—is on the high- way, adjacent to the Cheshire Lines, the London and North- Western, and the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Com- panies Stations with the additional advantage of the tramways passing the gates. The buildings will comprise— - The magnificent centre portion of the late Royal 4ubilee Exhibition, Manchester, or some other similar and suitable building capable of holding 10,000 persons andcovering 4,600 square yards ot land. This building will have intercepting naves forming a Greek cross, with the dome 90ft. in diame- ter and 15Crt,..high In the centre, and gables at each side flanked with towers. In front of this building and fading the lake will be a dancing floor, .180 ft. by 100 ft. fitted with anrings, and con- structed on the most approved and-setentific principles. Flanking the front, and on each side, will be a fine suite of dining halls . and tea rooms, built after the design of Chinese pagodas, each 120 ft. long by 30ft. wide, capable of accommodating 6,000 persons. A large refreshinent buffet, built as a Japanese pavilion, 115 ft. long and 30ft. wide, and divided into two rooms. , Grand stands underneath which will be lavatories and cloak rooms, mill rooms for the use of athletes, &c. Stone structure, 360 feet long and two storys high, replete with zoological specimens of every description. The vendor has secured a most advantageous arrangement with William Cross, Es., the eminent naturalist, of Liverpool, who will provide and' feed at his own expense one of the finest zoo- logical „exhibitions in the kingdom, and will alas supply keepers and attendants,sthus securing to the company a con- ' stant and -varying supply of zoological specimens. The ' vendor will provide all the accommodation for the collection. Aviaries, Monkey Houses, Lion House, 200 feet by 40 feet, Bead Pit, &c,; also Tanks and,Ponds for aquatic sped-1 meas. Circus, er.Reman Amphitheatre, 170 fcet in diameter, with an arena of 90 feet, or other special structure to be set apart for entertainments of performing animals. • The licensed house known as the "Plough Inn," serving rooms, kitchens, engine house, ,ne.„ and many other build- ings adding- to the requirements of thesgrounds. The Gardens, laid out in handsome fashion. and lighted by electric light. twill be provided with Athletic Grounds, with a splendid Bicycle Track. An-extensive lake for boating purposes, supplied from a brook in the.grounds, thus obviating the rates usually paid for the maintenance of large expanses of water. Fairy-Fountain, Grottoes and caves, Pyrotechnic pictures and displays covering 4,000 square yards of land. Switch- back Railway, tobogganning slides, atrial travelling cant, and novelties of every description. In short,the gardens will provide fte• all classes a resort at once intellectual as well as pleasurable, diversified in every de- gree, es may be exemplified by.the would-renowned Belle Vue of Manchester, which is now one of the best paying invest- ments of its kind. Aquatic, athletic, as well as cycling sports, will all receive due consideration 'as seasonable attractions; also contests of every description. Being .fully licensed, the grounds, and the buildings offer every imeilty for the supply of refreshments. The gardens are also licensed for music and dancing. The vendor has entered into a covenant to complete the work according to plans, specificaticns And designs prepared by Messrs. Maxwell and Tuke, aad to band over to the com- pany the freehold land, buildings, and •other properties pre- viously ,described,:finished and ready for Opening to the satis- faction of the directors, for the sum of £90,000t Messrs. Max- well and Tuke have had great experierioe in designing build- ings for exhibition.and pleasure ground' being the architects for the Brussels and Manchester Exhibtions, as well. as the Southport Winter Gardens. As there is no place of a similar kit 1-for out-door amuse- ments and recreation, the directors are Pdiafied that there is ample scope for the development of a ftelle Vue Gardens in Liverpool and surrounding district, corral rising a population of upwarcla of three millions of people. - Mi cuzzen Rutchut's t' boss o'er t' ship At's anchored you th' docks, Dischargin' sand an' yollo stooanes, I' th' length bi th' bottom locks. 0 them as co'd him "Dick" afooar Greet "Rutchut " wheer he gooas, He looks so bawd an' sailor like • t' plaisters on his nooase ! He's swaggeted reawnd aboon a bit, - Sin he geet full command 0 th' gallant bark at's plowed a way To mony a forrun land. Id name's on t' starn, it's "Busy Sly ;" Id engine's.one hoss peawer ; Th' next voyage eawt it's beawn to tek Some brickdust, tar, an' fleaur. Nea.w, th' engine's one o' t' spavind sooart- Spire topt, wi' fluted sides; It's thad as regulates t' ship's speed, N. matter wod be th' tides. It's fancy knobs o deawn id back, Id cost a creawn—or two! An' th' frigate's lost id compass, when Id hesn'd t' strength to pool Hey, th' Captain's fairly stuffed eawr fooak— His drink scooares they've to pay! He's t,owd 'em yarns o'er th' dangers An mishaps o' Mill Fiill Bay. Heaw t' ship i' th' midneet struck—'twur dark, Be cuddn'd see his hand,— An geet fast on a sunken cob Two yards away fro' land! He's tovrd heaw th' engine strayed away To th' haystack at a farm, And left ',m sweltered on t' wide sea. Wi' t' w9ather fearful warm. O'er navigation heaw he brags, He's one as likes his trade; His " Navigation's " up Mill Hill, An' th' ale-shot isn'd paid! Be cadges bacco to a stock, , An' sprees off "British Fours," \ lies ne'er no brass to pay his way, An' hard work he deplores. Last neet he spoke so pitiful

Mi mans was fit to Cry, BPcose he sed his shirt wur hung On t' main topmast to dry. Strag Dick fro' Fancy Row's his mate, Cook, crew, an' engineer; But Rutchut, th' famed boss wariner, Is t' boss as hes to steer. Last week ther wur a mutiny, , An t' crew an' captain fowt ; That's w beer th' bowd Captain's nooase wur dinged, He's one eye black as owl. For o he's sitch a lovely seet, Wl' lips like Nigger Joe. He's looked on as a hero brave Bi th' nayburs in eawr row. He's towd 'em o, when he gets wed, Ther'll be a gradely do, For he'll tek th' lot fro' th' "Saw Mill" brig, As far as Timbuctoo

Pedestrian: "You say you are a beggar by profession?" Beggar: "Yes sir, won't you help me a trifle to-day ?" Pedestrian "Why don't you try to get into some honest business?", Be„elar : "I'm afraid a change at my time of life would be disastrous. It does't do for a man to throw up a good thing for an uncertainty." Be discovering his prevailing deficiencies, and order- ing his life and habits so as to counteract them, a man may exercise that true self-control which is alone worthy of the name. No wiser or more valuable lesson can be ' learned in the whole system of education than thus to know self and to minister to its deepest needs. Bitter are a losing card, a losing horse. Bitter the public hiss, the private sneer. Bitter are old age without respect, manhood without wealth, youth without fame. Bitter is the east wind'stlast ; bitter a step-dame's kiss. It is bitter to mark the woe which we cannot relieve. It is bitter to die in a foreign land.—Benjantin "I had my picture taken to-day," said little Christine. "I crossed my arms and leaned on a chair, and the pic- ture man put my head in some tongs." "Why, you must have looked like a lump of sugar in sugar-tongs," laughed papa. "Why, so I must have," said Christine. delightedly, 'cause the man kept saying, 'what a sweet little girl.' A man in the path of duty is twice as strong to resist temptations as out of it. A fish is twice as strong in the water as on the shore; but a fourfooted beast is twice as strong on the lan as in the water. The reason is, because the water AM proper element of the one, and the earth ot the other. Thy work is thy element wherein thou art most able to resist temptations. "Darling," said he, tenderly, "I have made up my mind to ask you—to ask you—" "Yes," she whispered, breathlessly. "To ask you to become my wife. I know, dearest, that it is bold, it is presumptuous for me to do so.. You are so much superior to me. I am, I feel, un- worthy of you, but—" "Say no more, John. lam yours. You may be unworthy of me, but—" 'But what, dearest ?" "Half a loaf is better than no bread." AN Acroa AT WINDSOR PALACR.—In his "Random Recollections of an Actor," ,Mr. Frederick Bolton relates the following amusing incident which occurred at a dramatic performance, in Which he himself took part, at Windsor Castle:—" After playing Tom Hayday, in The Prisoner of War,' I had dressed quickly and wanted to look about. I ascended the stage from my dressing room, and found no one about. A sudden impulse seized me. The dais on which her Majesty, Prince Albert, and the Duchesieof Kent tthe Queen's mother) sat, was be- fore me, in a moment I jumped over the orchestra, ran lightly up the steps of the dais, seated myself in her Majesty's chair, and throwing my legs out thoroughly at my ease, exclaimed in a loud voice, Now lam King oil England.' Suddenly a side door opened, and then Colonel Phipps, with horror depicted on his countenance, exclaimed. DO you know, sir, where you are ? ' 'Very well,' I said, In her Majesty's seat.' • Come down, sir, come down; you ought to be ashamed of yourtelf.' 'What for ?' I said. 'No one, sir, is ever permitted to sit on any chair her Majesty has once sat upon.' I de- scended somewhat crestfallen at the enormity of my sin, reflecting what a vast quantity of useless chairs there must be in the palace if her Majesty was not particular where she sat." Tug Figsr Gas' ENGHTEER.—WiIIiarn Murdock was the son of a small farmer in Ayrshire, and when a boy he herded his father's cows, and he seems to have planned and executed a good many things when out in the fields. One of his contrivances was a furnace in a rock, in which he burnt pieces of hard coal taken from a seam above ground. It is thought that it was then, asle saw the gaseous matter in the mineral take fire and blaze away, that the idea first entered into his head to supply a gew method of street-lightivg. It was not, however, until long after this that he *as able to give his discovery to the world. One thing, however, he did while helping his father, and with his father's aid, and that was to make a wooden horse—not a horse to vault over, or a horse for Banbury-cross work, but one for use. It was a horse that went by machinery, and father and son used to ride on it, and all the country-side were amazed at the sight, as well they might be. When he grew to manhood, young Murdoch visited England and sought employment at the works of Watts and Boulton, the great engineers. He saw Mr. Boulton, and was told that there was no opening for him, as trade was slack, and of course he was very disappointed. But aa he stood there in Mr. Boulton's presence, he nervously twirled a hat that seemed very light and very hard. Boulton noticed this, and out of curiosity said. "That's a queer sort of hat you've got, my man; what is it made of ?" "Timmer, sir," said Murdoch, in his Ayrshire speech. " Timber ! Do you mean to say it is a wooden hat ?" "Yes, I do." "Then how was it made ?" "Oh I jist turned it myser on a bit lathe I have at home." That was enough for Boulton. He saw at once that he had no common workman before him, and a situation was found for Murdock. As time passed Murdock did a great deal to add to the fame of the firm that employed him. He soon knew all about engines, and the lad who could make a wooden horse go constructed in after years a steam carriage that ran along the road, and which might be called the first locomotive. This was more than a century ago. It was at Redruth, in Corn- wall where he was staying looking after engines used in the Cornish mines, that Murdocksexperimented with coal as he had done while a boy. In the yard attached to his house he erected furnaces and an iron retort, and here from coal he made gas, and carried the vapour through pipes into his house where it was consumed from burners, very much in the way that js done now. He also stored up quantities of the gas in vessels that could be carried about in carriages to give light at nights. Murdock afterwards conducted his experiments at the works of Watt and Boulton, and at the beginning of the present century these works were illuminated from end to end with the new light. Other manufac- turers asked to have it introduced, and one of the first mills to use it was that of Messrs. Gott, in Leeds. People began to think after this that what was good for mills and factories would be good also for houses and streets, and so gas companies were formed in most of the large towns, and the new light came into general use. It was A great boon. And as Murdock got nothing for his dis- covery—he really gave if` away—it is well that we should remember his name along with this wonderful invention. PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY HVGH BETTE. XXI.—THE SEA. [Concluded.] p

"Walking the plank" is supposed to be the blood- thirsty pirate's mode of making his victims amuse him. If you could kidnap a bloodthirsty pirate, and make him walk the planks in the Liverpool docks for about three days, I feel confident it would cure the plank disease in him entirely, and for ever. If you will kindly follow me up one more plank, you will see me get my berth on board the steamship "Canopus." Casting a nautical glance (copied in detail frem the Bay's Standard) over the "Canopus" I saw that she wasn't as much like a rope puzzle as some of the sailing vessels I had tried; but I wasn't near so severe a critic as I had been three days ago. The cap'n wasn't abOad, so saw the chief officer. He didn't want any boys. He referred me to the chief engineer. Now I didn't see what the chief engineer could want with a boy, but I thought that perhaps he might have charge of the powder magazine and the big guns, in which case I should be his assistant, and consequently second engineer. When I found the chief engineer, he was sat in his room, cutting his corns. Calculating that the corns came wt en the chief engineer was thirty, they would be about thirty-five years old. When I asked if he wanted a boy, he shaved off three slices of a corn very deliberately, and then said he did. With youthful ingenuity I drew his attention to the fact that I was a boy; whereupon he cut one more slice off the corn and looked at me. "Can you cut corns?" he inquired. I said I thought so. 'He balanced his right heel on his left knee, handed me his ponknife, and I commenced shaving a corn off the ball of his foot. Be cautioned me that if I made any slips he would skin me alive. Ha!!! He was some smuggler chieftain in disguise I felt certain; and while I trembled at his terrible threat, I I proceeded in silent awe for some time to cut myself into his good graces with a will; anti I did it. You have often herd of men carving their way to fortune, but I doubt if you ever heard of a boy carving a berth through a corn. The old chief was catechising me all through the operation, and by the time it was finished he had engaged me at a salary of £2 a month. His only objection to boys who hadn't been to sea was that they were sick. I assured him that I shouldn't be sick; I had never been sick in my life. He told me to get my togs ready* be at Lightbody-street at three o'clock to sign articles, and come back to the ship immediately after, as the ship said at high tide, and in the mean- time he had work for me. "Getting my togs ready" wasn't such a tremendous undertaking. I had a brown paper parcel containing one shirt and one pair of socks at the lodgings I had taken the first night I came; and although the woman was surprised to see me come back to claim them, she wasn't any more surprised than I was to learn that they hadn't walked down some hole in the floor. The rest of my wardrobe didn't require much looking after, for I was inside it. • When I fell in with the line of men at the shipping office, I was somewhat surprised to see no uniforms, and was more than ever convinced that :so (you must pardon the slight tinge of vanity in italics) were engaging in some desperate enterprise. I expected a rush of soldiers every minute, and the lot of us being made prisoners; but no, the articles were signed, and aeon afterwards I presented myself to the chief engineer. Instead of taking me through the powder magazine, the \ chief engineer proceeded to tell me in the most cold-blooded way that there were three engineers and a winch man; that I was their boy, and was to attend to their comfort while they attended to the comfort of the ship's engines. He showed me each of their rooms, the messroom, and the engine-room; and then with the most unnatural absence of feeling, he showed me where the soap, scrub- bing brushes, bath bricks, &c., were kept, so that when I wanted to use them, he said, I had only to "get 'em out of the locker." I may have overlooked passages in the Young Men of Great Britain relating to these useful articles, but I cannot remember their names ever being mentioned. The chief then passed me over to the winehtnan (more commonly known as the donkeyman, because his work was to tend the donkey engine used for the steam winches' a man named Ramsay. He taught me how to make the engineer's bed, an art which I learnt with the deepest disgust, for I didn't credit for a moment that such a thing as bed-making existed on board ships. None of my favourite authors had ever hinted at such a thing. The Young Englishman had shown that, after an action with the Portugese frigate, the crew went below to drink their grog, and then flung themselves down anywhere to snatch a few hours' sleep, and be ready for the next engagement. ' I had still a faint hope that all this menial occupation was a mere show till we were fairly riding on the foam- topped wave, so I bustled about putting the rooms in order while we were being tugged down the river. Ramsay gave me some useful information respecting my duties. Ile also explained that the two little brass guns on the quarter deck were the only ones on board, and were used for signalling. He believed the cap'n had a canister of gunpowder, but he hadn't seen it. The way Ramsay unravelled my notions of sea life was almost like sacrilege. By the time the tug•had left us, and the thump, thump of the engines, pronounced us to be in full swing, he showed me my hunk in a room next the fireman's forecastle, and informed me that the chief had told off a trimmer to waken me at three bells when I should have to get some hot coffee from the galley and take it down to the old chief in the engine-room. Before turning in I stood on deck watching the lights, ashore grow less and less; and somehow it seemed as if I could pick out the light in the kitchen window at home from amongst them. I tried to see only the light, and to shut out from mental vision the view of two quiet, sad faces that made my heart swell almost to bursting. Two forms sat, one on each side of the fire, silently rocking, rocking, rocking. Oh! if I could only have said Good-bye! to those two forms, it might have eased me a little. I am perfectly aware that the proper thing to do under these circumstances was ta whistle "The girl I left behind me ;" but honestly, I didn't think about it, and, if I had, the lump in my throat would have spoiled the tune. I turned in To wet with unseen tears Those graves of memory,— and to dream that I had let one of the chief's corns fall into his coffee, and that he had ordered one of the fire- men to skin me alive, which he was proceeding to do, when I awoke to the fact that I was being vigorously shaken by a man who,if I were to judge by his begrimed appearance and his abrupt lecture on sanguinary sleep as pertaining to my saneninary self and the sanguinary ship generally, might have been Satan; but as memory catne to my aid, I concluded be must be a trimmer. I beg to state that he was a trimmer. He was to such a degree a trimmer that I daren't put any of his remarks before you. After seeing that I was thoroughly awake, ho left me. I was just dozing off again when I suddenly thought of the possibility of being skinned alive. I was about to jump up with the alacrity with which you jump out of bed when you are going on a cheap trip to Wales, but it didn't work. There was a beam in the other bunk above me, and if I had known how hard and firm that beam was I should have padded it with cotton waste the night before. But we are keeping the chief waiting for his hot coffee. The iron steps that lead down into an engine-room are not coated with resin; on the contrary, each step is a skating rink on a small scale. There is a brass rail all along to prevent somersaults. When the ship rolls port you lie on your back on the steps. When she rolls star- board you hang on to the rail with as many hands as are not occupied in carrying hot coffee, in order to let your body hang at right angles to the steps. Considering that you are waiting to watch the chief engineer drink his coffee, I thought it best to mention the attendant phenomena: I may also tell you that, after I had broken three pots, and acted as a kind of blottieg paper on the coffee, the trimmer before men- tioned had to officiate. If you desire to know what the duties of an engineer's boy are, I might as well give a short summary here,as I couldn't take you through them consecutively for the few days that follow, during which was slightly indisposed. If I were a nautical novel writer I should worry you with stating the sime of day
and
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 21, 1888.

with each event in so many bells, as four bells for six o'clock and so on, but as I am only a dejected and dis- appointed engineer's boy I won't do it. I had to rise at 5 30, as shown, to make coffee; after which the day was divided into scrubbling the room floors (or, nautically, decks), making beds, cleaning brass- work, laying three breakfasts, three dinners, and three teas and in washing up pots and cleaning knives and forks until 8 30 p.m., when I was at liberty to turn in. The reasons for the triple meal were that one engineer was always below, and had a meal fur himself when he came up, and that the fourth and fifth engineers (meaning Ramsay and myself) stood on the order of their going. You must excuse me for remarking again that this routine was never given in the the "penny dreadfuls."

I have said that I felt indisposed. I can assure you that there wasn't any mistake about it. When a big vessel rolls it gives you a most unearthly sensation. I was once very much indisposed through smoking twist tobacco, and the same feeling began to crawl over me now. Life gradually began to lose its lustre. "Ram- say," I said, "I'm—l'm going to be ill." "Go to the lee side," said Ramsay. I didn't know which was the lee side, but I went to the nearest, where the wind blowing in ray face might have told me I was wrong; but it was too late to retract. I cast my bread upon the waters, and it was returned to me in a few second. Nature seemed to have revolted at herself; but in vain I tried to turn myself inside out. For hours I manfully stood to the pumps, until there was nothing left of me but the shell, when I lay down in the scupper, and mentally pronounced all sea stories and their heroes hollow mockeries. Only one hope was left—if I could reach my bunk. I reached it, and crawled in to die. I didn't even want to shake hands with anybody. My friend the trimmer bad orders not to let me stop in that bunk a minute, and he executed them. When he had dragged me out twice he threatened to throw me over- board if I got in agtin. With the little remaining reason left in me, I saw a happy way of release. I crawled in again, but he only dragged me out again, and cursed. I hated that trimmer as much as it was possible for a , blathering idiot to hate. lam glad to say that the men were kind to me. They offered me dainty pieces of fat pork; and as they had no smelling salts, they let me smell of lamp oil, and otherwise showed me every attention in their power. The old chief were especially kind to me. He fully earned the nautical man's characteristic of "rough-and. ready." Whenever the vessel pitched me into his bread- basket, he was rough to his own horny palms; and when he,gave me an order, and I only stared at him and said " Ugh ! Ugh !" he was ready to choke for want of lan- guage to properly classify me with. We were now crbssing the Bay of Biscay in a 'heavy gale, and as, with the seas we were shipping, any loose articles such as mops were liable to be washed over- board, I Was kindly rolled under, the messroom table by Ramsay, where I acted as footrest for the three engineers for what seemed like three years. I awoke one morning to discover that the messroom door and the skylight were not rapidly exchanging places as usual; and I felt very hungry, and very sore. I found that although the thump, thump of the engines continued, there wasn't the slightest motion of the ship perceptible. I had left home in my Sunday suit, the only suit I had brought with me. It, won't require an extraordinary imagination to picture what that suit *is like by this time. I was about to say "Richard's himself again," when, to make sure, I looked myself over, and tried once more to fancy myself a hero, but it wouldn't do. The most idolatrous youth couldn't have been deceived into such a belief; nay, I am sure that a "penny dreadful" couldn't have turned me into a third- rate hero. I cleaned myself as well as I could, and set about my humble duties as though to make up for lost time.

We didn't meet with a single pirate; we didn't encounter a single hurricane; we didn't even get wrecked; but I must belay, for the captain of this vessel has his weather eye on space. Although several "penny dreadful's" have been named in fullin these Papers, I can assure you that they haven't paid for it as an advertisement.—Yours nautically, HUGH BETTE.

ALT.F.GED FALSE PRETENCES AT WARRINGTON. At Warrington Borough Police _Court, on Wednes- day, a respectably-dressed woman, who gave the name of Rose Williams, and an address in Winder- mere-st., Liverpool, was charged in custody with having attempted, on the previous day, to obtain money by false pretences from George Millman, of 15, Gladstone-st., a clothier, whose place of business is in Winwick-st. The prisoner was represented by Mr. A. Browne.—From a statement made by the Chief Consthble (Mr. Runt) it appeared that on Monday the prosecutor saw an advertisement in a Liverpool paper setting forth that the sum of £3 lOs interest would be given by a lady for an immediate loan of £7 until the 25th inst., good security to be given. The address given was Mrs. Clarke, Conis- ton-st., Liverpool, and prosecutor caused a letter to be written in reply to the advertisement. As a result of the despatch of that letter defendant, on Tuesday, appeareci in person at 15, Gladstone-st., where she saw Mr. Millman, who had caused the letter, for a reason of his own, to be written with signature of Simpson. She produced the letter, and Millman asked what security she was prepared to offer. She thereupon produced tickets relating to various articles of jewellery in pledge,and stated th at she had a private income. She also represented that she had property in London, and gave the names of trustees. Prosecutor, who had previously had deal- ings of the kind with a woman whom he believed to be the defendant, was suspicious and gave infor- mation to the police. Mrs Williams was taken into custody on suspicion. In a satchel that she carried were found a large number of letters in answer to the advertisement. She had at the time the sum of £4 17s 4d in her possession. Mr. Hunt asked for a' remand in order that he might comniunicate with the London police as to the genuineness of the prisoner's information regarding her property and trustees in London. In answer to Mr. Browne, prosecutor, who gave formal evidence, admitted that he caused the advertisement to be answered in order to try and catch the prisoner: Mr. Browne submitted that as prisoner was prepared to deposit valuable securities there was no false pretence, but the magistrates said that they considered the case one for a remand. They therefore remanded pri- soner until this (Saturday) morning, allowing bail in the gam of £2O.
BAZAAR AT TIqLWALL HEYS.

On Tuesday afternoon a bazaar, for the purpose of raising a sum of £9O, to clear away a debt which exists upon the Cairo-st. Chapel. Congregational Parlour was, by kind permission of Mr. Wm. Long, held in the ground of his residence, Thelwall Heys. The parlour which was built some years ago at a cost of about .C 350 is a room used for special pur- poses in connection with the chapel and Sunday school. Through the generosity of members of the congregation and friends, the debt had been ze- duced to about .C9O, which it as expected to raise by the bazaar. Owing, however, to the extremely unpropitious+ state of the weather the expectation was scarcely realized, the sum amounting to nearly .C7O being realised, however, during the afternoon. The bazaar was opened about 3 o'clock, in the pre- sence of a very fine attendance. Mr. Wm. Long gave a hearty welcome to the friends who were present. He explained that the bazaar was the ladies' share of the struggle to clear away the debt incurred by the erection of a room for the accom- modation of the congregation.. Mr. W. D. llouomrox, in opening the bazaar, said he was pleased to see so many persons present, and took it that it was an acknowledgment of the kind- ness of Mr. and Mrs Long in throwing open their grounds for the purposes of the bazaar. It was also an indication of the kindly interest they were taking in the geod work carried on at Cairo-st. Sun- day School. The sale had been arranged for, and would be conducted entirely by the Ladies' Sewing Society, ot which their good friend Mrs Long was, and had been for some time past, president. That society had, he could assure them, worked most bravely and industriously for years past, and in a manner to be highly commended. He hoped that the result of the effort put forth that day would be the freeing of the room from debt. He had now very great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. and by way of starting the sakes he would commis- sion their treasurer, Miss Wheeler to expend a sum of £5 on his account, (Applause). The Rev. PRIESTLEY PRIME said before the pur- chasing began he would like to move that a hearty Vote of thanks be accorded to Mr. Houghton, not only for opening the bazaar, but for many other ways in which he had assisted towards the remp- val of the debt, and he coupled with it a similar compliment to Mr. and Mrs. Long for their kind- ness in allowing the bazaar to be held in their grounds. (Applause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL seconded the vote which was carried unanimously. Mr. HOUGHTON having duly acknowledged the the compliment,.ehe sale began, and was carried on till towards 8 o'clock in the evening, the various ar- ticles finding ready purchasers. The bazaar was held near the lodge, in a large marquee, one side of which was occupied by a stall containing many use- ful, ornamental, and artistic goods, presided over by Mrs. Long, Mrs. Winser, Mrs. P. Winser, Mrs. Jen- kins, Miss Wheeler, Miss Houghton, and Miss Valen- tine. The only other stall was devoted to a fine collection of fruit and flowers, attended by Miss Milner, Miss Long, Miss Dunkerley, Miss Dowson, Miss Thornley, and the Misses Wolfe. Tea, presi- ded over by Mrs. Allen and other ladies, was Novi- ded at the lodge and in the marquee. Mr Forsyth's orchestral band, from Manchester, played selections of music during the afternoon.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MR. T. K. RYLANDS.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MR. T. K. RYLANDS.

On Wednesday week a wedding which excited much interest in th'.: neighbourhood took place in the pretty little church at Woodlands, near Broughton-in-Furness. The bridegroom was Thos. Kirkland Rylands, Esq., tecond son of the late Peter Rylands, Esq., M.P. The bride was Miss Vith Nora Pennington, daughter of John Pennington, Esq., of Woodland Hall. Shortly before twelve o'clock the bridegroom arrived at the church, accompanied by his groomsmen, who were Finlay Dun, Esq., of Warrington, W. P. Rylands, Esq., and A. R. Pen- nington, Esq. The bridesmaids were Miss Penning- ton, sister of the bride, Miss Rylands, and Miss L. C. Y. Rylands, sisters of the bridegroom. The bride wore a dress of rich white corded silk, made with a Court train, and trimmed with silver sequin net. The bridesmaids' dresses were white Pongee silk, with hats to match. They each carried a bouquet of yellow roses and a staff decorated with white ribbon. On the arrival of the bride the service commenced with a hymn. The officiating clergy were the Rev. C/L. Reynolds, M.A., vicar of Wray, and the Rev. C. F. Reynolds, M.A., curate of 'Bux- ton, uncles of the bridegroom. The Vicar of Wood- land was also-present. The church was beautifully decorated with flowers. Crimson cloth was laid down on the walk leading to the church door. The weather in the early morning was anything but promising. Before noon. however, it cleared, and a brighter and pleasanter day for a wedding could not • have been wished for. After the service the wed- ding party drove to the Hall, where, after being photographed by E. W. Reynolds, Esq., they par- took of a sumptuous breakfast. About four o'clock the newly-married couple left in a carriage for Di- ver:got'. whence they proceeded by train to Crewe, en route for London. The wedding presents were exceedingly numerous, and, many of them very r costly.—Preston Guardian.

div.head: FORGERY AND_ EMBEZZLEMENT BY A
div.p: FORGERY AND_ EMBEZZLEMENT BY A

CLERIC. At the Borough Court at Warrington on Tues- day, James Williams (34), Barry-st., until recently employed as ledger clerk by the Castle Rubber Com- pany, Warrington, was brought up on remand on several charges of a serious nature—of forgery. embezzlement, and larceny. The case for the pro- secution was conducted by the Deputy Town Clerk, Mr. J. L. Whittle. who, in the course of his open- ing statement, said that there were other charges to those entered on the sheet against the prisoner, but they would not be proceeded with, as they could not indict a prisoner on more than three charges. There were three charges of em- bezzlement against Williams, but they would be reckoned as.one count. The prisoner came to Warring- ton about 12 months ago in search of employment. The Castle Rubber Company required a clerk at that time, and engaged him. He was an excellent penman, and was put in a position of confidence, in return for which he stole the trousers and overcoat of the manager, Mr. Tay- lor. After he had been in this employment for a time he received a warning as to his conduct, but, notwith- standing this, he committed the offenses alleged against him. In January last the company had dealings with the firm of Storey & Sons, Manchester, and the pri- soner made out a .cheque for £3 10s, payable to I. Storey. Mr. Taylor, as principal, signed the cheque. Prisoner, it was aileged, forged on the back of the cheque the name of I. Storey, and took it to Walker's vaults in Bridge-st., where he induced the manager to cash it. Prisoner afterwards intercepted letters from the firm to whom the money was due, and who were demanding payment. The other charges against the prisoner were that he, without authority, collected and appropriated the following accounts owing to the firm by which he was employed—£l Ila from Mr. W. P. Skelton, Horse- market-st. ; £1 is from Messrs Waring and Co. ; and 16s 6d from Mr. Edward Connor, Sankey-st. He was also charged with stealing the clothing mentioned. After, evidence in support of the various charges had been taken the prisoner was committed for trial to the Liver- pool Assizes. He told the magistrates that he was ex- ceedingly- sorry for what he had done, and that he was 'perfectly willing to repay the money and make every re- paration. He had unfortunately given way to drink, and that was the cause of what he had done.

div.head: MORE SUNDAY TRADING.
div.p: MORE SUNDAY TRADING.

At the Warringten _Borough Police Court on Mon- day, before Alderr.aan Harrison and other magis- trates. Edward Gough, a travelling photographer, was charged with having unlawfully exercised his worldly calling upon a Sunday, the same not being a work of necessity or charity ; another man, named James Leach, being summoned for aiding and abetting in the same. Gough was represented by his brother, bet Leach appeared. P.C. Dionog- ban said that on Sunday afternoon the Bth inst., he saw the defendant Gough taking photographs in a tent on some waste land near Chester-st. He looked inside the tent and saw thirteen persons sitting for their portraits. He cautioned defendant, who promised to leave immediately, but on visiting the place at 6 o'clock in the evening he found defendant still there and doing a good business. He had cautioned defendant the previous Sunday also. The Chief Constable said it was with great reluctance that he brought a case like that into court, but the defendant had caused a nuisance and would not be warned He had even then disobeyed the summon, of the magis- trates by not appearing in person. He explained that the offence committed by the defendant Leach was in being one of the sitters.. He had paid Is for the 'photo of himself and dog. Alderman Harrison: Some time ago a man was fined for selling cigarettes on Sunday; if we allow such a case as this to pa,ss it will be difficult to know where to draw the line. The Chief Constable asked the Bench to inflict the heaviest penalty in their power upon the defendant Gough, in consideration of his having been warned and having taken no notice of what was said to him.—The Bench decided to fine Gough 5s including. costs, Leach being discharged. i A writer n the "Sporting Chronicle" says—" War- rington is the place to live in if you want to be kept on the straight track for the beautiful shore. The police authorities in Warrington exercise so vigilant a super- vision over the doings of the inhabitants that.it is said the very amours of every tom cat are Chronicled in their archives and pigeon-holed for future reference. Yester- day a man named Edward Gough was charged with 'having, on Sunday, the Bth inst., unlawfully exercised his worldly calling of a photographer, the same not being a work of necessity or charity." James Leach was sum- moned for aiding and abetting. Gough was found pho- tographing people in a field, Leach and his dog being the sitters. Gough was fined ss, and Leach was let off with a caution. Wink happened to the dog is not stated, and the only reasofl3 thy a summons was not issued against the sun for ag and abetting the other criminals is possibly because old Sol has since the Bth inst. put up the shutters and retired from business—afraid, no doubt, of the Warrington police. A curious feature of this godly law of the right; reverend Charles the Second is that if Mr. Gough had refused to pay his fine, the magistrates would have, no alternative but—to put him in the stocks. I don't know if the Chief Constable of Warrington yet preserves a set of stocks along with the Act of Charles 11., and other antiquated fnve-a-brac in his backyard; but it does seem that if he means to go in for the Sunday Closing Law vrfth any degree of energy the resources of the town' are likely to be strained in erecting a few hun- dred of such convenient holdfasts for milefactors of the Gough and Leach stamp. That would be a really charming addition to the picturesque architecture of the Buttermarket ; and, while he is about it, he might add a few whipping posts for the reproval of the iniquit- ous Dissenters who still refuse to go to the churches as by law established under another clause of the same useful Act—also still unrepealed. Let us be thorough while we are about it, and put the whole of this truly lovely ornament of the Statute-book into force. Then we shall begin to realise whether we are really living in the nineteenth century or not—which in Warrington seems rather doubtful Just now."

There was a considerable improvement on morning iirtlie condition of General Boulanger, the fever having entirely disappeared. TILE VANDELEUR EVICTIONS.—The Vandeleur evictions were resumed on Thursday. Daring Wednesday night several bridges were destroyed on the way from Xilrush, and the Sheriff was compelled to take a circuitous route.

THE QUININE BITTERS MANUFACTORY CO. (LIMITED) , has just been incorporated under the Joint Stock Com- panies' Acts as a limited company with a capital of £50.000, divided into 35,000 ordinary shares of £1 each, and 15,000 deferred shares of £1 each. This company is eiltablished to' purchase the secret recipe or preparation known as "Quinine Bitters" and certain other pro- prietary medicines and articles and the well-known busi- ness of Mr. Gwilym Evans, of Lia,nelly, in connection therewith. The following are the subscribers to the Memorandum of Association, each of them taking 20Q shares :--George Robert Barclay, 95, Farringdon-st., London, managing director to Barclay and Sons, Limi- ted. Dan Harries Evans, of 10, Cornwall-terrace, Regent Park, London, also sf 314 to 320. Oxford-st., draper and silk mercer. Alfred Thomas; of Park-place, Cardiff, Membensf Parliament. Evan Morris, of 16, Peel-st., Princes Piirk, Liverpool, senior partner in the firm of Morris and Jones, wholesale grocers, 13, St. Thomas's Buildings, Liverpool. Owen Isgoed Jones, of Llanrwst, North Wales, chemist. 4"ohn Davies Penny, of 33, Red Cross-st., Liverpool, manager to David Jones and Co., wholesale grocers. Robert John Elliot, Ph.D., 69, Church- st., Liverpool, chemist. The Articles of Association pro- vide that :—The first directors are George Robert Bar- clay, Esq., Alfred Thomas, Esq. M.P. Owen Isgoed Jones, Esq., and Gwilym Evans, ELI. The qualification tor directors is not less than 100 shares of £1 each. Mr. 1 Gwilvm Evans will act as managing director.

A man's own good breeding is the best security against other people's ill manners. THE PalmaLtrrirs AND ME COMMISSION BILL.---At a conference of Parnellites, held on Thursday, at the coo- ference room of the House of Commons, it was decided to assent to the Bill on three conditions—(l) limitation of inquiry to letters, (2) a controlling voice in the selec- tion of at least one of the judges, and (3) judges to re- port to Parliament immediately their finding as to letters. These resolutions have the full approval of Sir Charles Russell, who, with Sir W. Harcourt, are under- stood to be aiding and advising Mr. Parnell.

div.head: WIMBLEDON MEETING.
div.p: THE WIMBLEDON MEETING.
TUESDAY.

A great number of competitions that have been in progress for many days are being continued this morn- ing. Besides these, the Albert, any rif' e, competition' at 600 and 900 yds., and the Army and Navy Challenge Cup competition, at 200 and 500 yards, occupy attention. The morning is warm and calm, and there is every pros- pect of fair weather for the final stage of the Queen's Prize this afternoon. The following have been posted as winners of first prizes :—Atkinson suite of library furniture, Major Mc. Rerrell, Ayr; War Secretary £lO, Captain Barnett, Oxford; St. Leger, ,tie. £7 each, Mr. Gauby, Irish Rifle Association, Major Glendonwin, Hythe Staff, Major Godsol, 4th Oxon, and Captain Murphy, Irish Fusiliers; Armourers Company £lO, Sergeant Pries, 4th Rants; Evening Prize, Martini Henry, £7, Captain Cortis, 2nd Sussex.

The shooting in the last stage of the Queen's com- menced just after the afternoon gun fire at the 800 yards range, in dull, cloudy weather. Sergeant Bates, Ist Warwick, led at the close of the 800 yards range in the Queen's, with an aggregate of

At the end of the fifth and last round of the Queen's Prize, the highest were : Private Fulton, 13th Middlesex Private Cooper, let Devon 259 Corporal Noakes, Ist Berke 219 Private Pattison, 2nd Argyle 259 Sergeant Bates, let Warwick 2i7 Corporal Jones, 2nd Cheshire Colour-Sergeant Comery, Bth Lanark 254 Colour-Sergeant Ingram, Glasgow Corporal Chicken, Glasgow . Private George Fulton is 30 years of age and an en- graver, and has been six years in his battalion, and was in the Queen's competition last year, but was counted out of the 300 at the end of the first stage. He tied for the St. George's Challenge Vase last Friday, and was ninth in the tie for the silver medal in the Queen's second stage. Corporal Noakes, who had pressed him so hardly in the competition, was one of the first to con- gratulate him upon his success at the conclusion of it. Fulton got a most enthusiastic reception in the Metro- politan camps, round which he was chaired. The greet- ing in the Queen's Westminster was of the utmost cor- diality, the delight of his comrades being unbounded. WEDNESDAY. The Mother Country team won the Bajahof Kolapore's Cup and £24 with 687 points. Canada was second with 674, and wins £BO, as the highest team outside Britain. Jersey was third with 655, and Guernsey last with 609. Thr United Service Challenge Cup and £4O were won by the Volunteer team of eight with 724 points at three ranges. The Marines were second with 683, the „Army third with 674, the Navy fourth with 651, the Yeoinanry fifth with 648, and the Militia last with 592. The Chan- cellor's Plate was won by the Cambridge University team of eight men with 645 points. Oxford's score was' 626.
THURSDAY.

The Irish team of eight won the Elcho Challenge Shield with 1,652 points. The English team was second with 1,642, and the Scotch last with 1,568. The Clifton Col- lege team won the Ashburton Shield, and the Public SchOols Veteraus' Trophy was won by the Cheltenhani team. The Yeomanry Inter-Regimental Cup was won by the First Ayrshire.

div.head: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
div.p: HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
BY MRS. J. K. SPENDER, Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," " Both in the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.

CHAPTER I. WIND AND WORDS. "I call it a crying shame," said Peggy, as she bounced the rollipts-pin on the rickety wooden sable, forgetful of the fact that, it was weak upon its legs ; "I call it a shame to be all foi his own self. I have no patience with his velvet coats, his long 'air, and foreigueering ways; and she—poor lamb—a precious deal too good for k- though she be that wea and wheezy, she minds me at times o' a pair o' bellows." The comparison was not an elegant one, but the neighbour who answered more guardedly let it pass as she looked at Peggy with her red arms dusted with whise flour, her cap awry, and her honest face as red as a rising Sun, pausing to take breath in the intervals of her pastry making. The pastry when it was turned out was apt to be as hard as lead, and had more than once to be broken withsa hammer, if tradition were to be trusted. Peggy's culinary skill did not equal the warmth of her heart. Yet a blackberry pie was so rare a luxury in the gaunt old kitchen that the little girl who peeped from her book with eyes as round as marbles—sometimes to listen to the passionate dialogue and sometimes to watch the red hands dabbling with the flour—was prepared to do full justice to this mystery of cookery. The child had the digestion of an ostsich ; as most healthy country children have who are brought up to ' rough it in all winds and weather. "And to come back to her for money when I work all I can, as no nigger can ha' worked, it's scarce enuff they blessed elates has to put in their insides —well born though they be. Wasn't the last couple o' chickens killed, and the cabbages dug up the last time he come and seed her? Itminds Inc o' avampyre, that it does—sucking their very blood." Peggy's voice had grown shriller, and seemed to mingle wili that of the wind, which was roaring and blustering on the open flank of the hill, changing its tones from a moan to a shriek as it mounted and tore at the leafless trees. "And say it I will—let alone who hears me—like a vampyre I calls it—which they sez is a sort o' bat thing sucking their life-blood !" cried the angry woman, rather pleased with her comparison, as she stripped the stray bits of dough from• her bare and muscular aims; "and it's the dainties he wants, whilst that poor delicate lamb—" Swish ! went the wind, coming with a rush like the , angry noise of the tide, and whirling some of the dead leaves outside the door till they seemed to go round like the spokes of a wheel. " Husli—sh !" said the neighbour, as she got up to give a push to the door, glancing meaningly at the child curled on the window-seat with her book. The furniture in the room was so dilapidated and scanty that the old red cushion on the window-Seat with its frayed edges revealing the horsehair stuffing was the favourite resting-place of the little girl. From it she usually had a good look-out on the pre- cipitous lane, in which seine dead leaves from the previous autumn still lingered on the boughs of the trees, and which was surrounded by green pastures and picturesque cottages. But to-day an amorphous curtain of mist, monotonous in its colour, veiled hill and dale, leaving the outlines of the little grey church, with the leaning gravestones of the church- yard, half-way up the hill, but faintly indicated. " Mind the child," said the neighbour, warningly, looking at the round eyes opened more widely than usual, and at the flush on the plump cheeks. - Swish ! went the wind again, rattling the diamond-paned glass of the cottage window. It seemed to blow away the mist. Reflected grey lights were gleaming on the pools between the pebbles in the wet lane and on the coats of a carthorse, making it look glossy as it plodded UP to a distant farmhouse. , "Don't you be afeared ; she never takes "no notice," rejoined Peg,gy in a lower tone, with a hasty glance at the little maiden who had been biting her lip 4 hard, and trying to sit still without fidgeting or making angry, restless movemsnts as she heard blame cast on her absent fathe:, and knew that she would not be allowed to relieve her pent-up feelings. . "Little girls, should be seen and not - heard," Peggy bad once said sharply, whln She had tried to lift up her piping voice in profs st. There was silence for a minute or two, during which the women spoke in subdued murmurs, varied only by occasional thumps from the rolling-pin, creaks from the wooden table, and whistles from thewind, which waxed more furious in theintervals of shrewish Inimansspeech, twisting and contorting the trees outside into every conceivable shape. The twigs were proddingeach other with a scraping sound, and a few dry leaves and blosld-red berries falling from the straining branches—which were scourged till they were laid bare of 'all their remaining adornments, and the ground strewn with dead and broken frag- ments. Then the wind seemed to grow solid like a man in a rage ready to throw stones. The door opened with a sudden bang, letting in a rush ' of the cold outside air, and revealing the prospect, which had now cleared, with the rounded shoulders of the distant trees crouching together beneath the hollows of the hill, as blast after blast fell on them, cutting like whips. Peggy closed the door, standing with her ample back to it, and apologising to her gossip with much grumbling about the ramshackle sort o' a barns". And after a good deal of head-shaking as well as hand-shaking the gossip departed and the child returned again to her book, not without a heart- ache, and not without a strange recollection which the little girl coupled in a way she could not have explained with the conversation she had overheard —a recollection of a sudden appearance like a shadow darkening the sunshine, pf sharp words and of a fainting - fit, followed by a fall. After the fall came angry words, which the child had overheard in the intervals of her broken sleep, continuing to a late hour of night, and then a ringing of bells, and a man's voice calling for sal volatile and other restora- tives, kept by medical orders in the cottage. The walls of the cottage were so thin that the angry words could be easily overheard, and Ursula 's imagination had been haunted till long afterwards by the sound of a'gentle voice raised in passionate pleading—an im- pression on the imagination, which had been intensi- fied by the ,fact that Peggy had threatened her with the terrible probability that if she allowed her- self to get into passions she would grow up "like her father." Children are apt to lake the part of the calum- niated, and the reiterated prophecy had a curious effect on Ursula's mind, inchningher to take the pert of the absent and much-maligned father, rather ' than that of the sickly mother who was rarely able to see her, and who had, a nervous ailment constantly on hand to give employment to one of the doctors in the neighbourhood. She asked questions of the doctor, who of course had heard all the gossip; but as a doctor was bound to affect ignorance of such reports. He petted the child and supplied her with fairy tales, instead of satisfying her curiosity. Take care of your little brother," he said, as he patted her head; "wait till you grow up to become a member of the meddling sisterhood." She did not half like the. doctor,' who wasnot handsome—with thick under:lip, and rather full face, indicative of his benevolent disposition. "Handsome is as handsome does,'' said Peggy, to whom she confided her prejudices, and who had a feminine liking for a rounded aphorism in the shape of a homely proverb. It was not easy to tell the little girl that the good doctor, like so many other unselfish members of his philanthropic profession, was ready to giveihis ser- vices to a sick and penniless lady for nothing, driving over in all weathers from the city of Abbey- ford, which was a few miles off, to help her, and that moreover he was deeply interested in the somewhat neglected children' preferring the resolute and quick-tempered girl dto the shy and retiring boy, who was a couple of years younger. Dr. Havard was a rich bachelor, and could afford to humour his bene- volence. "Poor little chap," he would say, as he looked at the sallow face of the boy, from which eyes of the colour of wild hyacinths, fringed with long black lashes, met his own so timorously, "he will never be able to battle with the world; heredity, all heredity I Gifted with his mother's beauty, and yet inheriting from no long-forgotten ancestor the artistic temperament which already distinguishes him from other children. How well I remember the father, with his ardent love for natural scenery, and how his own people discouraged it; how it was met with perpetual antagonism in every fashion I Well, genius, is a curious thing—too often allied to mad- ness ! Give me instead that science which is common- sense at its best; but if ever a lad was ruined in his childhood, it was poor Leonard Campion, who i had once so much good n hisn." In spite of his roughly-cut features—which looked as if nature had forgotten to finish her chiselling— the doctor waasas tender-hearted as a woman. And so finding the ill-fated children cooped together in the cottage at Langhorne • in wet weather, with no

Hitherto there had been nothing to play with but an old violin, which the father had left unstrung, and a couple of paint-boxe9, which he had flung on one side, but which supplied sufficient paint—after dexterous sqUeezing of St old tin tubes—to daub, the walls and disfigure to" half-finished canvasses which Campion with his usual carelessness bad left behind him. There were n° other toys in the kitchen, which was the most attree' tive part of the cottage, monopolising the grent'er part of the ground floor. But there was an aUnor phere of goodness and kindness about the buxel' ,Peggy, which, if alternated by fits of scolding, di something to make the young ones CO fortable. She did her best* to prephre fo° to tempt the palates of the children as well .99 the delicate/ appetite of her mistress, and if sae failed it was not for want of the best intention She never interfered with the reading aloud of tl* new versions of Cinderella, Jack and the stalk, and the Little Mermaid, which were devourel greedily by both her charges—Ursula being perche° on a high chair, and using thewindow-seat-as a le_ei tern, whilst Peggy pared the pdtatoes or prepan the beans for the simple dinner, and Ray listen 7 open-mouthed, soon knowing the tales by beef; "Bless the little innocent dears—if they never to know no worse!" said the furtively ' wiping her eyes with a corner of 0,„'" rough apron as the two prattled of their beliefs w gardens planted with flowers which never with and birds which sang perpetually, or fairial took care of fountains of diamonds, and print- in enchanted palaces. " But, lor, the sight i trouble there s in the world. ,They'll cum on' giants and dragons jist as their poor mother rstead o' they fairies." Peggy had done her best to help the children spell out their lessons during the long illness of ' delicate mistress. Mrs. Campion - had tried superintend their education when her health I allowed her to do so, teaching them to pronoin Englishwithout the Somersetshue brogue, which tb had picked up with juvenile readiness, and tai infinite pains to instruct them how to enter a. l'°°, properly, to address strangers without clowin manners, and to answer when spoken to Mith° abruptness. " Oh, it is all of no use," she would say Wile- times, with a burst of tears, "how can I ell that they should be anything but vulgar absurd, brought up with such surroundings ? diamonds would not be known from pebbles bedded in such mud." Dear and lovely as Mrs. Campion was to her lit ones—a sort of minor divinity, emThrined sanctuary of suffering, still retaining its fastidi ness, and some of its dainty love of luxurY--- children who entered her sick room on tiptoe often with bated breath, were conscious of a sort 0' thraldom in her presence fatal to their ln" glow /of spirits. Ray was the least to hide his sense of the oppressive pliere making his baby wants known in an sistent and noisy manner peculiar to his and afterwards betraying a readiness to be b°l which was shocking to his more faithful little sif Young as Ursula was, it went to her heart ,h 0 the delicate mother say in' piteous tones: "Take them away, Peggy, they will be 110,0 downstairs with you. It is dark and dull for here. Why should they know dulness be time ?" Peggy had always agreed with her mist' it as her opinion, that if "they was ID in the semi-darkness of that invalid room grow up white as young plants as was I lars ;" but often little Ursula would creep a, she was not noticed and sit by her mothei reading; her favourite books. One day when she was learning her geob ventured to ask Mrs. Campion where wi chanted country where lived the fairy gra with the silver locks, and was surprised to instead of answering, the invalid gave unusual fit of weeping. Peggy had to he summoned for the ba.._ and the child felt-naturally aggrieved at short, when she repeated her question, by servant, who bade her with unusual acerbity her lessons and not bother with nonsensical "It is not nonsense,"- retotteansula.- knOws, li everything ; I thought, of course,: • "You may talk to her about anything else, bli4f, about fajry grandmothers," insisted Peggy, sharpness which set Ursula vinegar-like sha thinvoist Was it the fairy grandmother who jiad driven t through their village with silver harness. her white horses, and who. had nearly kn over little Ray, and then noticing kis blue eyes had drawn down the blinl of her riage and ordered her coachman to drive on 113 less of the cries of the frightened boy? TlLn_.°o, grandmother lived at the manor house of St. Art 00' miles away over the hills. Ursula had fonna by asking questions, but not of old Peggse answered her tartly whenever she alluded to t° cident. The old woman was disconcerted by tlitic:oo usual keenness of the little maid. But PeggLO sidered herself a match for anyone, and rer severely— ," Talk to your mamma about anything not such stuff as fairy grandmothers. (To be continued.)

THE SITUATION IN ZULULAND.

The Earl of CARNARVON asked the Secretary for the Colonies whether he had bad any recent intimation of the progress of affairs in Zululand. He quite trusted that his noble friend apßreciated the gravity of the case and would lose no time In sending an ample force. He took the opportunity of expressing the.regret he felt at the death of that eminent man, Sir John Brand. _ _

)Lord KNDTSFORIN at a latel: period, stated ti at the following telegram had been received from the general officer commanding at Etshowe :—" I have :relieved Pretorius by flying column under APKean. Ifir.Torrinanz moved an adjournment to call atten- tion.ito the violent attaas 'made by the police upon peaceful and unoffeinfrng persons in Trafalgar-square, on the afternoon of Saturday, the 13th June, and on Saturday the 14th instant.

Vermission haring been given, MeCONYBEARE pro - eroded to speak in support of his motion. lie only asked for the proper regulation of meetings in Trafalgar'. square, and unless the Government would try a con- ciliatory solution of this question 'the matter would grow worse and worse. Mr. MArrnaws,condemned the conduct of the agita- tors in Trafalgar-square, and said ttra„t no right of meet- ing had been established in the coats of law. After further debate the closure'Vras applied, and 'the motion was defeated by 255 to In.
THE GOVERNM'ENT AND THE-CHARGES AGArNST MR. PARNELL.

Mr. Suannnts inquired of Mr. W. H. Smith whether the Government had held any comrounication with the lead- ing counsellor of The Times in' the case of O'Donnell v. Walter with respect to the charges brought by that journal againSt members of the House, and whether be was prepared to state to the House the na- ture of such,communications. •

Mr. %nett said it was absolutely without precedent to make any statement with regard to private communica- tions between 'members of the Government. If the question -was intended to suggest that the Government had received any communication from the Attorney- General as 'to the'facts which had come to his know- ledge as counsel for the defendants, he desired to state most distinctly that there was not the slightest founda- tion lor any such suggestion. (Loud Ministerial cheers.) The AeroallEv-Gatinasc desired to say that he had not received•the slightest communication, direct or indirect, from Her Majesty's Government. Mr. PARNELL asked whether the position of the bill regarding the appointment of a commission of judges, Which stood after 31 orders of the day and five notice of motion;was a`test, of the measure of the importance which the Government; attached to the bill? • Mr. W. H. SMITH said the bill was introduced in re- sponseto the offer which he made to the hon. member and to those associated with him. It was for Mr. Par- nell to say whether he would accept the proposal of the Government. The Government did not desire to debate the proposal, and he put it down in order that it might be accepted or rejected. If the motion was accepted the-bill would be immediately printed and circulated. Mr:Painceta, asked leave to move the'adjournment ot the Efnuse in order to call attention to the statement of the right hon. gentleman. The SPEAXER said it would be a violation of the rules of the House to move the adjournment when a motion in relation to the same question was down on the paper. Mr. PARNELL replied that his motion had referefice to the position on the paper of the bill, and not to the merits of the bill.
Mr. GLADSTONE askedwhether the motion was to be , taken that night. Mr. W. H. SMITH replied that he had hoped it would have been taken that night, but if it was opposed it could not be taken.

Mr; PAR- 111M-1.--e-x-Pressed his surprise at this statement, and emphatically asked, amid cheers from the Irish benches," Are we to accept as sheep the judgment of a jury of butchers ?" Mr. W. H. SMITH said if there was opposition to the bill it could not be•taken after 12 o'clock. Sir WILFRID Lewson suggested that the motion shonld be the first order for to-day; but Mr. SMITH refused to not upon the suggestion. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
The House then went into committee on the Local Government Bill, and, some other clauses were added to the bill.
Clause 63, which transfers the property and liabilities of the county to the county council, was considered and passed ; as were clauses 64 and 65.

An amendment, moved by Mr. RTTCHIR, limiting 'the borrowing powers of the County Council to one-tenth of the annual ratable value of the ratable property in the county, was agreed to; but an amendment, moved by Mr. WHARTON, limiting the period for the repayment of loans to 30 years instead of 60, gave rise to some•dis- cussion.—Mr. RrEcnix and Mr. STANSFIRLD assented to the amendment, but Mr. H. arOWLER and Mr. Cot, LINOS urged the Government to extend the period to 40 rears, or even to 35 years. nr. RITCHIE, however, refused to give way, and, n division being taken, the amendment was carried bv 1'253 to 136. After this the Committee adjourned until I re-day. Leave was given t 6 Loki R. Churchill to introduce a hill for the more effectual prevention and punishtnent of bribery and corruption of and by members, officers, hr servants of corporations or other public bodies.

div.head: 7WWiES ALLEGATIONS.
div.p: THE 7WWiES ALLEGATIONS.

Mr. Smrrri then rose and moved for "leave to bring in .1 bill to constitute a Special Committee to inquire into the charges and allegations made against certain metn- hers of Parliament and other persons by the defendants in the recent trial of an action entitled O'Donnell v. Walter and Another ; the Commission to have power to examine witnesses on oath, to compel full disclosures of all facts and documents, and to grant certificates protect- ing from all further proceedings other than proceedings for perjury Ibitnesses who may have committed them- selves by such disclosures, the parties to be represents:l by counsel if they think fit." _ - -

, • , M. PARNELL, who was greeted with Opposition cheers, , said: I was surprised that the right hon. gentleman should have moved this bill in silence after having in- formed the House in this reply to the question that he would expect us to accept or reject the bill before it was ‘ minted., (Irish cheers.) And it turns out he expects unto : 'accept the bill before he has even ,explained it, or told us . anything about it.—(Ministerial cries of "Oh," and Irish cheers.) A more monstrous proposal was never made. This is not a question for me. It is not a question for the rights hen. gentleman (Mr. Smith). If these letters are trw and genuine, if they were ever dictated by me, if they ' were ever signed by me,l, whom you call honourable. , in this House am dishonourable and dishonoured. The , Attorney-General, in dealing with this matter in his ' speech, and referring to one of those totters in which an I alleged facsinti/e was published last year, said that, without doubt, if untrue, it was the worst libel ever ' published on a public mall. (Ministerial cheers.) If these libels are true, if these letters are genuine, if the right hon. gentleman believes that they are genuine, then instead of making bargains with me he should have come-to this House and said,' The Government are de- termined to have this investigation—(lond Irish cheers) —and whether this alleged criminal likescit or not—the Government will investigate this matter to its very sources and its vary roots.' (Ohe,ers.) That would have been the language,of a, Minister—(cheers)—.representing a great nation and a great country. But Ile, the First Lord of the Treasury, head in this House of a.great party and of the Government,comes and says to me—this Bill Sikes—" it is for the hon. member to say whether he will accept or reject it." He offers me this as a sqb- stitute for a jury. He says I sin to accept this tribunal without knowing the names of the 41e n j s who will be placed on it, or their umber, , in the case of a jury we should have the chance a the fortune of a ballot. We have nothing except the very vague terms of his rderence tea jury of 'Judges nominated by himself. (Laughter and cheers.) Why should I trust the right hon. gentleman—(cheers) knowing that he and his party and his Attorney-General have made themselves accomplices in these foul and scandalous and disgraceful libels— (cheers)—and that his organs in the press have made themselves accomplices? Yet lam to trust the right hon, gentleman blindfolded to do me that justice which he says he was willing to do. (Cheers.) The Govern- ' ment desire to put the cart before the horse. They desire, following the example of their Attorney-General in the recent trial, to keep the question of the genuine- ness and authority of these forged letters in the background (cheers) —to investigate any other question as to what Tom did and what Dick did and what Pat did and what Harry did all over the country before they come to the investigation of the question of what I did. This has become a public ques- tion. The r4lit hon. gentleman will not be allowed to bank oat of the investigation. (Cheers.) I will hold the

right hon. gentannan to an investigation. (Rentrood cheers.) I will give him no chance of creeping ant, but I will claim my right when this bill reaches Commlttee, if I find that its details will not afford that fair investi- gation which I claim and demand— (Ironical cheers from the Ministerial benches, responded to by loud cries of "Oh" and " Order " from the Irish members, and one voice, "A neck of cads.") The SPEAKER: Order, order. Mr. PARNELL': I claim my right. The Marquis Of CARMARTHEN : I rise to order. (Loud cries of "Order" and "Sit down.") The SpEalan (emphatically); Order, order. Mr. PARNELL : I have just finished. I shall claim my right when this bill reaches Committee to influence the judgment of the House upon its details if 'I think it necessary to do so, and I shall decline to make any bar- gain with the right hon. gentleman to withdraw the bill from the judgment of the House as to its final shape and effect. (Loud and continued cheers from the Irisa members.)

• Mr. W. H. Smtvn reminded the hon. gentleman that the ercvernment had Always declared And still believed that the proper tribunal was a Courtrof taw, and it was because he had declined this tribunal that the bill was brought in. He declined to say anything which could intimate that the Government had formed any opinion on the subject., but he promised that the names of the memburs of the 'Commission would be stated in Com- mittee.

Sir W. HAROOURT expressed his satisfaction that the Bill was to be debated, and Mr. Dirzwvn dissented alto- gether from the proposed tribunal, thinking the House had sufficient powers of its own. Mr. SEXTON and Mr. LABOUCHERE made some remarks and Mr. W. 111. Slum fixed Monday or the second, reading. .

On the motion to go inth Committee on this bill, relating to the formation of joint stock companies, Lord HERSCIIELL moved that it be referred to a Select Committee. The bill, he said, was saturated with good intentions. and for that very reason was fraught with ranch danger to commerce. The Earl of KIMBERLEY tnought it would be better t attempt legislation after, than before full information had been obtained.—The Marquis of EALISBURY stated that the bill was only intended to 'attack shams, which Were obstacles to honest enterprise. If the nokie and learned lord required information, why did he not move for a Select Committee earlier.
Earl GRANVILLE saw no advantage in proceeding with the bill.
The House divided For Lord HerechelPs amendment ...44 Against The House then went Into Committee on the bill.
The bill was---1;er'1;ally amended, and when the 7th Clause was reached the Committee stage was adjourned and the House resumed. BILLS ADVANCED.

The University Bill passed through Committee. The Supreme Court of Judicature Act (Ireland 1877) Amend- ment Bill, giving increased Ministerial power to the Court of Appeal was read a second time, and Lloyds Signal Steamers Bill -passed through Committee. lhe House adjourned AO 20.
. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—T 7. ESDAT. The Speaker toot the chair at 3.p.m. . QUESTIONS.
In answer to Mr. Powell Williams, Mr. itrroang said that the Government would give to the House the whole of the information with which it was supplied by the Boundary Commissioners. _ . .

Mr. SsxroN inquired if it was true that the Irish Government had detailed an army, of 500 men to assist at 100 'evictions in County Clare the next day.— Mr. Dextrous replied in the affirmative, and added that he believed every effort had been made by agita- torsto produce resistance to the law, but he hoped the efforts would fail.—Mr. Barret;: By whose authority do you make that statement P—Mr. J.
