The committee divided, and there were—for the clause 174, against 229, majority 55.—The Government, on the motion of Mr. HOIIHOUSE, accepted a clause providing for the transfer of the appointment of ooroner from the freeholders to the County Council. A new clause dealing wlth the power of County Councils to appoint medical officers of health was then agreed to, The -clause dealing with the,.qualification of medi- cal officers was under discussion at half-past five o'clock, when the proceedings of the Committee were adjourned. 'The Liability of Trustees Bill, was read a second time; and the House adjourned at twenty minutes to six o'clock.

HOUSE OF 1.19RD5.--Tinraseax. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four, o'clock. A telegram was read by Lord KNUTSFORD indicating an improvement in,the condition of affairs in Zululand. A question was asked as to whether children would be allowed to use the Playgrounds attached to London Board schools on Saturdays, and Lord CRANBROOK promised to make 'inquiries. Several bills were advanced it stage; and their lordships adjourned at ten minutes to six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tuurcsnex. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. The Lords' amendments to the Lancashire and York- shire Railway Bill were considered and agreed to. Tim PARNELE COMMISSITON.--Questions were asked on many subjects, from female clerkship examinations to the magazine rifle and Chinese immigration to Australia. But the most interesting were the inquiries relative to the Attorney-General and the Parnell Commissioir.—Mr. Summers Mr. Sexton, Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Mr. P. Stan- hope, dr. Labouchere, and other members put question after question to the First Lord of the Treasury, and kept him busy in reply until hiS patience was well-nigh exhausted, and there were decided indications of annoyance in his tone. He de- clined to give any undertaking that the Attorney-General should not attend another Cabinet Council at Which any question with reference to " Parnellism and Crime" was under consideration, nor would he make any statement as to the course the Government would pursue about consulting the hon, and learned gentleman. The Gov- ernment, he said, hp. 4 not supplied the leading counsel with any information; nor, he added in reply to Mr. Sexton was the offer made last session of the Attorney-General as counsel to the Irish members in proceedings against the " Times " still open. He retained to the Government full liberty of action, on their own responsibility, as to the course they might take in constituting the Commission, and he informed Mr. Parnell that he had no intention of putting down the bill as the first order for Monday. Complaint was made as to theconduct of the Government in not supplying members with information as to the charges; but Mr. Smrrix referred them to the newspaper reports, and alto- gether laid the foundation for a lively night on the se- cond reading. In reply to Mr. Gladstone, Mr. SMITH -said he proposed to take the pommission Bill about nine or ten o'clock on Monday.—Questioned by Mr. LABOU- aim, be did not contemplate the discussion occupying more than two or three hours; if it did, there was the al- ternative of suspending the standing order, but he should be very sorry indeed to take that course. Quesnoes.—Further questions were asked, as to laun- dry work in schools, the meetings in Trafalgar Square, the Oaths Bill, and limited companies.—Sir J. FEacius son, replying to Mr. Redmond, said the Government were in negotiation with regard to the question of Chinese emigration, and that they had reason to believe those negotiations would be satisfactory to the Austra- lian people. Local. GOVERNMENT BlLL.—Committee was then re- sumed on the new clauses of the Local Government Bill. A clause for the appointment of properly qualified medi- cal officers of health was agreed to.—Mr. WiLmazis moved that the County Councils should have power to name fit persons to be county magis- trates. An interesting discussion followed. Mr. SAMUEL SMITH took part in it, and said his experience in Wales had convinced him of the necessity of a change of the law. In Flintshire the magistrates were almost ex- clusively Tories and Chnrclunen, and the great majority of the population Liberals and Nonconformists. More- over, the representations of the people on this subject had been treated with contempt, and they were con- sequently very discontented. When the Committee divided the clause was rejected, 168 voting for and 217 against it. Several new clau6es of local interest were agreed to, and before midnight the bill as amended was ordered for report amid loud cheering from both sides of thellouse.

' At Wednesday's inquiry at Tullamore Dr. Moorhead, who visited the late Mr. Mandeville in gaol, said the de- ceased suffered from sore throat and diarrhcea, and wit- ness made frequent recotnmendations s to his medical treatment which were disregarded. The witness spoke to finding the deceased one day walking in his cell with no covering but the bedclothes, and also to the deceased complaining the next day, when suffering from rheuin tism, that the bedclothes had been taken away from him and that he had been left naked for twenty-four hours. He thought that the treatment endure& by Mr. Mande- ville was sufficient tb undermine the strongest constitu- tion. , The coroner's inquiry into the death of Mr. John Man- deville 'was resumed on Thursday morning at Mitchels- town. Among those present on Thursday were Mr. Condon, M.P., and °Mr. Featherstonhaugh, governor of Tullamore Gaol.—Dr. Edward M`Craith, Mitchelstovm, was examined, and gave it as his opinion that Mr. Man- deville's constitution was injured by his being left naked in his cell whilst suffering from a sore throat. Bread and water was not a proper diet for a man suffering from sore throat, rheumatism, anddiarrhcea. After his release Mr. Mandeville consulted him. He was then very thin and nervous. Dr. Ronayne, a visiting justice who saw Mr. Mandeville in Tullamore goal in November when he , was on punishment diet, said he warned the Governor that he was going too far and that there might be a sud- den collapse.

div.head: 'LOCAL _GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: THE 'LOCAL _GOVERNMENT BILL.
At four o'clock the 'Hone went into Committee ,on the. Local Government Bill, , _ _
Very rapid progress was made. Several clauses re- garding district councils wece debated, and many amend- mentsto other clauses were never proposed. . . . . . .

• Clauses applying to the Municiu pal Act to County Councils, and ,incorporating such Councils, were passed with little comment, but on the clause providing for the appointment of Finance Committees, Mr. CONYBEA RR moved an amendment extending to those bodies the administrative work of the County Councils in the intervals of .the latter's sittings. This proposal Mr. Ritchie objected to and. it was not pressed. _ _

Clause 100 was reached justipefo;e 8 p.m., and added to the bill amid cheers, the progress made 17 the .sitting having been exceptionally rapid. On Clause 101, Mr. WEBSTER proposed an amendment providing that the selected councillors (county aldermen) shalibe•elected by ballot, and that an elected councillor should only be able to vote for three-fifths of the total nunaber of selected councillors to _be appointed. —Mr. Floanonse favoured the idea that the elected councillors should .only have power to vote .for one county alderman or selected Donn- cillor. Mr. Ravin:lona considered the ballot -entirely out of place when the-voter was representing a constituency.—The Government proposal was criti- cised by other members; but Mr. RITCHIE declined to accept either of the suggestions •put before trim.— Mr. WEBSTER, agreed to remove from his amendment the words as to the ballot, and intimated that he would take a division on the rest. Mr. H. H. Fowram pointed to the various _difficulties which were likely to arise on the selection of County Aldermen, since a brief preponderence of one party. at the first election might determine the balance of Dower for years. Be suggested the desirabilit3r of introducing' the transferable vote.—Mr. RITCHIE urged that the question should not be divided on that night. but should be considered at a later stage.—After con- siderable further discussion, Mr. Webster withdrew his amendment. ' Several other clauses were rapidly added to the bill, the amendments being of a purely technical character. and consequential upon other emendations previously made.

Clauses 116 and 117 had reference to the duties and salaries of the Clerks of the Peace under the bill, but most of the amendments bore more particularly on the home counties, and the clauses were not in the end . materially modified. On the motion of Colonel Guicres,•it.was decided to add to Clause 117 a sub-section providing that the per- son who at the appointed day was the clerk of the gaol sessions in Yorkshire and Lincolnshire should, it he held office at the . time of the passing of the Act, continue to be the clerk, and should also be the first clerk of the Joint Committee for the County Councils of the three ridings or divisions of those ,eounties, and should hold the office by the same tenure, and have the same power (if any) of acting by deputy as heretofore. When Clause 119 was reached great amusement was caused by the circumstances that the names of Sir John Dorington and Sir Trevor Lawrence appeared in con- nection with a whole string of amend ments•none of which were moved. Mr. Ritchie. himself became,confused in consequence of the constant recurrence of the name, and there was a loud burst of laughter when he rose to state his view on an Amendment which had not been moved. The clause was added to the bill, as were also Clauses 122, 123, and 124. Go which verbal .amernimttnts had been set down. With Clause 125 there ended the consideration ,of the tnani body bf the bill. -Upon this clause Mr. Woodall and Mr. Conybeare both spoke, the latter amid derisive cheers from Ministerialists, but shortly before midnight the clause was disposed of, and the Chairman, amid general cheering, reported progress. There remains for consideration only the seliedule•of the hill, and some new clauses, which will betaken to- day (WednesdaY). The House adjourned at 12 10. HOUSE OF COMMONS, WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes After twelve o'clock. , THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL._

The consideration of the Local Government (England and Wales) Bil in Committee was,resumed. The original clauses having been got through at the previous sitting, consideration was given entirely to the new clauses_ Mr. CRANKING moved a clause the object of which was to make the payment of local rates more equitable as be- tween landlord and tenant—ln the discussion that fol- lowed Mr. Rathbone, Mr. Ritchie, Sir W. Baxttelot, Mr. Stansfield, Mr. H. Fowler, and Sir William Harcourt took part. The latter said the division of rates was the prin- ciple at issue. The proposal had been described as in- opportune(' but he reminded the House of the words of Felix to Paul—"Go thy way for this time; when I have . a convenient season I will call for thee." Why in a bill settling the principle of local government should they not settle .the principal of local rating? It was a gross injustice to make the tenant pay for permanent improvements from which the owner derived advantage. Mr. Goscitsri charged the right hon. gentlemen with trying to set owners against occu- piers and with endeavouring to create bad blood between them, remarks that were received with Ministerial cheers and laughter from the Opposition. Sir J. GOLDSMID urged the Government to undertake to deal with the , question next session.—Mr. &qui said the Government could not go beyond the promise nude to deal with the question at the earliest possible moment. Mr. GEnon. who followed, had rather an exciting time of it. He started amid cries of "Divide," continued his speech in uproar, and the closure was twice moved before he finished it.—Lord HARTINGTON, who said that the whole question of rating was of sufficient importance to form the subject of a separate

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

John Mc.Oonnell has died at Oldcastle, county Meath, at the age of 112 years. The deceased took an active part in the rebellion of 1798. At a special Crimes Act Court, at Sligo, on Monday, Mr. Nfe.Hugh. Mayor of Sligo, was charged With inciting to intimidation. On the applicatitw. er the defendant the 7.ase was adjourned for a fortnight. - - • ' • -

'Judge Andrews, opening County Cork Assjzes, said ;here was nothing in the criminal statistics to prevent niro from stating that the improvement observable in other counties WAS also apparent in county Cork. A Perlis mentsry return issued on Monday shows that in die quarter ended June 30th the net number of agrarian putrages reported to the police in Ireland was only 172, pf which two were murders and eight cases of firing at he person. The add resa of sympathy, sighed bra large number of Gladstonian members of t'arliament, and presented to qr. John Dillon at the time of his appeal trial, has since neen written upon vellum, all the ordinary signatures neing repeated. When completed it will be illuminated ind bound. _ . .

On Sunday evening, while some boys were fishing in :he Royal Canal, Dublin. one of the hooks caught some- 'mug very heavy-. fin pulling it out on the bank it was ound to be the body of a murdered infant, h large stone raving been tied round its neck. The body now lies at the morgue awaiting an inquest. On Tuesday-afternoon the Dublin Corporation presented an address to Archbishop Welsh expressing gratitude for his chamnion,thip of the Irish cause in Rome. Arch- bishop Walsh replying, denied that the resolutions adopted by the Irish party were au insult. lie cordially endorsed many parts of these resolutions, and said that Papacy was not hostile to any movement that would benefit Ireland.

Fold play is suspected in connection with the mysterious death of an Orangeman named Greenaway, whose body was found' on Monday on the railway metals near Gilford, County Down. There is now little doubt the man, after being murdered and the body mangled in a shodking manner, was carried on to the railway line, so as to make it appear be had been killed by an early morning train. The police are carefully investigating the affair, and a number of arrests ath expected. THE 'DEATH OF MR. MANDEVItLE.—INQUEST. The inquest on Mr. John MandeVille, of Clonkella House, Mitchelstown, was resumed at Mitcbelstown, on Tuesday, at 11 o'clock, before Mr. Coroner Rice. The Mc.Dermot and Mr. Timothy Harrington, M.P., appeared for the next of kin, and Mr. Morphy appeared on behalf of the General Prison Board of Ireland. The Mac. Dermot said relatives of the deceased hoped to prove Mr. Mandeville!s death was due to unreason- able hardship ,put upon him by those in whose power he was.

The Coroneresplained at the outtlet that he held the inquiry at the solicitation of deceased's relatives. Mrs. Mary Mandeville, the widow, said the deceased told her his throat was sore during the whole term of imprisonment It was so sore that he dould not eat his brown bread. The prison doctor did not relieve him, but certitled that he was fit for punishment. He suf- fered greatly from hunger, and at times his mind wan- dered from hunger. He had prayed to Heaven that he might die before he went mad. On one occasion a war. der, taking his meal outside the cell, threw in a piece of meat, and deoeased told her he never enjoyed anything so much in his life. One prisoner, he said, tiglitened his waistbelt. He became more and more hungry. Since his release he frequently complained of sore throat and weakness.

Cross-examined by Mr. Murphy Since Mr. Mandeville entered politics he was frequently out from home at night. She only once saw her husband under the influence of liquor, and he promised her this should never occur again. Mr. O'Brien entered court while witness was giving evidence.'

Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., said on the way to the county gaol he had a oceversation with Mr. Mandeville, who said he would not wear prison dress or perform menial work in prison. He urged Mandeville to leave the fight to him, as it would probably be a life and death struggle, and there would be more hesitation about maltreating him than Mandeville, as the latter was.a man of magnificent physique. They would think it safe to experiment upon him and use brutalities with less scruple. If be died, officialism alone would tell the tale. Nothing would induce Mr. Mandeville to promise this. On the second morning in Cork Gaol he saw Mr. Mandeville, who suffered from diarrhcea, and had been deprived .of his clothes by force. When in the train he asked Mr. Mandeville if he ever saw anything more like wilful murder, and the reply was, "I suppose that is just what they are up t 0.7 When leaving Cork for Tullamore he asked for a medical examination, as he knew they were going where there were no witnesse.s. Mr. O'Brien detailed is treatment in Tullainore Gaol, and the attempt to make him wear prison clothes. He met Mr. Mandeville at mass in the prison. and he then appeared unwell. After he was released he met Mr. Mandeville, who was shockingly altered. He was a different man—shrunken. and extremely nervous. Previous to Mr. Mandeville's imprisonment he never saw a more magnificent specimen of a man. When in prison he heard on one occasion that Mr. Mandeville WEiS on punishment diet in Tullamere Gaol. He (16. O'Brien) cautioned the Governor that the punishments to which he could be subjected were defined and limited, and that no rule of the Prison Board 'autliorised violence. Mr. Morphy said he would delin* his cross-examination at Mr. O'Br]en until the next morning, and the court • thou adjourned.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

It is stated that many members of Parliament have secured "pairs" for the first week of August, and that the attendance will be greatly reduced after that date. The Ministerial whips are trying- to discourage the pro- cess as much as they can, but, owing to the lack of in- terest in the legislative work and the prospect of an autumn sitting, members are, says a London correspond- ent, disposed to take their departure at all hazards. More than 80 resignations were received on Monday by the "Four Hundred" of the Birmingham Liberal Asso- ciation. The announcement was hailed with loud cheer- ing, and the President of the Association expressed satis- faction that the party was now clear of dissenters. The resignations included those of Dr. Dale, the Rev. Dr. Croeskey, and Mr. Bunco, editor of the Daily Post. Next week the new members for Ayr and Spalding will speak In Mr. Matthews and Mr. Bright's divisions. Mr. Michael Devitt writes stating that lie has no recollection of having promised, in Mr. Parnell's name, every assistance to Mr. O'Donnell in his action against The Times. He remembers offering personal aid, and also premised to do his best to persuade Mr. Parnell to render some financial assistance, but Mr. Parnell refused to give any monetary aid, as the case had been deter- mined upon without consultation with him, and in a spirit which he believed unfriendly to his interest. Mr. Parnell expressed himself willing, however, to give evidence, and to facilitate the access of Mr. O'Donnell's solicitor to the Land League books. Mr. Davitt adds that he had nothing to do with inducing Mr. O'Donnell to take the action against The Times; but, believing he had been libelled, he felt bound to render any help in his power in what he believed was a bona fele action on the part of Mr. O'Donnell. • MR. H. GLADSTONE AND MR. O'DONNELL. The Press Association issues by permission a summary of the correspondence which passed- between Mr. Herbert Gladstone and Mr. F. H. O'Donnell in April, May, and June, 1882, respecting Irish administration and remedial legislation. Mr. O'Donnell having offered his counsel and opinion on Irish affairs, Mr. Herbert Gladstone had an interview with him on April 22nd, and wrote a memoiandum of the conversation, which shows that he was informed that the Irish extremists were ready for a compromise if the political subjects were released, arrears settled, and the Bright clauses ex- tended; that a declaration in favour of law and order by the leaders of the League might be made the occa- sion of the release of political prisoners, and that the Irish detested and repudiated the notion of separation. Some further correspondence followed, and after the in- troduction of the Prevention of Crimes Bill, Mr. Glad- stone wrote depreeating Mr. O'Donnell's hostility to the measure, and promising that remedial legislation would follow. Further correspondence includes letters written by Mr. O'Donnell on April 24th and May sth, 1882, the latter, it will be seen, 24 hours before the Phcenix Park murders. In this communication. Mr. O'Donnell warns Mr. Herbert Gladstone to remember the real difficulties of Mr. Parnell's position. These difficulties, the letter state', were threefold—John Dillon, Patrick Egan at Paris, and Ford, the Irish World proprietor, in America. Ford had already had the impudence to wire to Mr. Parnell, say- ing, "Rumours of compromise in circulation. Deny them at one. No compromise with the British tyrants. No rent for ever. The triumph of the .people certain." If, wrote Mr. O'Donnell, Government did not hurry on the settlement of arrears and evictions, they. might endanger Mr. Parnell's power to bring the crisis to a close. The writer added, "We do not understand Lord Frederick Cavendish's appointment. Personally we like him. The time has come for a decisive step and a magnificent speech. Your father can accomplish both the one and the other. We stand at a turning point in history, and your father to-day holds in his hands the balance of two nations' destiny." SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN ON IRISH AFFAIRS. On Saturday, a large garden party was held in the grounds of the Wildwoods, North End, Hampstead, the residence of Mr. Samuel Figgis, at which Sir George Trevelyan spoke, and among the audience were Sir W. Lawson, Mr. O. V. Morgan, Mr. T. W. Dickson, Mr. Biggar, and Mr. T. P. O'Connor. Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN, referring at length to the speech of the Duke of Argyll in the House orLords, said: For the manner in which the movement against excessive and unjust rents is conducted the Nationalist. party is responsible, but for the fact that the move- ment was to be conducted nobody is responsible except the Government and their supporters for the last two years. (Hear. hear.) The Duke of Argyll said the in- spiration of those who spoke on behalf of the tenants of Ireland came straight from hell. (" Shame.") Be did not use those actual words; but I listened to his polished, and covert, and elegant phrases in which that odious imputation was couched; and when I heard the nobles of England, without one representative of the Irish tenants among them, applaud I thought how little there was of chivalry and courtesy, how poor a sense of justice and how little sympathy with thtsufferings of the Irish people within those gilded walls. (Hear, hear.) And then the ..puke of Argyll attacked me. I was on the steps of the throne, and would have given £lOO to have been able to reply then and there to his face. He proceeded to charge inevaith attacking Mr. Balfour for his Manner of speaking of the Irish members. What I said, and say again, is this, that the Ministers have put political op- ponents in prison; that they treated those opponents as common criminals and not as political prisoners, and then when they have gone to public audiences they have jeered and laughed at, the sufferings of the men whom they had under lock arid key. (Hear, hear.) And I defy the Duke of Argyll to say it is not true; and if he says that is the way rulers should speak of the people committed to their charge, all I can say is this— that he is not the Duke of Areyll of old who sympathised with Italy, who was the advocate of the negro slave ; he is not the Duke of Argyll who, amid the sullen discon- tent of his own order, was the entertainer and friend of Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe and General Garibaldi. (Cheers.) In his attempt to make out that in the old days I was as Mr. ' Balfour and Lord Spencer as Lord ~alisbury lie cannot say that we ever deliberately said an insulting word against any man who could not answer. He brings up one passage picked from every- thing I said, in which I charged the Irish members with making too highly of crime. In the terrible revolu- tionary times between 1880 and 1884 Irishmen of b.ith sides and parties were too irritated to speak with indulgence of some things that were done by people who professed to have the same political opinions as themselves. Sir George Trevelyan I proceeded: Two years ago the mass of the people were ' unwilling to exclude the Irish members from Parliament, and now the whole Libefal party with its leaders are ready to keep those Irish inembers. Two years ago the mass of the people were not ready to buy out the land- lords of Ireland at the risk of the British taxpayer, and when Mr mitli comes with his proposal to get another £5.000,000 of credit to buy out the I;ish landlords, he will find that the people are still of the same opinion. (Hear, hear.) But the great body of the English people have come round to the firm persuasion that you must govern Ireland by conciliation and confidence, and not by coercion and distrust.

Snoexixo DRATR.—Mrs. Leese, of Kidsgrove, was crossing the railway at Harecastle Junction on Tuesday evening with her two children, when one stopped on the line. The mother pushed the child off the rails, but was herself caught and cut to pieces by an express train. div.head: OEN EItAL NEWS.
div.p: OEN EItAL NEWS.

The total number of admissions to the Glasgow Ex- hibition up to Saturday last was 1,856,513. • Sir Morell Mackenzie left Windsor Castle, on Monday, on the conclusion of his visit to her Majesty. The London correspondent o' the Freeman's Journal says that Mr. F. H. O'Donnell has gone abroad for the benefit of his health.

--- It has been decided by the Salford Libraries Com- mittee to open the reading rooms in the borough on Sun- days, commencing in September next. At Nottingham, on Saturday, a man, named Stawson, was committed for trial for forging an endorsement to a cheque from George Barrett, the jockey. Capt. Argrove, ex-marine superintendent of the?, and 0. Steamship Company, has received a commission a 3 honorary commander in the Royal Naval Reserve.
Further attempts were made on Saturday to hold meetings in Trafalgar-square, London, but the police succeeded in frustrating the objects of the demon- strators.

About 900 Dundee excursionists had a narrow escape on the river Tay. on Saturday. The steamer conveying them struck on sunken rocks and immediately begat' to sink. The passengers were transferred to another steamer. _

.„ ..... „.. Mrs. Slaughter, the wife of a Worthing publican, blew down the lamp ehiatney with the object of ex- tinguishing the light. A terrible explosion followed. Mrs. Slaughter was so shockingly burnt that she died in a few hours.

A public inquiry respecting the local charities of that part of Derbyshire extending from Glossop to Chapel-en le-Frith is to be held by the Charity Commissioner, Many of these charities, it is alleged, have been misap propriatod. A case of suicide came before the Coroner of Liver- ' pool, on Saturday, in which a woman named Bridget Burke dPstroyed herself by taking a dose of carbolic acid whilst labouring under temporary insanity caused by excessive drinking. .

The Duke of Cambridge will, on August 10, unveil the memorial which the corps of Royal Engineers are placing in Rochester Cathedral in memory of the late General Gordon and the officers and men who fell in the Relief column to Khartoum.

Great•excitement is created in the extensive mining districthf Ebbw Vale in consequence of work being sus- pended at the collieries. Upwards of 1,600 miners have "struck owing to a dispute with the coalowners regarding the removal of dibris in the mine.

Mr. Justice Denman, in charging the Grand Jury at Monmouth Assizes, said the calendar was the most ex- traordinary one that had ever come under his notice in a county containing a quarter of a million inhabitants, tnasmuch as it did not contain a single charge of fraud, stealing, forgery, false pretence, or burglary.

On Monday morning a little girl, 14 years of age, named Emma Millward, was charged at the Birmingham Police Court with attempting to commit suicide. She jumped from a bedroom window to escape a beating from her mother, and afterwards tried to drown herself in the canal. She gave a shocking description of the way she was treated at home. Her body was covered with bruises. The case was adjourned so that the mother's conduct might be inquired Into. The adjourned interview between the directors of Bryant and Mays and a deputation of members of the Trades' Council took place, on Tuesday afternoon, at Bow Atter a lengthy discussion, the directors conceded prac- tically all the demands of the strikers, including the abolition of fines, and payment for stamps and brushes. In the evening, an open-air meeting of the match girls was held at Mile End, at whiph the surrender of the directors was announced, amid enthusiastic cheers. In the Court of Session, Edinburgh. the judge granted a decree of divorce in the Aberdeen bookseller's case, in which there were eight co-respondents. The husband, who, it was alleged, allowed his wife to dance in skin tights before mere was ordered to pay his wife's ex- penses. He claimed £lOO damages from each of the eight co-respondents. The judge allowed no damages, but ordered each of the eight men to pay his ow ex- penses. MR. AND MRS. GLADSTONE'S ARMEE WEDDINCL—The Daily News says Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone are approaching the jubilee year of their married life. The opportunity will be taken by a circle of personal friends and col- leagues in both Houses of Parliament to make an inter- esting presentation. Mrs. Gladstone will receive the portrait for which she is now sitting to Mr. Herkomer, and Mr. Hull's portrait of Mr. Gladstone, which forms a feature in the Royal Academy of the present year. has , been purchased for presentation to the right hon. gentle- .

TEN CHANGE AGAINST A CANON OF WORCESTFR.—The 'Rev. Robert Hall Baynes, honorary canon of Worcester, and late vicar of Holy Trinity, Folkestone, was brought up, on remand, before the city magistrates at Oxford, on Tuesday, on a charge of obtaining goods and money from Oxford tradesmen by means of cheques on a bank at Folkestone, at which he had had no account since 1884. After a lengthy hearing the defendant was com- mitted to the Quarter Sessions, bail being accepted in two sureties of £lOO each, and himself in £2OO, an application to lower the amount being refused,

DARING PACAPE FROM A WORKHOUSIL.—A daring escape from the Kirkby Stephen Workhouse was made early on Saturday morning by a woman named Sewell, who is 85 years of age and quite unable to take care of herself. Early on Saturday moraine she was missing. A ladder was planted against the inside of the high wall and it was found that She had reared this up, and had ascended the wall and dropped down on the outside, a great height. She was,' some hours later; found, in a public.house narrating her adventure and expressing her determination to walk to Carlisle.. , ThE EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A Mile-op-WAR'S MAW—At Chester, on Monday, the inquest was resumed on the body of James Pole ot Laytown, Ireland, an able seaman, who died -from the result of injuries received near Chester while travelling from Holyhead to join the fleet at Portsmouth.. Several of the deceased's com- rades were with him when he/ell from the express, but in response to telegrams the coroner received a reply that they had gone to sea with the fleet, and the inquiry was adjourned. Detective Hughes produced a boot and cap found on the railway, which deceased's wife failed to identify. A MANCHESTER BOOKMAKER SENT To 'PENAL BERVI- TDDE.—At Down Assizes, on Saturday afternoon, Thos. Parkmore or Parker, a bookmaker, bailing from Man- chester, was indicted for assaulting John Archbold, on the 11th April, at Downpatrick Races. The evidence was that the prisoner was making a book, and that subsequently a disturbance took place, when Archbold found the prisoner's hand in his pocket. The prisoner got off, taking with him £5 10s. of Archbold's money.— The jury found the prisoner guilty, and the Judge said that as prisoner had been previously imprisoned for five, years, he must now be sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. THE DEFENCE OF THE MERSEY.—A commission froth the War Office and the Admiralty—at the head of it being General Sir Lothian Nicholson, K.C.8., and Admiral Sir Vesey Ilemilton, IC.C.B.—visited Liverpool on Monday, and addressed a conference, convened by the Mayor, of merchants, shipowners, and representatives of public bodies connected with the city ad port, on the subject of the defences of the Mersey. In his address, Sir Lothian Nicholson indicated the scheme whioh the Government contemplated for the better protection of the Mersey and the ships and commerce of the port. A local committee of representative shipowners and merchants, with power to add to their number, were appointed to consider the subject.

AN INHUMAN CAPTAIN DESERVEDLY PUNTSHED.—At Plymouth, on Saturday, David E. Mahony, master of the ship Mary Stewart, of Nova Scotia, was sentenced by the Board of Trade assessors to be deprived of his certificate for three months forcruelty to his mate and' a seaman. The case with regard to the former was that the captain confined him to the cabin when he was ill, keeping him without food, and . refused to supply him with medicine. Eventually ' this man was left behind, at Brunswick, with fever, and was still in the hospital. Concern: leg the seaman, the evidence was that he lay in his bunk three weeks, --seriously ill with consumption, anti the master refused to give him other than salt pro- visions, and limited his supply of medicine. The result t was, the crew alleged, that Svenson died in consequence. The Board of Trade intimated that other charges will be instituted against the defendant. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' INQUIRY:STARTLING EVIDENCE —The House of Commons Select Committee on friendly societies met for the first time on Tuesday, Sir H. Max- well presiding. Mr. Ludlow, Chief Registrar of Friendly Societies, gave statistics as to collecting societies, as dis- tinct from ordinary friendly societies. The largest ool- lecting societies were gradually working out the next largest. It was practically 'impossible for them to re- lieve sickness. They could give benefits only on death and burial, and a vast official network was created, tending to absorb an increasing proportion of subscrip- tions. Their public meetings were a farce, and the delegate system should be compulsory. The Friend* Societies' Act needed strengthening, and the powers of the Chief Registrar increased. The collecting system tended to increase infant mortality, and familiarised parents with the idea of the death of their child. For insuring infant life he suggested some branch of the Post Office. In Manchester and Liverpool children were sometimes insured in more than one society. DISGRACEFUL SCENE AT A FUNERAL.—An unseemly display of popular sentiment was witnessed at Penzance Cemetery, on Sunday. Thomas Oates, who had only been mfirried twelve months, committed suicide on Tuesday right by throwing himself into the deepest part of Penzance Harbour with licwt. of old iron round his neck, to which it was secured by a piece of his mother-in-law's clothesline. The deceased, his wife, and one child lived with this wife's mother, and popular opinion attributed the suicide to an unhappy home. Two thousand persons attended the funeral. Until Pre- bendary Hedgeland moved from the grave there was nothing more indecorous than loud talking and laughing. When the prebendary left the mob tried to hustle the young widow and her mother into the grave. Failing this, they stripped the younger woman of her widow's dress, bonnet, gloves, and wedding ring. A policeman got her into the sexton's house, and he and three volun- teer preservers of the peace saw her safely home. They were followed by a jeering and shouting crowd, the chief offenders being women.

TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT-A... FOUR WOMEN KILLED,. A frightful accident occurred shortly after Saturday midnight on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line, by which four women lost their lives and many other passengers were more or less injured. The train to which the accident occurred consisted of an engine, six or seven earriagm, and two brake vans, and left London Road Station, Manchester, for Glossop and other stations via Guide Bridge. It is an ordinary passenger train, which is generally well filled with people who have been visiting Manchester from the out districts for business and pleasure, and there was a Lair complement of pas- sengers. When the train arrived near to the engineering works of Messrs. D. Adamson and Co., near Hyde, at a point where there is a junction of the line, a goods train struck one of the carriages and smashed it to atoms, literally strewing the line with splinters and other material. A quarter lot a mile before the collison occurred, the carriage, which was afterwards struck by the goods train, oscillated so fearfully that the occupants tried to attract the attention of the guard, but apparently without success; and it is believed that from some cause not ascertained the carriage had left the metals. The right side of the carriage was struck with terrific force by the engine of the goods train, which was running in an opposite direction, and the passengers on this were partly buried in the rear of the carriage and shockingly mutilated. Those in some of the other carriages were shaken, and some of them received rather serious injuries. Those who were uninjured at once set about relieving their less fortunate fellow passengers, whose shrieks filled the air. Fires were lit on the embankment with the debris of the wrecked carriages, and passengers and officials from neighbouring stations were soon removing the wounded to the station near Hyde Junction, where the waiting- room was utilised as a temporary hospital. Four per- sons, whose bodies were shockingly disfigured, were found to have lost their lives—all women. Other pas- sengers, men and women, were attended to on the spot after a short afterval by medical men from neighbouring towns, who had been summoned as soon as the salous nature of the accident was realised. Several others in- jured were able to resume their journey after being attended to by the doctors, and others were sent' on to the Manchester Infirmary. The bodies were identified durirg the day as those of Mm. Middleton, Glossop; Mrs. Beard, Glossop; Miss Wilson, Glossop; and Mr. Ba.stien, of Hadfield. The list of injured includes James W. Ainsworth, Glossop; Frank Cellen, painter, Glossop; James Goddard, land- lord of the Victoria rioter, Glossop, who are at the Man- chester Infirmary; Mrs. Cellen, wife of Frank Cellen ; John Bennett, Hinting Vale, and his daughter, a young girl, who is somewhat severely shaken. The following Glossop passejgers were more or less hurt :—Louie Duffiey, Alfred Mellor, Eliza Ann Collins, Alfred Smith, Joseph H. Smith, and a young man named Be,ales, or Beald. Miss Wilson, who was killed, was to have been married this weak. The three persons at the infirmary are progress- ing satisfactorily, and no fatal result is anticipated. The most serious case is that of Cellen, suffering from a severe shock to the system and injuries to the head and back, but with spine uninjured. Ainsworth is also in a serious condition, having received a compound fracture of the arm, whilst Goddard is suffering from injuries to the thigh and head, and severe concussion, from which he had not recovered at a late hour last night. Break- down gangs from Gorton and other depots were sum- moned immediately after the accident, and in less than two hours had the lines so far cleared that traffic could ha ram, mart

• Statement:: made hy passengers ny toe train leave no doubt that the carriage which was run into by the goods train toppled over by reason of an axle breaking after it had oscillated violently for some time, and that the goods train caught the right side of it, smashing it to pieces. The occupants, alarmed at the oscillation, had for the most part gathered in the middle of the com- partments and thrown themselves on to the seats. Nearly all the injured—at any rate those most seriously hurt—were in this carriage. THE CAUSE OF THE ACCIDENT. The officials of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway Company have made a searching inspec- tion of the scene of the accident and the wrecked carriage. They find that the first mark of displacement on the line, showing the carriage first went wrong, 540 yards distant from the place of thel actual collision. A remarkable fact is that, although the carriage turned over, neither the couplings nor the connections of the automatic brake gave way, and the only injury to the permanent way was the breaking of a chair. It is the opinion of the officials that a sudden jolt or jar caused the axle to break. The axle was a perfect one, and seems to be of the very best steel, without any flaw or air bubble to indicate weakness at the point of fracture. The fracture was a clean one, as clean as if the axle had been caught. It is believed that the driver of the passenger train had become aware that something was wrong, and was pulling up his train at the time of the accident, but he has not been examined. The brake was applied just before the collision occurred, and too late to avert it. It would take 120yds. for the train to pull up after the application of the brake.

THE INCH 'ST., On Tuesday afternoon, at Dukinfield, Mr. Johnson, di- trict coroner:opened an inquiry touching the deaths of Mrs. J. Middleton, Miss Jane Wilson, Mrs. aria Bestian, and Mrs. Blard, who were killed on Saturday night by the railway collision near Hyde Junction. After the jury had viewed the bodies, Mr. E. Chapman, one of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Di- rectors, expressed their profound regret at the lament- able recurrence, and their sympathy for the bereaved and injured, and promised to facilitate the investigation in every possible way. Evidence of identification was afterwards given, and the inquiry was adjourned. Major-General Hutchinson, of the Board of Trade, arrived in Manchester on Monday night, and yesterday, along with the leading officers of the company, he in- spected the line and the broken axle, which lies at Guide Bridge Station. At London-road Station, Manchester, he examined some witnesses, but the proceedings were private.

div.head: TRIAL OF JACKSON.
div.p: TRIAL OF JACKSON.

The murder of Assistant Warder Webb in Strange- ways Gaol engaged the attention of' a jury at the Manchester Assizes during the whole of Wednes- day. Very few fresh facts were brought before the court on the part of the prosecution. The main interest of the proceedings centred in the theory of the affair advanced on behalf of the prisoner. Briefly put, the suggestion made by Mr. Wharton, who appeared for Jackson, was that the warder in stepping forward to investigate the stage at which the convict's work had arrived stumbled on the rolled-up carpet, and in falling his head came just beneath the hammer Jackson was bringing heavily down on a chisel with which he was prising up one of the planks in the floor. Then, seem what had happened, Jackson fled, in the belief that he would be charged with having struck the man wilfully. The jury, after a consultation of seven minutes' duration, found Jackson guilty of wilful murder. Mr. Justice Grantham in passing sentence said that although the crime might be wanting in those revolting and cruel circumstances which sometimes surrounded and accompanied crimes of murder, yet in this case the very absence of any motive beyond the desire to escape the short remainder of a short term of imprisonment, the very absence of anger or passion, the very absence of any wrong to be revenged, the very absence of strife or of ill-will against the unhappy warderincreased the enormity of, the crime, and left it one of the most cold-blooded and heartless murders with which the pages of our criminal annals were stained. His Lordship passed sentence of death. The prisoner held his handkerchief to his face daring the pass- ing of the sentence, and maintained the impassive demeanour which has characterised him throughout the day, except when' on the admission to court of his father he burst out sobbing. The condemned man has grown a beard since his arrest, and lost flesh. He is thirty-three years of age, and is des- cribed as a plumber and painter:- •

Ouzo Mum:mi.—At the Kent Assizes, at Maidstone, on Wednesday, Fanny Hancock pleaded guilty to mur- dering her child by drowning it in the sea at Sandgate, on the 9th inst., when she also attempted to drown her- self. She persisted in her plea of guilty, and Baron Huddleston sentenced her to death, without hope of mercy. Mn. GLADSTONE ON CURRENT POLITICS. - Mr. Glad- stone met at Sir Wilfrid Lawson's town house on Wed- nesday evening the Liberal members of Parliament for constituencies in Northumberland and Cumberland, and replied to an address which expressed confidence in his policy. The right hon. gentleman first'spoke of the work of the Parliamentary session. He said the Vocal Govern- ment Bill was undoubtedly a great measure as contain- ing an outline which it would be the duty of the Liberal party when in a majority to fill up. He was encouraged by the progress Of Liberalism as shown in the by-elec- tions which had taken place since 1886. He believed that such progress ' had never been made by any party within two years as had been made by the Liberal party during the last two years. Taking these by-elections, he found that:the Liberal gains were 30 per centon the results of them. This was encouraging when they considered that the Government now in 'office obtained their posi- tion through a majority of only 8 percent. on the total poll at the general election. He did not, therefore, agree with the Chancellor of the Exchequer wheit he stated recently. that Home Rule had fallen into the back- ground. He,would not recommend Hie rejection of the Parnell Commission Bill, but it would be the duty of the House of Commons to see that definite issues were sub- mitted to the strange and unheard-of tribunal about to be set up. As to the retention of Irish members at Westminster, he saw no objection to it. There might be some executive difficulty, but it was subsidiary to the maid question of setting up an lush Parliament to deal with strictly Irish affairs, leaving the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament untouched.

• Important and exteipsive Sale of second-hand TIMBER and OTHER MATERIAL, from the Liverpool Exhibition.-- New Galvanised Corrugated Iron Sheets, Iron Roofs, Sheds,, Rouses, and Buildings, Ac.—By MR. CHARLES COSTIGAN, OR TUESDAY; the 240 JULY, and Two Pow.°Wpm Days, at Eleven o'clock each day, at the WINDSOR IRONWORKS, SPEKELSND-ROLD. EDGERILL, LIVERPOOL. About 1,600 tons second-hand TIM- BER from the Liverpool Exhibition, comprising about 150,02 feet run deals and Joists, 61n. by 3tollby 3; about 400,0° feet flooring boards, rough boards and lining boards, 100,0001; scantling, various sizes. All the timber is thoroughly dry al°, mostly in good condition. 40,000 feet 260 x. clear glass, I°' floors, mouldings, about 130,000 galvanised corrugated roofing sheets, 60 . iron roofs from 30 by 15 feet to 100 by 30' complete sheds with iron roofs, wood columns and framing for hay, corn, agricultural, manufacturing, and general pro; poses, same sizes—all the roofs and sheds strongly framed and braced; about 60 miscellaneous buildings, comprising churches, mission rooms, workshops, cricket and other pavilions, garden huts, offices, the buildings strangli constructed and well finished • a few wrought-iron field gale., and other varied and useful goods; also the richly-decorated, handsome, tasteful, and costly wood and glabli pavilion, about 70 feet square, used by Messrs. Kirkland as refreshment silo dining rooms at Exhibition, which will be offiefed in four lots, as follows :—Pirst. Portion known as bakery, about 45 feet 5/ 30 feet, suitable for mission room, school, cricket pavilion, do° Second. Open portion with glass roof, about 60ft. by 25f' Third. Central portion, about 42ft. by 32ft., containing re: freshment bars, counters. ac. : this portion is richly decoratr__: with carved woodwork. Fourth. Smokeroom above, 23ft...°Y 171 t., suitable for billiar+roorn, cricket or tennis pavilion, a';'. —These four lots are very high-class work; were erected ro enormous expense. They are now standing in Exhibitioo grounds, but may have to be removed before day of Oak% Intending buyers may inspect any day between two ano four on applying to Messrs. Dixon's representative at the Exhibition.

The timber framing, flooring, lining, doors, windows, ana glass of all the structures are of second-hand materials frog` Liverpool Exhibition ; the corrugated iron in all cases nett' The timber is thoroughly dry and in good condition, and the buildings equal to the very best. All the materials will be in bandy lots to suit all classes ni buyers. bad Catalogues will be ready a week before sale, and may be of lake° Drxox & CO., Windsor Ironworks, Spekeland-roset.
