div.p: needs to be sifted is the evidence, if there is any, that the Nationalists leaders have encouraged crime and been party to crime; and, more particu- larly, the nation desires to know whether Mr. PARNELL has writtdn the letters which the "Times" alleges are either written by him or signed by him. There has been enough of beating about the bush; let the case be brought to trial upon a legitimate issue and in a legitimate way.

" THB Westminster Review" for July contains an interesting and carefully-written article on some of the avoidable causes of mental deterioration. The writer cannot he said to belong to any parti- cular school of thought; he is dispassionate in his treatment of the subject, and discusses it from the standpoint of he opinions of the highest living authorities. He ranges the causes of mental de- terioration in the following order :—" (1) the habit of thinking alcoholic fluids; (2) the -habit of smoking tobacco; (3) the habit of smoking opium) (4) the habit of taking morphia; (5) excessive mental work; and (6) insufficient sleep." Alcohol takes the first place as a mischief-maker, and as such we propose to note some of the writer's ob- servations. This Westminster Reviewer, to begin with, cannot be said to argue as a teetotaller, for he has a good word to say for the use of" alcohol under certain circumstances; but he adds :—"Be- cause quinine, opium, and chloral are potent medi- cines, they are not necessarily beneficial agents for daily use. In our opinion the proofs are abundant and decisive that healthy men and women are most likely to preserve their health by abstaining froiri the use of alcohol altogether, and, that they can do more, and more continuous, work without alcohol than with it." This is testimony of a very specific kind; and it would be easy to ad- duce ample evidence in its support. Lord WOLSELEY is not an abstainer; but he has found in his various campaigns—and notably in the Red River Expedition—that troops are stronger and hearthier, and accomplish long marches better, with- out alcohol than with it. The same conclusion has been arrived at by those who have had command Of the expeditions to the North Pole; and it is not unreasonable to infer that that which is a cause of bodily weakness is likely to prove a; source of mental deterioration. As to this, authorities are emphatic in their, testimony. Dealing with the causes of insanity, Dr. MIKE places intoxication first—" intoxication, whatever the poison employed may be." Dr. BLANDFOICD, in his work on "In- sanity and its Treatment," says :—"lf we could ac- curately ascertain the statistics of insanity in other countries—civilised, semi-civilised, or barbarous— I think it probable ,ive should find insanity in pro- portion to the use of intoxicating liquors or sub- stances." This may be regarded as more or less speculative; but as regards a limited and still an important area, there is something -like solid evi- dence. "In France Dr. LIINIEit has shown that the consumption of alcohol nearly doubled between the years 1849 and 1869, and the cases of mental disease rose 59 per cent. among men and 0 per cent. among women." A fact of this kind, well- established and indisputable, outweighs any amount of argument. In the United States, some- thing similar was observed. For four years the ad- missions to the Worcester Asylum included 19 per cent. of cases "traceable to drinking habits. A tem- perance reform set in, and the admissions with drink as the cause of insanity fell to 4.5 per cent. It will be said, and rightly said, that there can be no question as to the injurious effect of alcohol When taken to excess; but the writer in the a- West- minster " procqeds to demonstrate that "the moderate use of alcohol habitually deteriorates the quality of nervous tissue, and therefore the quality and functions of the brain." It is not pleasant to learn that insanity is on the increase in this coun- try, and that those best qualified to pass judge- ment have come to the conclusion that this deplor- able increase is due to physical and mental deteri- oration•consequent upon drinking "riot only to the extent of producing intoxication, but in the moderate quantities taken by persons who regard thqmselves as especially temperate, and whose temperance is never doubted by those most inti- mate with them." This is sufficient to give us pause, for we are quoting not from a temperance lecture, but:. from a temperate high-class review. Temperance reformers may show themselves at times to be fanatical, but what if they have the truth on their siae ?

THE Women's Suffrage Movement makes pro- gress, though it has not yet achieved the victory for which it is struggling-- namely, the title to vote in Parliamentary elections. ' On Tuesday the annual general mating of the Society was held in London; and the nembers were in a position at any rate to congratulate themselves upon the fact that there has been no difficulty about extending women's suffrage to the county councils. This has been accomplished by what was described as the Local Government Electors Bill, which is now the law of the land, for it received the Royal assent on May 16th. It will thus happen that in the first election for County Councillors, women who are properly qualified will have votes as well as men. We can well understand-that this will be something of a shock to county magnates who have been in the habit of having ,things their own way without question from voters of any kind. The Tory section of them, who might be expected to disapprove of changes of this kind, are being consoled with the assurance that the majority of female voters will be found to be on the Tory side. We do not doubt that this will prove to be the case, especially for a time; but those who look ahead perceive thatsocial questions are coming to the front, and we think it is a mat- ter of course to say that wbmen in so far as they are reformers will be social reformers. But the main consideration is that, apart from party gains or losses, justice demands that women, who have as much at stake as men, ought to have a voice in making the laws by which they are governed. In- deed, there does not seem any room for argument on the question, for no one can say that the ex- tension of women's suffrage to matters municipal has proved injurious to the country. If a woman may vote for a Town or County Councillor, why not for a Member of Parliament P As the law now stands, it will sometimes happen that a widow who is left with a large farm on her hands, who has, mly be, the hiring and management of scores of labourers, will be shut out from giving a vote, while the very peasants in her service will be her superior on the day of a parliamentary election. This is an anomaly as glaring as it is unjust, and we may be quite sure that it will be one of the many evils that will be remedied as soon as Parlia- ment has got its hands free, by giving Home Rule to Ireland. \

NEWTON RACES.—" The Star," of Saturday last says:—" The ring and the back of the stand at New- ton was infested with thieves, and robberies took place in a most barefaced manner. Mr. Benzon had apocket book containing X2OO 'taken out of his coat pocket. The scene at the back of the stand was most disgraceful, it being unsafe to move for the cabs and traps, whilst the light-fingered gentry plied their trade unmolested.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULYI 21, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULYI 21, 1888.
"TOUCH AND G 0.." Warrington is nraldng progress; it has just been decided to extend the Wor'khouse.

It is reported that the Queen has taken a fancy to having Indian servants in her household. The Scotch have had their pull, and it is fondly hoped that "in the sweet by-and-by" the Irish will have a tu.rn. Ireland is (or ought to be) as near the throne as India.

If "it is a sin to steal a pin," it is more than a sin to put a pin in the ear. ABermondsey woman named Cornish died on Saturday night through pricking the drum of her ear with a pin. The slight wound caused meningitis, which proved fatal. The ear is a most delicate organ, and, like the eye, cannot be treated too carefully

Kr. Herbert Gladstone comes well out of the correspondence—just published—which took place prior to what was known as the Kilmainham Treaty. It would be interesting to see, side by side these letters, the communications which passed between the Tories and the Nationalists before the election of 1885. Will somebody who know S look the Matter up?

Let jobbers and robbers beware. Lord Ran- dolph Churchill is on their trac'.7. He has just brought in a bill for the prevention of bribery and corruption among the members, officers, and ser- vants of public bodies. It is backed at present by Sir H. James, Mr. Whitbread, Mr. Jennings, Sir R. Fdwler, and Mr. R. Power. If Parliament will only back it, it will soon become law—and a good thing too.

. It is suggestive of a primitive and happy state of things, that in the Isle of Man it is only of late that payment of poor rates may be made compulsory. Even now the law is optional, and at Ramsey, on Tuesday night, it was decided that the rst step should be taken in the direction of levying a compulsory rate. They have Home Rule in the Isle of Man, and they manage to settle matters without troubling the Imperial Parliament with things that do not concern it.

The fall of rain has been heavy for several weeks; but it has not yet mad %up for the con- tinuous drought. It will surprise many people to learn that, early in the week, the report as to Rivington reservoir,whichfurnishes water for Liver- pool, was that the stock of water was "only about one-half what it was at this time last year." Liver- pool is still on "short commons," for, although there is less fear of a water fathine, there is need to exercise economy.

A Local Government Board report, recently issued, strongly condemns back-to-back houses. In Warrington they were condemned by Dr. Bal- lard as far back as 1871. Some of these fever- breeding dens have been improved out of exist- ence • but some, we understand, are still per- mitted to continue d mischievous career. It would be interesting to know if any of these condemned houses are owned by Councillors, Aldermen, J.P.'s, and an M.P., and why they are still allowed to stand.

There has been a little sparring between the 1 Duke of Argyll and Sir George Trevelyan. The Duke spoke of the light which shone upon St. Paul as "a light from heaven," but he had his doubts as to the locality of the light which shone on Mr. Gladstone in his conversion to Home Rule. Sir George contended that if one light was from heaven the other must be from hell. "When," he says, "an orator refers to heaven, and to another locality' his meaning is as plain as when he speaks of the House of Commons and another place.'" •

Would it be inquiring to curiously if one were to ask which of the two Houses of Pailiament is to be regarded as "heaven?" There is a good story told of Mr. Disraeli, soon after he became Lord Beaconsfield. On being asked by a noble lord how he liked the Upper House, he said he "felt as if he were dead and buried ;" but, seeing a disappointed look, instantly added "and translated to Paradise." That was neat, want it? It wai DiZzy" all over.,

It is "dog's delight to bark and bite," and hitherto it has been understood that a dog might bite one person with impunity. But Judge.Eddis, of Clerkenwell County Court, has ruled other- wise; and has followed up his ruling by giving a, verdict of £5O and costs in favour of a person who had suffered a dog's first bite—that is the first bite known to the law. It was sufficient for the judge that it could be shown that the dog was of a vicious disposition. This sounds like good sense, and it is to be hoped it will prove to be good law.

It is well that we came to the aid of Sir Gilbert, Greenall in the matter of his bad memory. Since our reminder that he promised to hand over to the Infirmary the receipts for the privilege of fishing in the Walton reservoir, we find that £7 17s. 6d. have been received by the treasurer of that insti- tution, "being the amount of subscriptions re- ceived from the Walton Fishing Club for the privilege of fishing in Walton reservoir." This is good as far it goes. But Sir Gilbert promised to give the public permission to fish as of old. Is he prepared to redeem that promise?

Day as well as night is being made hideous in the neighbourhood of the ' Fair Ground by a horrible Steam Whistle, which is neither a whistle' nor a shriek, nor a howl, but a combination of all that is worst in all three. Its villainous voice doth —to call in aid the divine William- -harrow up the soul, freeze the young blood, Make startled eyes, like stars, start from their spheres, And each particular hair to stand on end, •Likequills upon the fretful porcupine. Where, oh where! is Norman? If he has not fled affrighted from the scene, he ought to turn on the demon and make it a case of touch and—go.

Newton race meeting has come and gone, and left behind it the average crop of police cases, so that, for the present, the inhabitants may say --" the trail of the [races] is over us all.' Thieves were Carefully plying their trade whilst honest visitors Were carelessly looking on. One young fellow, who gave the high-sounding name of Fitzgerald, was committed for trial, on Satur- day, for attempting to steal a watch and chain. They need to be sober and wide awake who go to Newton races, and to have in mind the old rhyme : He who his watch would keep ,two things must do— Pocket his watch, and watch his pocket too.

Mr. Brunner is doing good service in bringing the question of subsidence at Northwich before Parliament. It, is a downright scandal that the inhabitants of the district should know to a cer- tainty that their property is being serionsly in- jured by those who pump off the brine, and yet have no legal remedy. If there was but one putu- per, they would "go for" him, and the. Courts would give substantial damages; but because the mischief-makers are numerous, the sufferers art i to look on and see the mischief done. What a reflec- tion on the law, and what a travesty of justice!

Mr. Brunner concluded his questions, on Tues- day, by asking the President of the Board of Trade whether he will consider the advisability of bringing in a bill to provide a remedy? Sir M. Hicks-Beach e aid, in reply, that "he was afraid the Board of Trade had nothing to do with the subject, and he could not hold out any hope of the Bard dealing with it. The matter was one which might be taken up locally by those interested." Precisely, and that is just what Mr. Brunner was doing as representative of "those interested." It would have been more to the point if Sir Michael had answered the question as to bringing in a bill. The people of Northwich will, it seems„ have to knock louder, if they desire to be heard at West- minster. I

The Tories are the farmer's friends, of course; but they never do anything for him when they have the chance. It was left to a Liberal member, Mr. Channing, to propose certain enactments in the Local Government Bill, on Wednesday, with regard to the levying of rates, his object being to

W.aniEuNGTos Musgum.--Return for the quarter ending 30th June, 1888. Museum' number of visi- tors April-June, 1888, 11,256; April-June, 1887, .9,344. Reading-room, number of visitors (estima- ted), April-June; 1888, 8,700; April-June, 1887, 9,600; books issued, April-June, 1888,3,493; April- June, 1887, 3,857, Lending Department, books issued, April-June, 1888, 6,423; April-June, 18K, 4,758. VISIT or SA.SGER'S Clncus.—Mr. George Sanger's circus is to pay Warrington a visit to-day (Satur- day), when performances will be given on the vacant ground near the Post Office. There will, in addi- tion, be a procession through the principal streets of the borough. If the weather is unfavourable the _

hitt& item of the proceedings may be somewhat in- terfered with, but the performances are to be given under a waterproof pavilion. The circus is one that has gamed no small fame, and tho attrac- tions provided are so numerous and entertaining as to ensure success. _

MUSIC IN THE Panic —During the past week visitors to the Park have, Its is now the custom, been well supplied with music. On Monday even- ing the St. Paul's Band played selections of dance music, and on Wednesday evening Pletcher's band gained the applause of a numerous concourse of people. Last evening the well-known band of the Warrington Volunteers, under the leadership of Mr. Armstrong, occupied the band stand. The "League of the Cross" band will play a selection of music on Tuesday next, Weather permitting. THE CASTYLE RUBBER COMPANY, L/MITED.—This company was registered on the 6th instant, with a ckpital of I'sooo, in £5O shares, taking over the business of indiarubber and guttapercha manufac- turers, carried on at Warrington and elsewhere, by the firm trading as the Castle Rubber Company. The subscribers are :—John Vincent Taylor, War- rington, ; indiarubber manufacturer; J. Walker, Southport; T. A. llampson, Knutsford, wine and spirit merchant; Richard Walker, Warrington, coal merchant; Mrs. Taylor, 93, Chatham-st., Liverpool; W. H. Brook, Warrington, solicitor; Lewis Voisey, Warrington, chartered accountant. Most of the regulations of table A of the Companies Act, 1862, apply. ACCIDENT TO A WARIUNGTON STEAM LAUNCM. —A steam launch called the "Ontario," which has for some time been• kept in the river Mersey at Warrington, was last week taken to Chester by a boatman of that town to ply on the river Dee, and , has there met with a singular accident. The launch had been unable to cross the weir owing to her drawing too much water, and had lain high and ' dry on the causeway. She was pushed off into deep water, however, but as the forward ballast had been removed, and the boiler and engine weighed heaVy aft, the stern half of the boat disappeared under water. She was hauled to the side of the river near the floating baths, but attempts to float her were for a long time unsuccessful. ELECTRIC BELLB.—Garland, Bell Hanger, Bridge-M.: War- rington.—Advt. CROSSLEY-ST. SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The children attending this school were on Saturday entertained by the teachers and a few friends to a substantial tea. Afterwards, an adjournment was made to a field lent by Mr. Bridge,where the children enjoyed participatioh in various games. The general enjoy" ment was also increased by the distribution of a number of prizes which had been purchased by subscriptions of friends of the mission. Mrs. Qfielrett forwarded a cheque, and Mrs. Rowsou and the key. W. Warner presented the children with. a large sack of nuts. The number of children present was over 250. Before the proceedings finished, .cheers were given for the teachers, the new Rector, Mrs. Quekett, and other friends.

KICKED BY A HORSE.—During the horse fair on Tuesday, a man named Grant, who belongs to Newry, received serious injuries by being kicked by a horse. Grant, who is about sixty years of age, and who is a horsedealer, was at the fair on business and it was by one of his own horses that he was kicked. It appears that he was behind the animal, 'and struck it over the flank with the whip. The horse, a spirited one, kicked, and Grant was knocked down and kicked on the chest and arm. He was rendered insensible, and after brandy had been given him, he was taken in a cab to the home of a friend who lives in Winwick-road. The in- jured man is progressing favourably.

AN ADMINiSTRATION-ORDER RR'Font:P.—At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, John Collins, collier, ap- plied for an administration order. The applicant stated that he was a "coal drawer" for Mr. John Simpkins, Ashton. He usually worked four days per week, and his wages averaged about 15s for that length of time. He had a wife and three chil- dren, none of whom brought him in any money. He bad no means besides his wages and a reserve I pension of 4d per day until 1890. In answer to questions put by his Honour and by the creditors, the debtor said that hjs trade was really a striker, but he had been forced by slack times to work " underground." He had got married when he had no money. He denied that he had lived expen- sively and that he had moved from place to place to escape his debts, living upon credit when he was getting good wages. His Honour finally dismissed the application, remarking that he did not con- sider Collins a deserving object for an administra- tion order. BOWLING MA.TCH AT DITTON FOR £so.—Yester- day afternoon, on the green 'attached to the Ball Inn, Ditton (proprietor, Mr. John Hunt James Shaw, of Warrington, and William Ince, of Widnes, played a game of bowls, 101 up, for £25 aside. Both men are well known experts at this popular summer pastime, and the amount of the stakes at issue caused a considerable number of spectators to be present. Some heavy speculation took place over the event; but after the interval at half game, the partisans of Ince, who had been leading in the tint part of the game, came on the green and interrupted the play, saying that their man was "throwing them over," and declared all bets off. On the starting of the game the Widnes representative overplayed his opponent, and at half game the scores were : Ince, 51; Shaw, 30.. After the interval, the War- ringtonian played in his best form, and the men peeled at 55. Ince now commenced to play better, but was unable to lead his opponent more than a few points, the game being called 67 to 65 in his favour. The Warringtonian again put in some good work, and passed his opponent; eventually winning by 10 points. The scores at the finish were: Shaw, 101 ; Ince, 91. _

IN'TERES. TING RELICS AT THE PARISH CHURCH.— While a quantity of rubbish was being removed i from the cellar of the Warrington Rectory recently„ a window was found which formerly belonged to ; what—before the restoration of the Parish Church , in 1860—was known as the Boteler Chapel. The ' window consists of a centre panel of frosted glass, 11 which bears the arms of the Boteler family, around , which is a border of navy blue and ruby. The i window has been thoroughly cleaned, and yester- day was fitted in one•of the windows on the south , side of the Parish Church, nest to the Patten Chapel. This has been done by Mr. Peter Hill, of Church-st. A portion of the window bearing an inscription was shattered beyond remedy. The in- ' scription read as follows "Beneath this window Beth the body of Sir Thomas Boteler, of Bewsey, Knight, founder of Boteler Free Grammar School. Warrington. Sir Th omas died April 27, MCCOCCXXII." The following inscription has been added to the restored window :—" In memory of Sir Thomas Boteler, of Bewsey, Knight, who died April 27th, ' 1522, founder of Botelees nee Grammar School, re-erected by N. B. Percival, churchwarden, 1S88." There have also been discovered in the cellar of the Rectory a number of candle brackets and small_ 'candle sticks, suclr as were formerly used by the worshippers. A Boom PROBLEM.—At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, before Alderman Harrison and other magistrates, three lads named James Quinn (12), John Broderick (15), and James Broderick (13) were brought up in custody charged with sleeping out upon a ca* of hay on the premises of Joseph Ashton, the Bridge Inn. The Chief Constable re- minded the Bench that the boy Quinn was brought up on a similar charge a week ago, and was sent to the Workhouse. He then informed them that the lad's father, who lived at Widnes, knowing that he would probably have to contribute to the boy's maintenance there, had gone to the Workhouse, and having taken him out, had virtually set him adrift again. With respect to the Broderick& the father had undergone' a sentence of twelve months' im- prisonment for having attempted to murder his wife, Some time ago he had committed another, serious assault upon her, kicking out six of her teeth, and i was then n hiding from the police. In consequence of the injuries inflicted upon her, the woman had been obliged to go to the Workhouse, where she was at present an inmate. The mothert who attended, but only spoke with difficulty, appealed to the magistrates in behalf of her sons, stating that they were homeless. The eldest Broderick (weeping) : Please, sir, I wouldn't sleep out if I had a home to go to. The Chairman: We hardly know what to do ' with you. It was decided to detain the boys at the Bridewell until night, the boy Quinn promising on ' being set free to go to his father at Widnes.

FESTIVITIES are to be held at Massey Hall, Thel- wall, the residence of Mrs. Rylands, to-day (Satur- day), in honour of the recent marriage of Mr. T. Kirkland Rylands, son of the late Mr. Peter Ry- lands. M.P. PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.—We understand that at the half-yearly meeting of this company. to be held next Friday, the directors will propose the declaration of an interim dividend at the rate of 15 per cent. THE GAS ComathTEß.—lt is stated that at a meet- ing of the Gas Committee, held during the past week, it was decided that at the next meeting of the Town Council a vote of confidence in the com- mittee should be asked for; and that, if this were not granted, the members of the committee should resign in a body. It is, however, rumoured that one or two members of the committee disapprove of this

step. 1.0.G.T.—1n consequence of the gloomy weather, the open-air temperance meeting in connection with the Good Templars' Lodge, Latchford, was held in the Temperance Hall on Monday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. J. Langham, who, in the course of his address, viewed the temperance cause in its rescue work from a Christian stand- point. He appealed to the consciences of his hearers, and also to their patriotism as English men and women, to contend with the greatest of English foes.—Mr. Wrathall, of Leeds, the missionary of the Grand Lodge, next gave a stirring address upon the general aspect of the question; referring dis- tinctly to the physical deterioration, the mental de- gredation, and the moral debasement of the liquor traffic. Votes of thanks were given to the chairman and speakers.

A RAILWAY INCIDENT.—As a train journeying from Warrington was passing Great Sankey station on Saturday afternoon, some fragments of a large bottle were hurled into one of the compartments through the window, which was down at the time. There were several passengers in the compartment, and one of them—a well-known Warrington gentleman—was struck on the eye by a piece of glass. Dr. Gornall, W}io was on the train, afterwards examined the injured eye, and, acting on his advice, the passenger went to see Dr. the'oculist, of Liverpool, who gave it as his opinion that the eye was not seriously injured. Inquiries are being pursued with the hope of finding out the person who threw the bottle, which, it is surmised by the railway officials, must have first struck the arch near Sankey station, though there are circumstances which point to the conclusion that the bottle was directly and wilfully thrown at the train. •

SCARLET FEVER AND SMALLPDX AT WARRlNG- TON.—Considerable alarm is just now manifested with regard to the number of cases of scarlet fever in the town. The Medical Officer for the Borough (Dr. Gornall) states that the cases of this disease are increasing both in nrmber and severity, there being at present no fewer than 74 persons under treatment at the Infectious Diseases Hospital. There has also been an outbreak during the week of typhoid fever, three adults, all forgemen, having been admitted to the same institution suffering from that complaint. With regard to the smallpox, no fresh outbreak has been reported, there being now three cases in the hospital. All the patients are convalescent. Mrs*. Bibby, of General-st., has this week succumbed to the disease. Parents, on account of these causes, ex,perience great reluctance in sending their children to school, but no schools have, as yet, been closed on account of the disea- ses.

UNWELCOME VISITORS.-At the Borough Police Court, yestersday morning, before Mr. John White and other magistrates, John Hunter, a tramp, and a woman named Mary Taylor, were charged with hay- ing on the previous afternoon stolen from the shop of A.B. A. Smith, grocer, Lateliford,a bag of flour, of the value of 4d. It was stated that the prisoners went to the shop, begging, and as relief was refused them the female prisoner was seen to take the flour, and they both made off in the direc ion of Warring- ton Bridge, where they were subsequently appre- hended by P.C. Meacock. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said Hunter was what was often called "a had bad 'un," and he paid periodical visits to War- rington, where he had been in trouble before. The female prisoner was also of very indifferent charac- ter, and could well be spared from the tow/I.—Alder- man Harrison Could you manage to spare her for a month.—Mr. Hunt replied that she could well be seared for that period.—The prisoners were accor- dingly both sentenced to one month's imprisonment, with hard labour.

WILFUL DAMAGE BY BOWL—At the Borough Police Court, Yesterday morning, a number of boys, aged from ten to fifteen years, were brought up in custody charged with unlawfully &imaging certain palings' the property of Mr. William Owen and others, to the amount of £.3 3s Gd. The Chief Con- stable stated that about the end of last week the -Cast-iron heads of some palings in front of dwell- ing houses in Palmyra-square, belonging to Mr. William Owen, architect, and other gentlemen, were found broken off and lying on the ground. On Monday evening more damage was done, and from 40 to 50 knobs were altogether knocked off the palings. Information was given to the police, inquiries made, and several boys charged with/the damage. As these made statements implicating others, about a dozen boys were then arrested, and were brought up. The cost of replacing the knobs would be is 6d each. Most of the lads pleaded guilty, and they were each ordered to pay the costs, and to receive six strokes of the birch. Objections to this latter course were raised by the mothers of one or two of the lads; but on hearing that a fine of 40s and costs,could be imposed in these cases, the parents became extremely anxious for the iwhipping to be inflicted instead. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—EarIy on Wed- nesday morning a respectably-dressed middle-aged woman was found on the railway between Golborrie and Bamfurlong in an unconscious state, badly bruised and cat. She is supposed to have fallen from a midnight express from Carlisle to Crewe, as an empty third-class carriage door was found open on the train reaching the latter station. The woman is unknown. She possessed an excursion ticket from Glasgow to Warrington, issued on the 14th instant. There is a tattoo mark, "J. M'Eay," found on her left arm. She was taken to' the Wigan Infir- mary, and died there on Thursday. The body of the deceased has since been identified as that ofn War- rington woman. It seems that a young man named W. T. Smith, residing at 46, Napier-at., Warrington, was perusing a newspaper on Thursday evening, when he saw the paragraph giving particulars of the sad affair. The mark on the arm and the excur- sion ticket corresponded with a Mrs. Messenger whom Smith had seen off to Glasgow on Saturday last to see her mother, who was very ill. Smith im- mediately went to the relatives of Mrs. Messenger, and showed them the paragraph, in consequence of which he and the daughter of Mrs. Messenger came to Wigan. They were taken to the Infirmary, and there identified the body as that of Mrs. Messenger, aged forty, who resided at 58,, Napier-et., War- rington. The deceased was well-known in War- rington, having a stall in the market, and a shop in the town. A Coss. DBA_LER SUMMONED, FOR CRUELTY— At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- day, Thomas Berry, a coal dealer, was summoned for having cruelly ill-treated a horse, the property of Mrs Q wen, 'coat dealer. Mr. Percy Davies ap- peared for the defendant, who pleaded not guilty. John Owen, a young man of about 19 years of age, said that the horse in question belonged to his mother, for whom he worked. Oa Saturday morn- ing he went to Messrs. Ri'Chard Evans and Co.'s coal yard to load his cart and was directed by the foreman to fill it at two waggons from which the defendant Berry was also loading. On his attempt- ing to do so Berry became annoyed and kicked his horse in the stomach, raising a lump as big as his fist. He took the animal home and gave informa- tion to the police. Cross-examined by Mr. Davies, witness got into a most excited state, and com- plained that that gentleman was trying to make him tell lies. For the defence Mr. Davies said he believed that the witness's evidence was complete and deliberate, periury. The defendant was a mqst quiet and inoffensive old man, who bore a most, excellent character. He (Mr. Davies) wonld produce, if necessary, per- sons who would swear that the horse was not kicked by anyone in the yard that' morning. He could also prove that Owen was in the habit of ' kicking the horse. The facts of the case were that the defendant Berry on Saturday Morning was told by the foreman that he might have the two wag- gons of coal mentioned to himself. Soon after- wards, as Berry was engaged in taking his load, Owen came into the yard and attempted to force his cart between Berry's vehicle and the waggon. Berry objected to this, and led the horse and cart away. Owen had no business to have gone to limy at all, and nothing was heard of the alleged cruelty until the summons was issued. He then proceeded to call evidence in support of this state- ment. The magistrates, however, dismissed the case, the Chairman remarking that it was scanda- lous to bring a case like that into court.

LOCAL POLICE RATES.—At Liverpool Quarter Sea- 'ions, on Tuesday last, local police rates were leviet for, among others the following districts :—Prescot, lid in the pound, to produce £2,790 17s 8d; War-. rington, ltd. in the pound, to produce £1,743 Os 4d; and Wigan, lid in the pound, to produce £2,629 18s 4d.
ANNIVERSARY SERMONS AT BURTONWOOD.,-OR

Sunday last the anniversary services in ai-cf-of the schools connected with St. Michael's Church, Burton- wood, were held. The elements were altogether against large congregations, as in pre .% ions years, considerable help being given by sympathisers from Earlestown, but this year the outside attendance was very small. The Rev. G. Bartle, DD., D.C.L., of Southport, occupied the pulpit, and preached three excellent sermons. The collections realised £lO 6s 11d, being about £6 below the average. PICNIC TO DUNHAM PARK.—A picnic to Dunham Park, arranged by the Trustees of Simin's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, took place on Thursday afternoon. Mr. J. H. Lea, who is a member of the religious body, generously provided the velaicles free of cost, and in consequence the trip realised £B, which will be added to the Trust Fund. A 'bus, a brake, and two small waggonettess were required to accommodate the party of 90 persons, and a pleasant drive through beautiful country was ex- perienced. Dunham Park is at present occupied by Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor to the Ship Canal, and after passing Warrington the party had a good view of the Ship Canal operations. The return journey was accomplished by ten o'clock. RETUR.NING FROM THE RACES:—On Friday after- noon a bus belonging to Mr. W., G. Dixon, Bicker- ataffe-st., was returning from Newton Races with a number of passengers, and when passing the tram sidings, at the junction of Higher Parr-st. and Tra- verse-st, one of the hind weels caught in a rut im the road, knocking out all the spokes and causing the vehicle to decline on one side. About half-a- dozen of the outside passengers, and the driver, were thrown off. The driver, Samuel Molyneux,. fell on his head, and received two or three severe wounds. lie was as soon as possible medically at- tended. Robert Harwood, of Peasley Cross, sus- tained a severe shaking, but was able to walk home; and a man named Robert Watkinson had his side slightly injured. A DARK AFTERNOON.—The changeableness of the weather was very plainly demonstrated on Tuesday. There was summer sunshine in the morning, but in the afternoon there was a remarkable change. Soon after three o clock the sky became overcast, and a heavy gloom succeeded the previous hours of bright- ness. This, as the afternoon wore on, increased in intensity, until the darkness beeame, if not quite so black as night, something very nearly approaching it. Before four o'clock there was seen in nearly every street in Warrington the unusual sight, at this period of the year, of houses, offices, and shops with gas-jets lighted. The effect was somewhat novel, and it was certainly rather depressing. For some time a drizzling rain fell, and this was followed by a perfect downpour, after which the atmosphere be- came a little clearer. CYCLING NEWS.—The Warrington Cycling Club had arranged to entertain the Leigh Cycling Club at the Griffin Hotel, Horsemarket-st, on Tuesday, but in consequence of the unfavourable state of the weather, what would no doubt have proved to be a very pleasant gathering had to he abandoned, the Leigh riders being prevented from making the journey. The roads were in good condition on Saturday, and there were .a large number of wheel- men about. Warrington was a centre of attrac- tion, the Sandfield and Wirral Clubs having a run there. The North Liverpudlians turned up at the Ship, at Rainhill. Some fifteen members started for the Bootle Bicycle Club handicap (twenty miles) the route taken being from the Farmers' Arms, Club Moor, by way of Knotty Ash, Prescot, and Rainhill, to Sankey Chapel, and thence back to Prescet. On the termination of the handicap there was a " feed " at the Royal. at Prescot. SUCCESSFUL LOCAL ATHLETES.—At the annual sports in-connection with the Altrincham Flower Show, which were brought off on Saturday, several local competitors came to the front. The 440 yards flat race was won by J. R. Donaville, Sankey, the second place being secured by J. Robinson,Warring- ton. In the one mile flat race the premier place was obtained by A. Edwards, Warrington, and H. Hope, Warrington, was third in the half-mile flat race. In the half-mile race (over ten herdles), S. Morris, Widnes, who was scratch man, won the first prize. He got off badly, and at first it looked long odds against him, but when about fifty yards from the tape he spurted and won in good style by about a yard. At an athletic meeting at Eccles, on Satur- day. H. Allen, Warrington, again proved wriat an excellent rider he is. With only fifteen yards start he won the mile bicycle handicap by about a length, the time registered being 3 minutes 551 seconds. Allen also took the second prize in the two miles bicycle handicap at the same meeting. WARRINGTON HORSE AND CATTLE PAIRS,—The July cattle fair was held in Winwick-st, on Tues- day. It, Nvaa not only well attended, but better. prices were realised than usual. The price of calving cows was from £lB to £2O, barren cows from £l5 to £l6, stirks from £6 to £B, heifers from £l2 to £l6, and mUch cows from £l2 to £2O. The horse fair was held on the following day at the same place.. There was a large number of animals on sale, and although very good horses were rather scarce, tilos) there fetched good prices. The middle and inferior kinds of horseswere well repre- sented in numbers, but were not easily disposed of. Irish horses were plentiful, the numbers being greater this year than last, although the quality was not improved. Dray horses obtained prices up to £7O, good cart-horses up to £65, cab horses from. £l5 to £25, and ponies from £lO to .E 25 The usual pleasure fair was opened in the Fair Ground off Allen-st. on Friday. and is a source of attractiom to large numbers of people. It will last for seven or eight days. THE RIVER WEAVER AND TFLE VYRNWY SCHEME.. —Sir Douglas Galton, the engineer appointed by the Board of Trade to determine the method by which the pipe line conveying the Liverpool water supply from Lake Vyrnwy shall pass under the river Weaver, resumed the inquiry on Saturday, at the Surveyor's Institution, London. Mr. Pember, Q.C., appeared on behalf of the Liverpool Corporation, and Mr. W. H. Higgin, Q.C., for the Weaver Trustees. The latter body urge that a tunnel should be con- structed a considerable depth below the Weaver, in which the pipe line should be laid, while the Cor- poration contend that all practical purposes will be served by digging a trench across the river bed and sinking the pipes therein. Further evidence was called on behalf of the Corporation.—Mr. Iliggin then opened the case for the Weaver Trustees argu- ing that their sole object was a public one, that of maintaining unprejudiced a great and important high- way, which had already been largely developed, and was capable of further extension and improvement. The laying of the pipes across the river bed would be a dangEr to navigation, and bar the trustees from deepening the river, as they proposed soon to do. Witnesses were examined, and the sitting was ad- , 'owned to the 26th instant.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many instances, when they first find their eyesight failing, they purchase all kinds of in- ferior manufactured spectacles, which in the cud cause their eyes to burn and ache. ,To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, and 44, Market-st., Manchester, 143, Lord-st., Southport, and 60, Whitefriargate, Hull, has invented his "Per- fection" Spectacles, which he adapts at either of the above addresses at Is 6d per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to he equalled in the coun- try for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet " llow to preserve the sight " free on application.—Adrt, LORD WINMARLEIGIL—During the week Lord Winmarleigh has been visiting at Appleton Hall, the residence of Mr. T. H. Lyon. AT THE ROSE SHOW of the Manchester Royal Botanical Society, on Saturday, Councillor W. But- ton' of Warrington, took third prize in the class for six distinct single trusses. DARES/WAY SCHOOL,—About 230 children who attend this school were yesterday week entertained totes in the schoolroom. Afterwards they were taken to a field, where various sports' were indulged in, and where the Walton brass band played for dancing. 'THE FISHING AT TETE WALTON RESERVOIR.—The ,honorary treasurer of the Warrington Infirmary has received from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M P., the sum of £7 17s 6d, being the amount of subscriptions received from the Walton Fishing Club for the privi- lege of fishing in the reservoir at Walton. MR. JOHN J. WEBSTER, C.E.—A new footbridge over the river Ouse, at Bedford,. which was opened last week by the Marquisof Tavistock, was designed by Mr. John J. Webster, son of Alderman Webster, of this borough, who, it will be remembered, was also the engineer of the new Cauldwell Bridge, in Bedford. . _

_ ACCIDENT AT LONGFORD WIRE WORKS.—Yester- day morning a man named Samuel Perry, who is employed at Longford Wire Works, had one of his eyes knocked out by a piece of wire that flew into it. He wet taken to the Infirmary, and afterwards went to the Eye Institution at Manchester to have his injury attended to. WALKING DAY AT STOCKTON HEATH. Thurs- day was celebrated as Walking Day at Stockton Heath, and the school children had a procession through the village and neighbourhood. Afterwards they adjourned to a field, where amusements of vari- ous kinds were indulged in. ARTISTIC BRASSWORK Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Earlestown.—Advt. ScuooP TRIP FROM CROFT.—On Saturday the members of the choir and the Sunday school teachers in connection with Christ Church, Croft, had their annual trip, Llandudno being the place selected. The party, which numbered about 45 persons, spent a very pleasant day. The arrangements were under the control of the choir master and of Mr. Battersby, the stationmaster at Kenyon Junction. Tam NEW RECTOR.—The Rev. F. W. Willis, the ; newly-appointed rector, has signified his intention of taking up his residence at Warrington on Tues- day, the 31st inst. Mr. Willis" will be accompanied ' by the Rev. .1. A. Easterling and the Rev. A. R. , Wilson as curates. Mr. Easterling has officiated in ' that capacity with Mr. Willis at Wellingborough , while Mr. Wilson has been connected for a short time with Chester Cathedral, and has been strongly recommended to Mr. Willis by the Rev. Mr. Storr, of ,St. Peter's, Eaton-square, and by the Dean of Ches- ter, and other clergy. The rector will read himself in on August sth and preach in the evening. Sr. PAUL'S CHOIR ExcuusioN.—The senior mem- bers, with their wives, of St. Paul's voluntary choir, Warrington, had, through the kindness of the ' churchwardens (the Mayor of Warrington and Mr. T. Jolley) and a few other friends, their annual ex- ' eursion on' Monday to Blackpool. t The party, ac- companied by the vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, left Bank Quay at 6-0 a.m., arriving at Blackpool at 9-25, ?then they separated to enjoy the various attrac- tions of the place, meeting at mid-day at the Royal Hotel, where an excellent dinner was provided. After a very pleasant day, the party reached War- rington a little after eight o'olock. The boys ot the choir are shortly to have their excursion to North Wales. DEATH or Mn. JAMES GANDY, —The death oc- curred on the 10th inst. of Mr. James Gandy, of Ea- field Hall, at the age of 72 years. The deceased gentleman, who had resided all his life in Warring- ton or the immediate neighbourhood, was much es- teemed by a large circle of friends and neighbours. He was well known in the district for his business industry, and integrity. He had not taken any prominent part in public affairs, but was always deeply interested in religious and 'political ques- tions. In politics he was a Liberal, and he was a Nonconformiet in religion. Mr. Gandy had been a total abstainer for 55 years, and he was in private life an earnest and devout christian. His loss is mourned by a widow, to whom he had been mar- ried 49 years, and by two sons. The funeral took place yesterday week, at the cemetery at Warrington. The service was impressively conduc- ted by Mr. William Hudson, who was assisted by Messrs. T. Holbrook and W. Wright, in the presence of a large number of friends. The funeral arrange- ments were admirably carried out by Mr. Joseph Mounfield, of Warrington. WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE StioUCTY.—A quar- terly meeting of the members of this society was , held in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday. There was a good attendance, the president (Mr. T. Bir- chall) presiding. The usual balance sheet was sub- nutted, and from this it appeared that the sales during the quarter amounted to £13,280. The profits after meeting all liabilities, allowing for fixed stock, &c., allowed of a dividend of 3s 2d in the pound on members' purchases, and this dividend was recom- mended by the committee. The balance sheet was adopted. The number of members who had entered during the quarter was 160, the withdrawals num- bering 92. In the minutes of the committee it was mentioned that a contract had been entered into for the building of the additional premises at Town's- end. One of the recommendations of the committee was that a sum of .£25 or £3O should be taken from the reserve fund in order that a testimonial of the re- gard and appreciation of the members of the society might be presented to Mr. Birchall on his having filled the office of president of the society for twenty-one years. This proposal was well received by those present, and on the motion of a member it was unanimously agreed that,Xso should be taken from the reserve fund for the purposes of the testi- monial. The matter of making all necessary ar- rangements for the presentation was left in the hands of the committee. This was, the principal business. wuo's YOUR HATTER ? —Weil, that's about on a par with the stupid old would-be witticism, 'jibes your mother know you're out?' But if anybody honestly and truly wants to know who's my hatter, my hat answers the query. Who could it be but W. Hall and Son, the Leading Hatters, at 1, Market age, Warrington.—Acivt.

TILE SANITARY QUESTION IN WARRING/TON. Y Y'SA.NITAS." Being one of those "outsiders" whose opiiiions are not much valued by some Town Councillors, ex- cept for a few weeks prior to the Ist of November, you will perhaps permit me to ask, what is the atim and object of those who in the Warrington Town Council and out of it are so persistent in their as- saults on the Sanitary Committee? Is their griev- ance based upon some detail of management which &Tea not meet with their approbation, or are their efforts prompted by a desire to put an end to, or, it may be, to completely reverse, that which has been the sanitary policy of the to .87n for some years past? If they are bent on nothing more than the squaring of certain details of management with their own notions of propriety, I think the people of the town may very safely leave the points of difference to be arranged or compromised in the Connell, though one could not but wonder at the amazing amount of heat and noise that have been generated by so small a matter. If, however, on the other hand, it be the , intention of the mal-contents, as they may perhaps be called without offence, to reduce the Sanitary Committee to impotence in its 'struggle for the sani- tary welfare of the borough, it is, certainly time that the people of the town as a whole, and particularly the working population, which is the most nume- rous, and has everything to lose by bad sanitary conditions, made its voice heard in support of the committee. SANITARY POLICY fI7BTIFIED BY ITS RESULTS. For after all, and in spite of everything that has been said, the present sanitary policy of the town is justified by its results. If we are to act up to the good old rule of jadginga tree by its fruits, there is no further defence of the Sanitary Cominittee and its methods needed than a plain statement of facts. Ac- cording to the speech made by Alderman Burgess at the late special meeting of the Town Council, the death-rate in the year 1870 was 31 per 1,000; in the three years ending 1887—after what may be called the modern sanitary policy had had some few years of trial—the death-rate sunk to 20.8 per I,ooo—in other words there was a drop in the death rate of fully one-third. This, I venture to argue, is a very fair account to render of a few years of vigorous work. It is an account of which those who for the past few years have had most to do with the sanitation of the borough have some reason to be proud. Farthhr than that, it seems to me that those who appear to be quite ready to up- set, or at least to tamper with a system that has made such an account possible, are strangely ready to take upon their own shoulders a grave responsi- bility. It cannot be said in mitigation of the undoubted Success of recent sanitary policy that the pre-exist- ing arrangements in Warrington were in any way favourable to the bringing about of so great an im- provement, for in some respects Warrington is one of the last places which would be chosen for the making of successful sanitary experiments. The narrow courts, close confined alleys, and back-tp- back houses in the older parts of the town will, probably, for generations to come prevent the in- habitants from enjoying the full benefits of even the best devised sanitary scheme. In his report as to the condition of the borough in 1871, Dr. Ballard comments upon the numerous instances in which houses had been built back to 'back. "It is diffi- cult," he says, "to give any accurate idea of the fearful extent to which this vice in the construc- tion of small dwellings prevails in Warrington. It would appear as if, in the older parts of the town, 'the principal object had been to place a dwelling upon every available spot of groiind, leaving no more free than was absolutely necessary for ap- proaches." Nothing could show more clearly than these words of a competent and impartial observer the original—and still existing disadvantages which had to be encountered by those who took in hand the sanitary renovation of the town, and at the same time nothing could better heighten the cre- dit which is due to them and to the system they have worked, for the good results that have been achieved.

WARRINGTON "r. BEtouciarow.—Played at Broughton on Saturday, and after a very interesting game victory rested with the visitors by 24 runs. Crosfield and Rey- nolds began to the bowling of Shutt and Murphy. Rey- nolds scored one and skied one to cover. Tinsley came in, and commenced his vigorous batting at once, making two fours over the spectators. •At 73 Tinsley retired for 46, including seven fours. Clarke was out at the same total. Of the others Fleetwood only reached double figures, and played a good innings of 23. Crosfield's 36 was put together in a masterly manner, and he was seen in a new style—that of hitting to leg. The innings totalled 129. Of the bowlers Murphy was the most suc- cessful, with five wickets for 48. Murphy and Lyon. opened the Broughton innings, and before a run was scored Murphy was splendidly taken by Lister- Kaye from a hard hit to mid-off. Lyon was the next to experience Fleetwood's break. The ball pitched much to leg, broke round behind the batsman, and hit the top of the off wicket. King and Heap now were associated, but the former ought to have been run out at 12. Heap hit finely, while King was content to play on the defensive. Nine overs were sent down for 3 runs, and Heap was run out from a smart bit of fielding by Clarke-3 for 44. At 57 King was taken in the long field. Evans stayed while Royle hit, but at 83 he was secured by short leg running in. Fleetwood went on at the bottom end for Tinsley, and he soon disposed of the remaining five batsmen. The last five wickets were taken by him for 12 runs. King, Heap, and Royle had played good cricket, the former being very patient. Fleetwood's analysis.reads- -30 overs, 12 maidens, 46 runs, 8 wicket. Playing against Frodsham last week, S. M. Crosfield,. the Lancashire county cricketer, scored 111 (not out) out of a total of 221.

Warrington managed to defeat Broughton on Saturday by 120 runs to 105. Tinsley made 46, whilst Crosfield played a patient innings of 33, and valuable aid was ren- dered by Fleetwood. The last named pro. again demon- strated his power with the ball by taking eight wickets for 46 runs.

Allen, of Warrington, continues his successes, and his riding was one of the features of the bicycle races at Eccles on Saturday. div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
EASTHAM AND ELLESMERE

The rain during the last two or three weeks has proved a source of trouble, and made the banks of the cutting slip in several places, owing to the soil becoming thoroughly saturated. The lock pits at Eastham are being pushed on with much energy, there being now seven Ruston & Proctor's navvies, and one of Wilson's crane excavators, working on the site. The embank- ments across the foreshore and the cutting near Pool Hall are also showing great progress. The engineering staff has been augmented on this section by the appoint- ment of Mr. Stone as inspector. A new chapel has been opened at Eastham. Miss Simpson has been appointed head muse at the Ellesmere Port Hospital. The grounds in front of the hospital are being laid out, and every care is being taken that the poor tellows who have the misfortune to become inmates have every attention and comfort.

MOORE, Ste. There is not much-to report in regard to this section this week, although the work goes steadily forward. The German excavator at Acton Grange is making havoc with the soil, over 500 waggons being fated each day. This means a daily excavation of about 2,000 tons of earth. On the side of the railwaY nearest Warrington, where the ground is too hard, for the profitable employ- ment of the German machines, four of Ruston and Proc- tor's steam navvies are making remarkable progress. At this point of the works, in addition to the railway devia- tions there are several roadways to be made. The earth that is dug out of the cuttings is taken to a tip, to go to- wards forming a railway embankment.

RXPLOSIVES STORE AT TFIELWALL. At Lymm Petty Sessions, on Friday, an application was made on behalf of Mr. Walker, Ship Canal contrac- tor, to the Bench for permission to erect a store of dyna- mite and other explosives near the site of the proposed Latchford locks, and about 300 yards distant from Morris Brook farm house. It was explained that the canal works and a " tip " heap would be between the store and Thelwall-lane. It was also stated that the reason why explosives were required was that rock had been come upon on the site of the Latchford locks. The Bench gave permission for the erection of the stores, stating that they should then hold a special session, and inspect the premises.

div.head: , FATAL ACCIDENT.
div.p: , FATAL ACCIDENT.

1 Mr. Churton, coroner for Cheshire, has held an inquest lat Ellesmere on the body of a man who met with his 1 death on the.Eastham section of the Manchester Ship 1 Canal works. The deceased, who was a stonemason, but who was not engaged on the Ship Canal, was viewing the works in the neighbourhood of Ellesmere Port. The excavations here are carried on by blasting, owing to the great amount of rock. The deceased appears to have been viewing the work from the top of the cutting, when he by some means fell into the cutting itself. Ile fell on his head, breaking his neck, and causing instant death. Evidence to the above effect was given, and it was stated that the fall was occasioned by the unfortunate man missing his footing.—The jury at once returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death." The deceased was In the employ of a builder at Ellesmere. Mr. IManisty, the engineer of the Ship Canal works, notwithstanding the fact that the deceased was not employed under him, very kindly offered at his own expense to inter the remains of the unfortunate fellow.

THE NEW BILL. The Bill promoted by the Ship Canal Company to ob- tain powers to effect certain alterations at the Manches- ter end of the canal Q'as on Monday before a select corn- inittse of the House of Lords. Earl Beauchamp presided. The Bill was passed, with a proviso to the effect that the Manchester Racecourse Company should be entitled only to the same rights, if any, over the substituted works as they are now entitled to under section 62 of the Act of 1885.

THE CANAL AND THE INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS. This Congress will be held at Frankfort, on August 19th, and five followinc, days. The subject for the fourth day is "The economical advantages of Inland Navigation." The works of the Manchester Ship Canal will form the leading topic, and will be fully described by Mr. E. Leader Williams, Chief Engineer for the Man- chester Ship Canal Company. Oft the same day M. Go- bert will speak on the same subject.

div.head: EXAMINER, SITITRDAY, JULY 21, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SITITRDAY, JULY 21, 1888.
:NTERESTED,

There can be no doubt that the class of people whose interests are most deeply and vitally involved in this sanitary question is the working class, who form the great bulk of the inhabitants of the bor- ough. Gentlemen who have pleasant residences in Cheshire, and even those who live in the better class houses of the town, may carp and criticise, but they are the persons who would suffer least by any outbreak of disease which might result from the relaxation of sanitary precautions. Dr. Ballard points out that the epidemic of typhus from which the town was suffering at the time of his visit was " almost entirely confined to the poor operatives, factory hands and their families," and that front the epilemic of the same disease in 1866 the "fustian cutters suffered severely." And so it has always been. The well-to-do class of people can generally to 1 a cgisiderable extent protect themselves from , - disease out of their own resources, but the mass of • the people are entirely dependent upon efficient public sanitation for protection. There- are other • Fespects in which the evils that spring from bad . sanitary conditions present a much worse aspect • to the poor than to the comparatively well-to-do ' man. To the latter, an attack of sickness often ' means little more than the inconvenience of a tem- porary confinement in comfortably furnished rooms, [ but to the man whose family depends upon his weekly wage for their weekly bread, an illness : which disables him from work is one of the most , serious calamities. t One cannot help thinking sometimes that even the more intelligent and thoughtful of working people do not always quite realise the full benefit t that has been conferred upon them and their class • by the increasing efficiency of sanitation during % the last few_years. When the death-rate of a town • has been reduced as it has been in Warrington, it ' not only means that there are something like ten fewer deaths in the year per 1,000 of the popula- tion, but it means also that there are a much larger ; number of cases of sickness prevented that would 1 . lesseningotherw isethheaveoccurr death-rateeyd.ou Aast t oneehveesrayme ttime ekno lessenw s L there may be in ordinary diseases ten or twenty, or • even more, cases of sickness to one death, and by the sick rate. That is to say, when ten per 1,000 L are knocked off the year's death-roll, there may be • a hundred per 1,000 of more or less serious cases • knocked off the sick roll. This is a phase of the i question that deserves to be very closely considered ! by every working man, not only as an individual l who has much to gain or lose by the prevalence or L otherwise of disease, but also as a member—if he . be such—of one or other of the flourishing Friendly Societies of the town. To these societies the , decrease in the death and sick rates during the last ; few years must have represented a saving of hun- dreds of pounds, and a relapse into anything like former sanitary conditions would. inevitably,Anean . a corresponding loss. 1.13 IN THE £ OFF, ONE IN THE 1,000 ON. , From the continual harping of some of the critics of . the Sanitary Committee upon the cost of sanitation, . while carefully omitting to make any mention of the . benefits that are derived from it, one might judge that • with them the guage of success is not to be found in the healthful condition of the town, but. in the lowness of the rates. It seems as though they would be quke willing to have one in the 1,000 more on the death-rate if thereby they could have a penny in the pound taken off their sanitary rate. Between this class of people and the great majority of the inhabitants of the town there is no commuity of interest in this matter. With them, according to their own showing, the main object is to keep lucre in their pocket ; with the bulk of their co- residents the thing of prime and essential importance is the preserving of healthy bodies and healthy minds. And let nobody deceive himself or allow others to deceive him as to the means by which this great desideratum is to be attained. There is no royal road to public health. Eternal vigilance is said to be the pride of liberty, and certainly the continual and judicious, but not niggardly, spending of money is the price that is to be paid for sanitary advancement. We ani told by a sanitarian of more than national repute that "no malady, once originated, has ever actually died out." What is it then 1 that saves Warrington and other English towns from those dreadful visitations of plague and pestilence which are so frequently mentioned in the records of medieval towns, and which still afflict countries of backward civilisation? Clearly it is nothing but the removing or neutralising by sanitary methods of those conditions which breed and facilitate the spread of disease; and let me add there has never yet been discovered a way of ap- plying these sanitary methods without the spending of money, and often of very large sums of money. • Sanita- tion, in fact, is a continual warfare against an insidious and malignant enemy, and money is the sinews of this warfare. To object, therefore, to the necessary spend- ing of money is to object to sanitation itself, for the one is the sine qua non of the others RENT-PAYERS AND THE RATES. Those whose one object is to lessen the rates often tell usthat it is greatly to the interest of the working people of the town, and indeed to all rent-payers,to have low rates. They very correctly point out that rates are not paid directly out of the lancllord's pocket, but out of the rents he receives from his tenant, and then they either tell us, or suggest the inference, that if the rates were less rents wonld be reduced in proportion. This is a very plausible argument, and it may serve to gull some people, but it is entirely fallacious. Rents are not

fixed in Warrington, nor in any other town, according to the rates Chat prevail. There are towns in which, comparatively spealdng, rates are high and rents low. and other towns in which rates are low and rents high. A landlord in letting a house gets as high a rent as he can, independent altogether of the rates that are levied. If the rates are low so much the better for the landlord; if they are high so much the worse. It, however, makes no difference to the tenant. If a landlord can get £l6 a year for a cottage he will not let it for £l4, though the rates be never so low ; if, on the other hand, he can get nd more than £l4 for it, he will let it at that though the rates be never so high. What would -be the result, then, if, by starving the sanitary department of Corporation worfr, we were to reduce the rat is in Warrington by 6d in the pound? Simply this; at the end of each suc- ceeding year the owners of property in Warrington, and of cottage properth hi particular,. would have more money in their pockets, and the tenants of these houses would have had more sickness and more deaths in their 'families. One set of peple, few in number, and on the whole pretty well provided for, would be still better off, while another set of people,vastly more numerous, and in many instances already hard pressed for an existence, would be still more impoverished and depressed. And what is more, the gains of the one-set would not be equivalent to the losses of the other, for ope of the good qualities of sanitation is that, even front a pecuniary point of view, it benefits the community as a whole, a good deal more than it injures any particular class. It is quite evident, therefore, that this outcry against the cost cf sanitation in Warrington is not in the inter- ests of the rent-payers of the town, but solely and sim- ply in the interest of rent-receivers. For my own part I am disposed to think that landlords in Warrington are already very well recompensed for their outlay, and that it very ill becomes them to still endeavour to further aggrandise themselves very largely at the expense of poorer people.

div.head: TES PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: TES PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.

_ The amended report of Mr. W. Owen, architect, to the House Committee upon the subject of the accommo- dation of the Workhouse, was read by the CLERK, and was as follows At your last meeting, after consider- ing the report I made to the Board of Guardians on the subject of Workhouse extensions, you decided that the utilization of the Board-room buildings for Workhouse purposes, and the extension of the Tramp Wards and Pauper Reception Wards, should not at present be under- taken. You then considered what additional ac- commodation it was really nececssary to pro- vide at once in the Hospital and House, and decided that it must be for 165 inmates, divided as follows :—ln the Hospital, male 25, female 32; in the House, male 32, female, 76; total 165. Having decided this, you instructed me to prepare an amended report dealing with these figures for the accommodation to be provided, and also instructed me to prepare an ap- proximate estimate of the cost. The required additional accommodation can be obtained .by taking the present Fever Hospital for females, and the present workshops with a storey added, for male hospital patients; and by adding for the 32 extra males in the House two stories to the one-storey east-wing, and for the 76 females two ' stories to the one-Story west-wing, with an extension, also three stories in height, some 50 feet further towards the west. Increased staircase and lavatory accommoda- tion as will be necessary would be provided. A new Fever Hospital and new workshopswill be required. It was I suggested that the building nears the piggeries might be used for workshops, but I find it is fully occupied. On the ground floor tile ambulance wagon, fever cart, and , hearse are kept, and on the first floor bed Steads and ' straw for bedding. The best position for the Fever Hos- pital is decidedly on the land belonging to you on the west of the present Fever Hospital. The position for the \ new workshops I have carefully considered, together with Mr. Ward, the Master, akd we have come to the conclusion that, all things considered, the most con- venient would be the space in the Hospital and work- shops yard, now occupied by the timber store, a shed used for preparing the timber for chopping, and an un- used ashpit. A Tailor's Room, Joiners' Shop, and Wood- chopping room of ample size can be built with entrances direct from the men's yard, and with no connection with the hospital yard. , I estimate the cost of the additions you propose as under :—Hospital for males, £4BO ;' fe- males—for the corridor connecting the Fever Hospital, if found to be necessary £lOO ; House for males, £690; for females, £1,120; total, £2,390. A new Fever Hospital , will probably cost £B5O, and the new workshops £2OO. Your pre,sent certificate is for 383 (afterdeducting the Fever Wards) ; the addition you propose of 165 will give you certificate for a total of 548. The whole of the works could be carried out without interfering with the comfort of the inmates, only needing temporary giving up of the orie-storey day rooms in theeast and west wings."l This report was recommended by the House Committee for adoption.—Mr. Buzairuasrasked how many inmates there were at Present in the Workhouse.—The Wonx- noon MASTER replied that there were 304 in that morn- , ing ; the House was certificated for 407, including feVer wards. In reply to Mr. Isherwood he said that at pre- sent they had just sufficient accommodation for the in- mates on the female side of the house.—Mr. GREENING: Had you sufficient accommodation last winter ?—The WoMmousE MasTEA said they had not; the inmates I were crowded together two or three in a bed.—Mr. VOISEY pointed out that the question of increasing the I accommodation at the Workhouse had been brought before the Board by Mr. Henley, the Local Government Board inspector, and remarked that, as Warrington was a growing town, they would have to provide for an increase of pauperism.—The CLERK said that the grants in aid of the maintenance of indoor paupers under the new Local Government Bill *mild depend upon the Satisfactory reports made to the Government as to the condition of the Workhouse.—Mr. VOISEY also referred to the necessity of providing hospital accommodation at the Workhouse.—Mr. HARRISON thought that instead of building an infectious htspital at the Workhouse it would be far better to send patients to the Corporation infectious hospital. They contributed £139 to the muni- cipal rates of Warrington for twelve months, and they had as much right to send patients to the hospital as anybody. ,That was in accordance with the views of the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, who said that, paupers or no paupers, infectious cases should not be allowed tq be at large to the detriment of the inhabitants of the town.—Mr. JOLLEY said there had been obstacles thrown in the way of the taking of pauper patients to the infectious hospital.—The CHAIRMAN said he had re- collections of officers reporting in that room that the Guardians must find accommodation forpauper patients. —The CLERK said that some weeks ago a difficulty arose in consequence of a poor woman, whose sickness proved to be infectious, coming into the charge of Mr. Har- bourne. Dr. Spipks wanted to send the case into the Corporation hospital, but Dr. Gornall, on the other hand, would not receive it, and the Town Clerk got to writing letters on the subject. He (the Clerk) wrote to the Town Clerk that they would be quite will- ing to take that as a sample case in order to have the question settled in a court of law, but the view taken by the Town Clerk was that they could not go into a court of law. A complaint of the conduct of the Board of Guardians was then written to the Local Government Board. He (the clerk) desiring that there should be no conflict between the two bodies, called at the Town Clerk's office and saw the deptity town clerk, who was at first very stiff, and said that the Guardians were guilty of a good deal of selfishness and wrong doing, but before ha (the clerk) left the deputy town clerk took an entirely different view of it, and said the matter had been put to him in a different light, and he would report it to the Sanitary Committee. The effect of that was that, though they did not take that particular case, it was because the patient was too advanced in her sickness, but they had ' taken all similar cases since. He (the clerk) had reason to believe that the Local Government Board had practic- ally told them what he had told them; atall events they had decided upon the matter since. The clerk went on to speak in favfitir of having a hospital at the work- house, pointing out that inmates of a workhouse could not always be regarded as inhabitants of the place in which the workhouse was situated. He remarked that when travelling in Devonshire lately he had been very much struck with the considerable nurdber of hospitals provided by private eontributions ; he noticed ..his par- ticularly in Exeter. The result was that the Union there would have to make very little accommodation of that kind. Mr. BrAciutunsr : We want some philan- thropists here.--,-Mr. GREENING moved that the report of Mr. Owen be adopted, and that Mr. Owep be instructed to prepare plans in accordance therewith for submission to the Local Government Board.—Mr. VOISEY seconded the proposal.—After some further discussion, Mr. DARBY- SHIRE proposed as an amendment that those parts of Mr. Owen's scheme which provided an extra accommodation for 76 inmates on the female side, and for 25 and 32
