div.head: BELLE VITE, LIVERPOOL.
div.p: BELLE VITE, LIVERPOOL.

The prospectus of the Belle Vue Liverpo'-ol Com- pany, Limited, appears in another column of this issue. This company is formed to establish in Liverpool popular recreative grounds of the same character as the famous Belle Vue Gardens at Man- chester. Now, the Manchester Bella Vue Gardens are perhaps the most profitable property of the sort in the kingdom. Fortune after fortune has been acquired at therr turn-stiles, and it therefore seems extraordinary that no such place should exist in the great sister city of Liverpool. All the most attrac- tive out-door recreations, such as racing grounds for cyclists, &c., switch-back railways, toboganniiag, fireworks, electric illuminations, and pleasant gar- -dens will be combined with a really splendid zoological and ornithological collection. Specially advantageous arrangements have been made with Mr. Cross, the great Liverpool rival of Jamrach, to maintain the collection of wild beasts at the t highest standard of excellence, and keep it ever varying. Thus the company will stock without ex- pense Monkey Houses, Aviaries, Lion Houses, Bear Pits, Elephants, &c., &c., under the charge of one of the leading experts in the kingdom. The magni- ficent central portion of the great Manchester Jubilee Exhibition building, capable of accommoda- ting 10,000 persons, has been acquired. A licensed house, the Plough Inn, stands in the grounds, so one great difficulty is overcome, and a most valuable branch of businass secured. The gardens will be in direct communication with the Cheshire Lines (that is to say, will have through communication over all the system of the Midland, the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, and the Great Northern Railways), and also with the Londdn and North- Western and the Lancashire and Yorkshire. The tramway cars run by the gates, and the gardens are not only readily accessible from all parts of Liver-, pool, Bootle, and Birkenhead, but situated in a neighbourhood where the population is increasing at an extraordinary pace, and property is rising in value every year. The terms of the purchase and site chosen are, therefore, singularly promising. The chances of large profits amount to an absolute cer- tainty if the business is well conducted. There is no opposition, nor any chance of opposition arising. The board of directors is composed of men of the highest respectability and keen business experience. The capital is £lOO,OOO in £1 shares, and the offices of the company are situated at 34, South John-st., Liverpool.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY CELEBRATION AT
div.p: SALVATION ARMY CELEBRATION AT
WIDNES.

The sixth anniviarsary of the establishment or the Salvation Army in Widnes was celebrated by a series of services last week end. In a leaflet dis- tributed amongst the audience, Captain W. T. Monies, who is in charge of the corps, states that during the six years 'many have been rescued from lives of drunkenness and sin. Many of them have gone to become. members in other places of worship in Widnes; many are still in the local corps, who are not only saved from drink and sin, but are trying to rescue others." Tire celebration commenced on Saturday night, when a meeting was held in the Barracks. Majpr Kutch conducted Ilthe service, a special feature being the singing of ' the "Bristol Nightingale, with her guitar." On Sunday three well attended services were held lin the Drill Hall. In the morning a" Holiness meeting," in the afternoon "News the war," and in the evening a " Salvation meeting." Mrs. Bramwell Booth, of the Rescue Home, London, was the central figure on each occasion,andshe delivered several stirring addresses. On Monday Mrs. Booth conducted a Holiness Convention in the Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel, which had been lent for the occasion, and she was assisted by Captain and Mrs. Glover and Captain Monies. Subsequently about a hundred persons sat down to tea in,the Drill Hall, and in the 'evening a large audience gathered to listen to an address by Mrs. Booth on rescue work. Mr. J. Brock, J.P., occupied the chair, and in introducing Mrs. Booth he said he was there that night to show his sympathy with the work which was being done in Widnes by the Salvation i Army. (Applause.) He knew that n many quar- ters the methods of the Salvation Army were not I popular, and their methods might not be exactly his methods, but if they were doing good and bringing people to Christ that was enough for him. (Ap- plause.) As to the rescue work, he supposed that none of those who traversed the streets of our large towns in the evening but must be painfully con- scious how much necessity there was for this kind of work—work that was extremely difficult, requir- ing the greatest tact and a heart full of love. (Ap- plause.) Mrs. Booth then delivered an address, in which she described the work of the rescue home of which she is the principal in London. The total number received into the Home was 1,040, and of these 513 had been sent to situations, 131 sent home, 29 sent to a trade, eight married, five emigrated, 145 were un- satisfactory, Sze. There were now 100 girls in the homes. Speaking of the difficulty of obtaining situations for the girls, Mrs Booth said it was a ter- rible grief how few people banished drink from their homes. There were some ot the girls that she could not trust with a mistress, however good she might be if she ha q any of that stuff in her house at all. She could not let a girl go to a house where after praying "Lead Us not into temptation" she would have to go into the cellar and draw the stuff that had been her temptation. (Applause.) In conclusion an appeal was made for funds. Captain Moules appealed to the public to help hinito obtain a suitable and commodious barracks. - The various services were characterised by the usual hearty singing and enthusiasm.
A slight. shock of earthquake was felt early on Thursday morning in Dumfriesshire, shaking hpuse,s and furniture.
WNEOIK AND Loss or LIFE.—A Lloyd's telegram from Adelaide states that the British ship Star of Greece has gone ashore at Aldinga. Her back was broken. Part of the crew were saved.

' INSTITUTION OF THE VICAR OF WIDNES. In the presence of a large congregation at St. Paul's Church, on Saturday afternoon, the Rev. Geo. Henry St. Patrick, 8.D., was formally installed as Vicar of Widnes. The ceremony was performed by Dr. Ryle, the Lord Bishop of Liverpool, and the clergy present at the function.were the Revs. Dr. Oliver, Garston ; T. H. Ethel, of Castle Eden, Dur- ham; Rev. J. A. Le Bert, Incumbent of St. Ambrose; Rev. C. W. Wool', Vicar cf Ditton ; Rev. W. Edmond- son, Curate-in-Charge of Famworth ; and Rev. Mr. Ardell, Curate of the Parish Church. The service was full choral; and afterwards the Bishop preached a sermon from the text, "When we preach, warning every man and teaching every man m all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus," Colossians, i., 28 verse. The Bishop said they were gathered together that afternoon on a very interebting occasion. He had come there to give a public institution to the new minister of a very large and important parish in he diocese, and he thanked God 'for putting the desire into their hearts to come there that theyZmight help by their presence, and witness with their eyes all that was done. The strength of a church was'not in its en- dowments or Cathedrals, but was in the men who were its ministers and officers, and those who, de- sired to help forward the Church of England should always pray and use every effort to assist the clergy in their work. He would plead with them on be- half of the minister who now came amongst them for the first time, and would ask them to assist him constantly as much as lay in their power, and to strengthen his hands in every way they could. They mig4 depend upon it that when the laity and clergy woAked together great good would be accom- plished. His Lordship then performed the cere- mony of institution, and a collection having been made in aid of the church fund, the service con- eluded.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. J. Kenwright. There were also present Messrs. W. Middlehurst, J. Ranson, J. Ellison, C. B. Johnson, Fisher, Lowe. Swift, Joseph Burchall, James Burchall, T. Finegan, T. J. Hill, R. Tuson, and Stevens (Local Government Board Inspector). WORXHOOSIC STATISTICS.—The Workhouse Master re- ported that there were at present in the House 486 in- mates, as compared with 490 last week, and 428 in the corresponding period of last year. 64 vagrants had been relieved, as against 73 relieved during the corres- ponding period of last year. PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.—It was reported that the Building Committee had considered the remarks made bv Mr. Henley, Inspector of the Local Government Board, with respect to the increased accom- modation-at the workhouse. The committee had resolved that Mr. Gandy, architect, of St. Helens, be requested to mike a report to the committee, based on the remarks of Mr. Henley, with a view to giving effect to his sug- gestions. It was also resolved that the report of Mr. Gandy be considered at a future meeting of the Board. —This action of the Building Committee was approved on the proposition of Mr. 'Hill,seconded by Mr. Ran- son.

A VACANCY ON T'HE BOARD.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board to the effect that an order would shortly be issued authorising the special election of a Guardian for the township of Huyton-with-Roby, in the Presoot Union, in the room of Mr. W. J. Ashton, deceased. AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER'S EXPLANATION. The fol- lowing letter was read :L-" I beg to own the receipt of your letter, dated 6th inst, and to say that lam sorry, that my last month's statements were not sent to you sooner. I will take care that they are posted to date in future, and with regard to the Guardians' request that I should give a bond for £l,OOO I respectfully ask to be allowed an interview with the Finance Committee of the Guardians, in order that I may make to their a state- ment bearing on the' matter. Since the reception of your letter I have been in communication with a guait antee society, the result of which I think warrants me in seeking an interview with the guardians." The let- tet was signed by John Kitchen, assistant overseer for the Sutton district of the Union.—Mr. Hill said that he thought that before Mr. Kitchen sought an interview with the Finance Committee, it was necessary that he should put himself in a similar position to the other as- sistant overseers in the Union.—This being the opinion of the Board, it was resolved that Mr. Kitchen's request be not a,cceded to. THE BURDEN OF mirz Middlehurst had given notice that he would propose the following resolu- tion—" That in view of relieving the present heavily bur- dened ratepayers, the president of the Local Govern- ment Board be requested to insert a clause in the Local Government Bill, giving power to assess ground rents and royalties for local purposes."—Mr. Middlehurst said that he had proposed to bring forward the subject men- tioned in the notice of motion, fie saw by that day's papers, however, that a promise had been made by the Government to the effect that that question would be taken up. He thought, therefore, that it was not neces- sary to propose his motion. INCREASE OF SALARY.—Mr. Lowe proposed :—" That the salary of Mr. A. Pennington. relieving officer for the Sutton district, be increased from £lOO to £120." Mr. Lowe said that MPennington had been relieving officer for two years, and had done his work well. He considered that he was fully entitled to the proposed increase.— There being no objection made, the motion was carried unanimously.
ALARMING ACCIDENT ON TIIE ()SHIRE LINES RAILWAY.

Early on Sunday morning a serious accident oc- curred at Padgate station, near Warrington. on the Cheshire Lines Committees railway. • Although, very fortunately, it was not attended with loss of life or personal injuries, it resulted in considerable damage to rolling stock The accident occurred soon after seven o'clock in the morning. It appears that a train of empty goods waggons was in the sta- tion, moving very slowly, when another goods trails moviug at a good speed, came upon the same line of rails. The result was that it overtook and ran into the other train with great force. No fewer than eight waggons were overturned, and for the most part smashed into atoms, while on one side a length of the platform was torn tip. A portion of the other side also suffered damage, but in a much slighter degree. The men n Charge of the trains were for- tunate to escape without injury. The news of the accident was received at the Central station, War- rington, soon afterwards, and it was also communi.; cated to other stations on the Cheshire Lines sys- tem. A number of the officials from Warrington, and other places proceeded to the scene of the accident with all possible speed, and their oenergies were at once concentrated on the task of getting the line clear for traffic. Breakdown gangs were brought from Man- chester and other places, and by dint of hard work it was found possible to clear the line of wreckage sufficiently to allow of traffic being worked on a single' line in the course ot about an hour's time. It took all day, however, to get the line properly clear, and to repair the damage that required im- mediate attention. A visit paid to the scene of th., accident showed how complete had been the wreck of the waggons, some of which had been smashed to atoms. The way in which the platform was torn up was also evidence of how severe had been the force with which the one train ran into the other. It was stated that the accident was due to the driver of the quickly, moving train not being able to arrest its progress soon enough, because of the rails being made greasy by the rain. During the day many people visited the place, and at times there was quite a crowd Of peiple viewing the ruin from the eminence of Padgate Bridge. Had either the trains contained passengers the result must have been disastrous in the extreme. but as it was, although considerable damage was done, traffic was very little interfered with, and the trains, with the exception of one, ran as punctually as usual. The signalling gear became somewhat disarranged dur- ing the progress of removing the debris, but this was soon remedied. Mr. Meldrum, the general manager, inspected the scene on Monday. It may be added that Mr. Rees, a student at the Manchester College, who had arranged to preach at Wycliffe Congrega- gational Church on Sunday, was delayed by the accident, and was in consequence unable to preach at the morning service. His plate in the pulpit was taken by Mr.- Theodore London, who should have gone to Manchester tol preach at a place of worship in that city, but wthi also prevented by the acci- dent. Mr. Rees preached at Wycliffe Church in the evening.

The Northampton Liberal and Radical Union on Wed- nesday night unanimously passed a vote of confidence in Mr. Bradlaugh. The celebration of the Armada tercentenary was com- menced at Plymouth on Wednesday night with the open- ing of an exhibitiOn of Elizabethan relics.
Ihe Prince and*Princess of Wales opened the newbuild- ings of the Great Northern Hospital. in North London, on Tuesday. The streets were crowded with spectators, and decorations were plentiful. . _

PnEsracrerioN.—Since the departure of the Rev. 0. A. Jones from Rainford, to enter upon the curacy of Whippingham, a few of his friends in Rainford have subscribed towards a testimOnial as a token of respect and in consideration of the manner in which he fulfilled his arduous duties as curate-in-charge of Rainford for seven months. The testimonial takes the form of a marble timepiece, supplied by Messrs. Reyes and Co., St. Helens.

belt, which she produced. As the defendant did not ap- pear to be perfectly sober, he was remanded until Satur- .

day.' EQUALLY AT FAULT. Mary Coyne was charged with beating Julia Ann Shields in Dial-st., on the Monday pre- vious. It appeared that there had been a quarrel and "scrimmage " between the parties, and the Chairman re- marking that he considered one as bad as the other, dis- missed the case. THREATS.—Mary Ann Morris was summoned by Mar- tha Jones for using threats to her. She. was ordered to be bound over for 6 months, or, in default of finding a surety, to go to gaol for 14 days.

WARRINGTON COUNTY TTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall and H. Bleckley, junr. "ELLEN TEarev" IN TIZOITI3L33.—A woman named Ellen Terry was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly on the 14th inst. at Warrington. Defendant said some friends came to see her and they became con- vivial. She was fined 5s and 8s cOsts. DmvEas FINED.—John Atherton, for having been asleep in his cart at Rixton, on the 29th, was fined 2s ed and costs; Thomas Dunbobbin, for driving a two-horse waggon without reins at Orford, on the 14th inst., was fined is and costs as a warning. MM./K.—Thomas Leech, for having been drunk at Sankey, ond the 2nd July. was fined 5s and costs. THE WAY HOME .—Thomas Craik, labourer, and James Handley, bricklayer, were charged with having been drunk in Church-st., Golborne, on the I.Bth inst. Both pleaded guilty, but objected to having been locked up. Craik said "I wanted the constable to show me the way home and he said he would, and then he locked me up.?. Prisoners were each fined 5s altd costs.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs, W. Long, H. Stanton, and C. Lister. REFUSING TO QUIT. Joseph Hurst and Joseph Win- stanley were charged with having been drunk and re- fusing to quit the licensed premises of John Scattergood, at Lymm, on the 30th June. Hurst did not appear. Winstanley was also charged with assaulting P.C. En= nion at the same time and place. For having been drunk and refusing to quit Winstanley was fined is and costs' the charge of assault was dismissed—Joseph Hurst, for having been drunk and refusing to quit the Plough Hotel, Lymm, was fined lOs and costs. DRUNRENNESS,--JOhn Concannon was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Broom Edge on the 17th June, and was fined 2s 6cl an costs. A LOCOMOTIVE CASE.—Joseph Frewen, of Manchester, was charged with having driven a locomotive on the 16th July, at Lymm at a greater speed than four miles an hour, and was fined 20s and costs. CYCLIST FINED.—John Hamilton Taylor. a young man, was fined ss, including costs, for having ridden a bicycle ' without a lamp at Lymm at 10 o'clock at night on the 11th June. DOG CASES.—John Brearley was charged with having allowed a dog to be at large at Lymm on two occasions, on the 13th and 20th June respectively, in contravention of an order now in force. P.C. Dutton gave evidence, and stated that on the 20th defendant allowed his dog to attempt to worry rats in the streets. Inc the first case a fine of ss, including costs, was imposed; in regard to that of tho 20th a fine of 20s and costs was imposed.— Dr. Fox, of Lymm, was charged with a similar offence on the 14th June. He admitted that the dog-t—a mastiff —was not led or muzzled, but he added that "his dog was like the centurions servant; he said do this and it doeth it, he said go and it goeth." (Laughter.) A fine of ss, including costs, was imposed.—John Forster, for a similar offence at Rush Green, 5s including costs; Major Brown, similar charge, Bth July, discharged, the dog .having been destroyed. For similar offences Thomas Hood, Eccles, was fined 5s including costs ; Alfred Jones, Lymm, 5s and costs; John Halton, butcher, Lymm, 5s including costs; Alfred Clark, a navvy, es including costs; Aaron Salmons, a navvy, Sc including COSta. FOACHING.—Aaron Salmon, Frederick Salmon, Philip Bedford, and William Shackleton, ship canal navvies, were charged with trespassing, on the 16th July, on land in the occupation of Edwin Massey, in pursuit of game and conies. .They were also charged with a simi- lar offence on the same day on land in the occupation of Daniel Massey. Bedford was the only defendant who appeared, the others, it was stated, having absconded. From the evidence it appeared that three hares had been caught by a dog on the occasion referred to.—Bedford' was fined 108, and costs 245; warrants were issued against the other defendants. ASSAIILTS.—Jane Ardern was charged With having as- saulted Mary Ellen Ledward, at Oughtrington, on the lath/June, and was fined 2s 6d and costs. Defendantt Well, that is not much.—John McTighe and Thomas McTighe were charged, the former with assaulting Peter Brooks and the latter with assaulting Henry Percival, on the sth July at Lymm. John McTighe did not appear. Defendants and complainants were each bound over to keep the peace for six months.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. TurEsnaY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst. Thomas Jannion was brought up under a warrant, charged with having, on the 19th March, been drunk and disorderly, and refused to quit the Three Crowns Inn, King-st. Ile was fined 20s, and costs 16s 4d, or a month. The money was paid.—Joseph Blackman, an engine driver on the Ship Canal, was fined 5s and cos's for being drunk in Portland-st., on the previous day.
r . WkDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. T. S. Tirnmis and Mr. J. Brock.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence the follow- ing were each fined 5s and cOsts :—James Tallon, Eliza- beth-st. ; Ellen Crowley, 30, Barn-st. ; and James Mc- Dermott, of Wwington.—John O'Neil, who made his 24th appearante, was fined 10s and costs.-eatrick McCreese, of Appleton„ and Thomas Rawlinson, of Sutton's-lane, were each bound over to be of good be- haviour for three months on separate charges of commit- ting breaches of the peace. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brock. DRUNKENNESS. James Duffy, of Liverpool, was fined 5s and 'costs for being drunk on the previous , night. BLEEPING Dim—Richard Ryder, Lawrence Pender, and John Dolan were each sentenced to seven days' hard labour for sleeping in chemical works.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. G. Lloyd Drams AND DI.SORDERLY.—Catherine Egan, William Jolley, Sarah Ann Meakin (27th appearance), and Thomas King, were each fined 10s and costs for this offence. A fine of 5s 'and costs was imposed upon each of the following :—Ellen Dolan, Henry Chesters, Francis O'Brien. Margaret Martin made her fifth appearance and was fined £1 and costs or a month. The defendant, who was very boist,erious in court, said she "would do the month."—For being drunk whilst in charge of a horse in Mersey-st., on the 14th inst., was fined lOs and costs. Martha Hampson pleaded guilty to using pro- fane language in Jackson's-laiae, on the 3rd just, and she was fined lOs and costs.

WIDNRS PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock. A BEGGAR.—Edward Connolley, an old man was charged with begging in Ball-lane, Ditton, on the pre- , vious day, and he was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. DEUNICENNESS.—The following persons were charged with this offence, and were each fined in varying amounts :—Eliza Glasheen, Caroline-St.; John Queeney, 9, Elizabeth-St. ; William Winders, 6, Chesterest.; William Connor, Midwood-St. •, Michael Mullen, 20, Bridge-st. ; and John Cassidy, and Louisa McKenna, Ann Martin, and Mary Black, all of 2, Elizabeth-St.; and Catherine Kennedy, of Lunt's Heath. Catherine Webb, of Char- ,lotte•st., was charged with being drunk. She was de- fendpd by Mr. Knowles, and the case was dismissed. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Andrew Doyle, Caroline-st., John Harrington, Travis-st., Thomas Tomlinson, Terrace road, and William Beresford, 11, Irwell-st., were each charged with committing a breach of the peace. The case against Harrington was dismissed, and the other defendants were bound over to be of good behaviour in the usual sureties. OFFENDING CARTERS.—WiIIiam Forster, of Edward-st., was fined lOs and costs for having been drunk whilst in charge of a luny and two horses.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed upon Robert Johnson, of 12, Westfield-st., for being asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart. Doos AT LARGE —William Walker, 37, Davies-street, Henry Humphreys, Anne-st. West, and James Howard, Wellington-5t., were summoned for allowing their dogs to be at large unrauzzled, and were each fined is. and costs. MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN.—John Quinn was sum- moned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his son, who is an inmate of the industxial school.--The -defendant offered to pay -6d. per week.--Superintendent Johnston said he could not ask for more, as the man's income at present was only 13s 9id per week, and he had a wife and three children to keep.—Order made accordingly.—Francis Garbutt, salt .', cake worker at the works of Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co., was ordered to pay 2s per week towards the support of his son in an industrial school.

LOCAL NEWS. (Continued from page 5.)

A BADGER, said to weigh from 17 to 181bs., has been killed on • the farm of Mr. Henry hunt, of Glazebrook. It had killed a hen, and eaten part of it. As the badger is. in England becoming very scarce, Mr. Hunt intends to have his specimen stuffed to keep as a curiosity. APPROACHING FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE.—It is

stated that a marriage that has been arranged be- tween Mr. Charles Mulville, late captair 3rd Dra- goon Guards, and Edith Galfrida, eldest daughter of the Hon. Leopold and Lady Mary Powys,of Bewsey Hall, Warrington, will shortly take place. THE LANCASHIRE DRAMA " GRELLEY'S MONEY," which is so well known to Warrington playgoers, has this week been reproduced at the St. James's Theatre, Manchester, and has attracted large audien- ces. "Soft Tommy Shutdeworth," the amusing character of the piece, was admirably delineated by Mr. Brinsley Sheridan, of the Theatre Royal, War- rington, who, it may be mentioned, has performed it nearly 2,000 times. It is no wonder that by this time he 19 most thoroughly at home in the part. A DIVORCE DECREE RESCINDED.—In the Divorce Division of the High Court of Justice on Friday, be- fore Sir James Hannen, the ease of Cartledge v. Cartledge and Slicer Was heard. The petitioner, who resided at Openshaw, had obtained a decree nisi for divorce from his wife. The Queen's Proctor now intervened to prevent the decree being made absolute. Evidence was given showing that the petitioner had committed adultery with Mrs. Dea- kin, wife of a joiner formerly of Openshaw, now of Widnes. His Lordship rescinded the decree nisi, and dismissed the petition. A CHILD KILLED ON THE HIGHWAY AT MARTlNS- caorr.—On Tuesday Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry at Martinscroft, touching the death of a child named David Platt, aged two years and seven months, who was run over by a horse and trap at that place last Saturday. It appeared from the evidence that the child was playing in the high road, and as a horse and trap belonging to Mr. Wm. Marsh, farmer, was passing, it ran into the middle of the road and was knocked down and killed. The jury returned a ver- dict of "Accidentally killed." THE BURNING FATALITY.—Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-st., on view of the body of George Henry Ayland (4), the son of George Hopkins, a brakesman, of Ernest-st. The deceased died at the Infirmary on Friday in last week, as the result of serious injuries received on the Wednesday previous. From the evidence given to the jury it appeared that the deceased slept with a sister who is nine years of age. Early on the Wednesday morning in question, before their mother was up, the two chil- dren went downstairs together, and the elder one made the fire. She put a box of matches on the table, and the little bay, picking it up, struck a match and set fire to his night dress. The mother, alarmed by his screams, came quickly downstairs, and, with the assistance of a neighbour, extin- guished the flames. The injuied child was at once taken to the Infirmary, where it ultimately suc- cumbed to its injuries. The jury returned a ver- dict to the effect that the deceased met his death by accident. Tam BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OFOYARRINGTON. For the week ending Saturday, July 14th, 1888. The mean temperature was 531 Fahren- heit, and therefore 1.8 deg. colder than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature, 64 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 9th inst, and the minimum temperature, 42 Fahrenheit, on the 13th inst. The rainfall measured .84in. The general direction of the wind was N.E. During the week, which was the 28th of the current year, 43 births and 7 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 7.5 per thousand, against 18-8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 181 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from rheumatism, 1 from ery- sipelas, 1 from phthisis, 1 from brain disease, and 1 from drowning. Twenty-three cases of scarlet fever, 2 of typhoid fever, and. 1 of smallpox were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JoHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health. THE NEW Sr. HELENS RAILWAY.—A few weeks ago the directors of the new St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Company considered the desira- bility of at once commencing work in S. Helens, and Mr. S. W. Pilling, the contractor, was instruc- ted to report upon the matter. Since then numerous] inquiries have been made as to how the works at Lowton are getting on, and what are the chances of an early start being made in St. Helens. Mr. W. B. Tracy, the business manager of the company, says anyone who likes to go as far as Golborne can see one of the best illustrations of pluck and enter- prise that a small public company has ever been able to present. Under the direction of Mr. Pilling, the contractor, the works for more than two miles are in rapid progress—cuttings, embankments, bridge foundations, drainage arrangements, &c., being visible. The present determination of the com- pany is to push on to Haydock to commence the coal traffic, the land arrangements up to this point being in pi2cess of settlement. As regards the start in St. Helens that (Mr.Tracysays) could be made without difficulty, as the circumstances generally are favour- able. To do so, however, would absorb £3,000 or ..£4,060 in as many months, which was not much, but the higher question was whether it would be wise to withdraw capital from the Haydock end, which represented a definite piece of work that would at once become contributory, to start another section, and then have to pause for connections. MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AND THE LAND SUBSIDENCE AT NORTHWICH.—In the House of Commons, on Tuesday night, the vexed question of land subsi- dence at Northwich formed the subject of question and answer. Mr. Brunner: I beg to ask the Presi- dent of the Board of Trade whether his attention has been called to the report of the sudden subsi- dence of the ground under the out-buildings of the Wheatsheaf Inn, at Northwich, on the 6th instant; whether he is aware that this inn had to be rebuilt a few years ago on account of a similar subsidence, that a considerable length of road has had to be raised, and that several shops near by have had to be entirely abandoned and pulled down; whether he is aware that the rock salt, which is the founda- tion of these buildings, is pumped from below them in the shape of brine, and afterwards, as salt and alkali, pays toll on the river Weaver, the surplus funds of which go in relief of the county rate; whether he is aware that the freeholders in the salt districts of Cheshire, who suffer by the serious and continual destruction of property through subsi- dence, have no legal remedy against the pumpers of the brine ; and whether he will consider the advisa- bility of bringing in a bill to provide such remedy? —Sir M. hicks-Beach: I am afraid the Board of Trade have nothing to do with the subject referred to in the question, and I cannot hold out any hope to the honourable member of the Board dealing with it. The matter is one which might be taken up locally by those interested. THE REV. F.E. HOPWOOD.—Lord Derby has pr.:- sented the Rev. Frank Edward Hopwood, M.A.. rec- tor of Badsworth Parish Church, Pontefradt, to the rectory of the parish church, Bury. The rectory of Bury is not only one of the most important in Lan- cashire, but in the kingdom, the value during the late Canon Hornby's time having been about £4,500 per annum. It is understood, however, that the new rector accepts a reduced income. The appoint- ment carries with it the patronage of the Bury livings, the office of one of Hulme trustees, the office of feoffee in Chetham's College and Library, and most likely the office of rural dean of Bury. Mr. Hopwood is the eldest son of Canon Frank George Hopwood, M.A., rector of Winwick, near Warrington, and grandson of the late Mr. Robert Gregge Hopwood, of Hopwood Hall, near Middle- ton, the intimate friend of Lord Byron. His mother was Lady Eleanor Mary Stanley, youngest daughter of the thirteenth Earl of Derby. He was born in 1843, was educated at Eton, graduated at Christ Church, Oxford, in 1865, and during his University career was coxswain of the "Oxford Eight." He was ordained in 1867 by Dr. Pelham, Bishop of Nor- wich, his first curacy being under Canon Nevill, at St. Nicholas, Great Yarmouth. In 1869 he

was presented by the Crown to the incumbency of St. James's, Congleton, Cheshire, and in 1879, by his cousin, the present Earl of Derby, to the rectory of Badsworth, Yorkshire. During the nine years Mr Hopwood has been at Badsworth he has been very popular. DEAFNESS CU/tED.—A very interesting 132 page Illustrated Book en Deafness. Noises in the bead. FISHING AT WALTON.

Sir,—The Treasurer and Committee of the Warrington Infirmary owe you a vote of thanks, for getting Sir Gil- bert Greenall to hand over £7 17s 6d for fishing in Wal- ton Reservoir. If you had nvt reminded the hon. baronet of his agreement, the funds of the institution would have been so much the worse off,—for some time at least. But £7 17s 6d for fishing at Walton! I wonder what the majority of the fishermen think of their 2s 6d invest- ments. Methinks the quiet roads round about the reser- voir must have resounded frequently with the groans and sighs of the anglers as they reflected upon their losses,— money, time, and bait; and I know of more than one lover of the gentle art whose first payment has been his last. It is not every piscatorial disciple who can afford to follow his hobby with the payment of a fee equal to the rate of pay of a brewery day-labourer, and if Sir Gil- bert Greenall had desired to preserve his domain from the foot of the poor and weary townsman, he could scarcely have fixed a more prohibitive charge. Perhaps, however, Sir Gilbert is anxious to keep people from breaking the commandments, by coveting things only a baronet can own. July 18th, 1888.

div.p: A PLEBEIAN.

Sir,—You will remember, at the "special meeting of the Council held to hear the statement of the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee," a resolution of the Council was passed that the information asked for should be cir- culated at least one week before the adjourned meeting. The meeting ought to be held next Friday ; but up to the present no information has been given, and, as far as I can gather, will not be given. It is the same story over again; the Sanitary Committee sets at nought the resolutions of the Council, and takes no notice of their request for information, except such as Alderman Bur- gess chooses to give them. On public grounds, I think a dead set should be made against any one committee taking up such a position. Whether you care to stir in the matter or not, I leave you to judge.—Yours faith- fully, Warrington, July 20th, 1888.
F. MONKS.

[lf there is yet time to prepare and presentareport, it cer- tainly ought to be done. We have reason to believe Alderman Burgess, as Chairman of the Committee, has been getting together the requisite material.— ED. Ex.]

ALLEGED DISCOURTESY AT THE INFIRMARY. Sir,—l am sorry to have to ask you to insert another letter on the subject of the Infirmary. I would not ask you to do so but that I feel bound, in justice to myself, to reply to Dr Gornall's letter in last Saturday's "Examiner." As soon as I had read the letter,l wrote to Dr. Gornall asking him if he had made inquiry as to what the imper- tinence consisted of, but though he kindly replied to my 'letter, he omitted to answer the question. I wrote to him a second time, pointing out to him that he had not answered the question, and repeating it. I had a second very nice reply, but still no answer to the question. Now, sir, I most distinctly deny having used any im- pertinence, and I challenge the doctor to prove it. There were two men in the room at the time who can prove what I say, if they are asked. It is very easy to write " Father Impertinent," but it is quite another thing to prove it ; and I contend that Dr. Gornall was not justified in publishing the entry in the accident book without first taking steps to see if it was correct.

I have no feeling whatever in this matter, and no object in view except the comfort of those for whom the Infirmary was founded. It is a most useful and neces- sary institution. It deserves to be supported, and it is because I desire to see it better appreciated and sup- ported by the people that I wish them to be treated as civilly and courteously as possible when they are necessitated to go there, whether on the occasion of an accident or otherwise.
H. E. HAWTHORNE.

THE REPORT OF THE SANITARY COMMITTEE. Sir,—There seems to be a division of opinion in the town as to whether the Sanitary Committee will, or will not, present a detailed report (as ordered by the Council) of the working at Longford since the introduction of the "Manlove, Alliott, and Co." system of machinery. As a body of English gentlemen whose word is their bond,' I feel assured that the Committee will carry out their promises and give the Council the fullest informa- tion they possibly can, and so afford an opportunity for ' 1 the proper discussion of this important question. The advantages accruing from such a policy will be obvious to all your readers. In the first place the rate- payers will be made acquainted (through the medium of your valued pages) with the material dealt with, and the method of manufacturing and disposal of the resultants. This information will also be of great interest to those who are desirous that the work should be carried on In the most efficient and economical manner. Secondly, the sanitary Committee by presenting a plain unvar- nished tale of their trials in the past, and their hopeMor the future, would do more to disarm criticism than they know of. If on the other hand their report is to be of a pimilar style to the statement made to the Council by Alderman Burgess on June Ist, 1888, and dealing with the question in a purely historical :manner—avoiding the main issue and treating it in an off-handed way—having the information but giving none—then I think that the Committee should be taught that they are only carrying out duties delegated to them by the Council, who again are only carrying out duties delegated to them by the ratepayers; and having these facts in mind, I hope the ratepayers will initiate a policy that will compel gentle- men appealing for their suffrages at the November elec- tions to pledge themselves to a line of action in the Council Chamber which will have the effect of showing to every Committee that it is subject to the control of the Council at all times.—Yours truly,

div.head: SIMPLEX.
div.p: SIMPLEX.
TRIUMPHANT ARISTOCRACY.

Sir,—The Duke of Argyll, speaking recently on Home Rule in the House of Lords, said: "The conversion of St. Paul was a remarkable one, but in that case a light had shone from Heaven, whereas the light that shone on Mr. Gladstone came from the Irish members, and he doubted whether the two localities were identical." Per- haps, if he had not been a "noble duke "and in the pre- sence of" lords spiritual and temporal," he would have put the simile thus: "St. Paul's conversion was from heaven, heavenly, but Mr. Gladstone's was from the devil, devilish." Again, in the same speeph he says: "There were some questions on which he would repose confidence in the masses, but on this (Home Ruler ques- tion it was not the uneducated masses, but the educated classes who must be consulted and entrusted with the carrying out of the work." In this last sentence we learn by implication that in this case the noble Duke would entirely ignore the masses—this being a question too intricate for their blunt intellects. Therefore, should the masses at the next general election give Mr. Gladstone a majority (which they will) with.the view that this Home Rule questiori be settled on a basis satis- factory to the Irish Representatives, he (the noble Duke) would rejoice that he and his noble colleagues had the hereditary privilege of vetoing the decision of such ma- jority, and wolild probably raise a horse-laugh at such futile efforts on the part of the masses to better their, and our, Irish neighbour's condition in life. Sir George Trevelyan said a short time ago, in a speech to the Welshmen—" The Conservative party show at I every turn that, though they have to accept representa- tive government, they do not really believe in it." "They are deeply impressed with the idea that the smaller country gentlemen, who are called squires, have a divine right to administer the affairs of the county, and the larger county gentleman, who are called ' peers, have the divine right to administer the affairs of the nation." This being so, surely it is foolish for the masses to trouble themselves about politics, and, we may almost reasonably include our Liberal M.P.'s, especially the Irish. Lord Salisbury's estimate of the mental calibre of the latter is a very low one, viz., any one member of his Cabinet being equal to eighty-six. Ought we not, therefore, to submit to the dictation of the" educated classes," and try to remember that we are an inferior order (" residuum"), and that the only functions that these noble lords will tolerate are those of working, pay- ing, and lighting? _
TOILER.

div.head: BRITISH WORKINGMAN.
div.p: THE BRITISH WORKINGMAN.

Sir,—! should like to know the expenence of some of your readers of the British workingman as he exists in Warrington. My little experience of him is such that I am exceedingly loth to employ him. Ile has such irrita- ting and senseless ways that one gets disgusted with him before he starts on a job. His sole object seems to be to get through what should be the working hours with the smallest possible amount of labour, and to make the job

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 21, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 21, 1888.

last as long as possible for fear it should be the last. The idea of getting the work in hand done never seems to enter his head; he has got a job and means to stick to it. If you engage, say, a joiner, for a verysimple job, and tell him explicity exactly what you want, he cannot for the life of him comprehend what is required, but must waste time by coming to look at the job. Then he goes to the 'shop for his tools, and when he brings them finds he has forgotten something. Off he goes to the shop again for a hammer, then he has to go again for nails, and so he proceeds wasting the time that should be bestowed on your job in walking to and from the " shop:". . .

My latest experieace with the genus was the other day, when a slater came to doctor my roof.. He came at 7 a.m.,with a long ladder on a.truck, which he left in the street for an hour, and then came to ask where the job wa.s. On being told, he said he must go for some one to help him to rear the ladder, and half an hour was occupied in fetching a man. The ladder up, another half hour was required to make it safe, and after a loss of about two hours the work was proceeded with. But the best came at the end. Having at length finished, the slater came to ask for his "allowance." "You must ask the landlord; I'm only the tenant, I didn't engage you." I "Oh, we always get a glass of beer from the tenant," he I said. "Well, you'll get none from me. I find water plenty strong enough. Besides, the cheek of the thing. You I get paid, and well paid, for your work, and why want more? Nobody thinks of paying me extra for any job i I do." "Well," chimed in the labourer, "a bottle of pop, then?" "Not a drop; I don't believe in it. My faith is in water." "Well, how would a bit of • baccy do ? " "No, nor tobacco, either. I don't believe in that." "Well, you are hard," remarked the labourer. "I don't see it," I said, "you get paid for your work, and that's enough I should say,' on which one man turned to the other, and in a most disgusted tone observed "Come along." If this be the genial way the British working- man carries on, it is no wonder the sober, intelligent foreigner is gradually but surely supplanting him.—l am, Ice., J. G. B. S. Warrington, July 11th, 1888.
ANOTHER SERIOUS SEWER ACCIDENT.

It is stated that on Thursday evening, at about five o'clock, a serious accident took place at the Gas Works at Longford, which was, however, happily unattended by fatal consequences. It being neces- sary to repair, or to move, something in a sewer at the works, a man named Harding, who lives in Warburton-st., Orford, descended into the sewer by means of a ladder, leading down from a man-hole. He had scarcely descended the ladder a few steps. however, when he was overpowered by the gas, and fell to the bottom. The foreman, )Ir. Parkinson, who was present at the time, seeing the catastrophe, called for help, and himself descended the man-hole. He. too, was overpo ered by the gas before he reached the bottom, and fell upon Hardy. His shout, however, had attracted the attention of some men working near, who, coming to the rescue, speedily hauled the men from the bottom by means of ropes. They were removed to their homes in an unconscious state, and Dr. Fox was called in. Under his treatment they at length recovered their senses. Mr. Parkinson was enabled to resume his duties yesterday, and it is expected that the other man will also in a few days have completely recovered from the effects of his accident. It is certain that had less promptitude been exercised in extricating the men from their position, the result would have been fatal to both of them.

putting out was reduced to the lowest figure named in the report. However that might affect the masters it was not likely to affect the men. It had not made and was not likely to make any difference to the workers. The merchants would most likely take off the amount which the master cutters had been putting into their pockets over and above the rules of the trade, and if any one was to blame for driving away the trade from Lymm it was the extraordinary dealings of these masters. Mr. James Buckley said he was glad to be able to say that a consideiable number had become members of the society, and had paid him their contributions during the week. He had found that many who had had work the previous week were now without, and vice-versa. As at the meeting held three weeks ago the society had been only formed tentatively, he thought the success they had met with justified them in recommending that the society should now take a permanent form. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Johnson asked if anything was to be done with those masters who worked the women and children all hours.—The Chairman said perhaps it might as well be announced at once that they meant to deal with those who systematically violated the law. There were shops in Lymm that were not closed from Monday morning to Saturday night, and women and children had to work alongside tho men. This had been going on for years. In fact, some masters never attempted to carry out the law, and it was time this state of things was brought under the notice of the authorities.— Some formal business having been transacted, the meet- ing closed.

div.head: "THE ONLY GENUINE LIBERALS."
div.p: "THE ONLY GENUINE LIBERALS."

Sir,—We are told in your last issue that " before the election in 1885, Mr. Gladstone said that if the Irish peo- ple were united, under the extended franchise, in demanding a certain thing, it might become neccess- ary for Parliament to make such changes as would go to the very foundation of the constitution. It is obvious to those who are not wilfully blind that Mr. Gladstone had Home Rule in his mind then, and, if so, his conversion was the result of evolution—and not miracle." Were the Nationalist's wilfully blind? for even they construed Mr. Gladstone's speeches in the election in 1885, when ho I appealed to the country to give him a clear majority over the Conservatives and Parnellites combined, that he meant to rule them with firmness. He made the same appeal in 1880, and got it, and we know the result. The Nationalists' were not alone in their construction, for the whole country did the same. Well, we all know the re- sult, viz :—Mr. Gladstone had only a clear majority of about three, over the Conservatives and Parnellitcs corn- bined,—that he had not a working majority. Hence in order to obtain the support of 85 Nationalists, he sud- denly turned round upon his previous opinions in order to get that working majority. I should like to know who expected any other result than the return of 85 Nationalists to that Parliament? We could not pick up a single paper,'whether Tory or Liberal, but what antici- pated and confessed before the election that the Nationa- lists estimate of 85 would be verified. Even Mr. Glad- stone himself thought so, for on the 9th of November, 1885, speaking at Edinburgh he said :—" Let me now suppose—for argument's sake I may suppose it possible —that the Liberal party might be returned to the com- ing Parliament,—that is rather a staggering supposition, —(laughter)—but I beg you to indulge me for an instant —(laughter)--might be returned to the coming Parlia- ment in a minority, but in a minority which might be- come a majority by the aid of the Irish vote; and I will suppose that, owing to some cause, the present Govern- ment has disappeared, and a Liberal party was called to deal with this great constitutional question of the gov- ernment of Ireland, in a position where it was a minority dependent on the Irish vote for converting it into a majority. Now; gentlemen, I tell you seriously and solemnly, that though I believe the Liberal party to be honourable, patriotic, and trustworthy, in such a position as that, it would not be safe for it to enter on the consideration of a measure in respect to which at the first step ef its progress, it would be in the power of a party coming from Ireland to say, 'unless you do this and unless you do that, we will turn you out to-morrow.' (Cheers)." What! not safe in November 1885, during the heat of the election, and then in a few weeks to be absolutely safe to surrender to the party of anarchy? What consistency forsooth! But what of that? It is the sort of consistency that has become fashionable with the Gladstonians ; and yet, when Mr. Gladstone tells us ser- iously and solemnly, that though that minority might become a majority, it would not be safe to entrust them with that power, we who have taken Mr. Gladstone's adVice as he wanted us, seriously and solemnly, to con- sider the Irish question in that spirit, are now to be ridi- culed and not to be considered as Liberals, simply be- cause we have seriously and solemnly considered this question in all its bearings. Sir, it is the Liberal and Radical Unionists who are the only genuine Liberals at the present time. Mr. Glad- stone's prophetic words in November, 1885, describes with marvellous accuracy the present position of the real Liberal party. We believe Mr. Gladstone spoke the truth when he said it would not be safe in 1885, and we believe it would not be safe in 1888, and I appeal to the Glad- stonians to take Mr. Gladstone's advice, and consider this question seriously and solemnly, as no doubt they did at the time.—l remain, yours respectively
RADICAL UNIONIST. [Our Correspondent is apparently unable to see that there
is a wide difference between the Nationalists accept-

ing Mr. Gladstone's proposals, and Mr. Gladstone be- ing forced to accept what they might think best. If "Radical Unionist" really believes Mr. Gladstone had in his mind the possibility of applying Coercion and not of turning to Rome Rule when he spoke of making a change which might go to the foundation of the constitution, we will not say that he is "wilfully blind " ; his blindneGs must 1;9 natural.—Ed. Ex.]

div.head: VACCINATION AND SANITATION,
div.p: VACCINATION AND SANITATION,

-- • Sir,—lf I may claim a space in your paper, I should like to say a word or tWo on the sanitary condition of the town. In your issue of the 14th inst, I saw the letter of , the Medical Officer of Health, coinplaining of the negli- gence of the people who live in the rural districts to re- port CAWS of fever and other epidemic diseases when they are abroad, saying that all his efforts are frustrated by their carelessness. Our Medical Officer has no need to go to the outskirts of the town. If he will go now and ; again through Winwick-st., not 100 yards from the Cen- tral Station, he will find stenches too horrible to des- dribe ; also in Pinner's Brow and Lythgoes-lane. If some morning shortly after breakfast, he will go down Lyth- goes-lane, he will find it a difficult task to keep his food on the stomach. In fact, Mr. Editor, I have wondered a few times whether we have Nuisance Inspectors or not and if they are paid to keep away from this part of the town; for if we have to have these centres of disease in our midst, all the medical faculty and all the physic they can bring will ao nothing towards destroying the causes of disease. But one thing it certainly will do, that is, fill the pockets of the vendors of medicine.

On Sunday, as I was passing through NVinwick-st., I saw posted on the wall a placard headed "Vaccination." stating (I)that children were vaccinated as a protection against smallpox; (2) that hundreds of children die of smallpox for the want of vaccination; (3) that those who, after vaccination, take the disease, recover with- out the blindness and scarring so common ia smallpox lin unvaccinated children. It also says that diseases can not be conveyed by vaccination. The bulk of these statements are, I contend, utterly false. Let us see with regard to the first point, that is vaccination as a preven- tive of smallpox. Vaccination was made compulsory in 1853 and still more stringent in 1867, and 1871. Now, one would reasonably suppose that after 20 years' trial lwe should see some good effects. I find that between the years 1853 to 1873 that there were three epidemics; the first in the years 1857-58-59, when there were no less than 14,244 deaths from smallpox; second in 1863-64-65. there were 20,059 deaths from the same desease ; and in 1870-71-72 there were 44,840 deaths from smallpox. If after 10 years' trial under compulsory vaccination we have no better results, I want to know where its protec- tion comes in ? With regard to blindness, pitting, &c., i any medical man knows that when these occur it s the fault of the treatment, and that only. This point we will leave as it is subterfuge. Tile next point is —we will take the words • from the There need be no apprehension that vaccination will injure health or communicate any disease." I find in a return made by the medical department itself No. 50 (session 1877) that out of 16 infants vaccinated at Misterlon, in Lincolnshire, six of them were dead within a month from erysipelas. Ah, but some would say, these are only exceptional cases. I could give hundreds, but your spale will not allow. But one more I will give. Dr. Cory, an officer of one of the Medical Departments of the Govern ment, vaccinated himself ttoin a child known to have syphilis. The result was, the local symptoms of that disease. Now, Mr. Editor, if these statements are facts, which all men may prove for themselves, what does it mean? It means nothing more nor less than we are being misled by the medical faculty. Still, we admit that there are honourable men among them, and it is a great pity that their calling has been made into a busi- ness to barter away life to the highest bidder. I ask what has to be done to be rid of the diseases from our midst? Each home will have to take measures for itself. We shall have to keep onrselves clean. We shall have to eat clean and pure food. We shall have to get rid of the stagnant cesspools from our midst, and if there has to be any compulsion we shall have to compel those who would keep filthy refuse to remove it from Social centres, and, not least, we shall have to pay our medical,staff according to the health and purity of the town, instead of when dissbn see are rampant, it proving their harvest.—l am yours, Sm.,

div.head: MANCHUSTE Et SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHUSTE Et SHIP CANAL.
(Continued from page 6.)

, WESTON. There are now upwards of 800 men employed on this section, and work is proceeding briskly. Two steam navvies have been fitted up, and are forging their way through the soft soil of the Marsh towards the Ince sec- tion, and preparations are also being made for the river operations. The village of huts in course of erection by Mr. T. Kirkham is approaching completion. RUNCORN. . _

There is nothing of importance to record on this sec- tion. Owing to the recent heavy rains a considerable quantity of water has accumulated in the trench, and the work of excavation has been much interfered with. Pumping operations have been kept up; and the steam navvies will be in full action in a day or two. At the edge of the river channel, behind the works of Messrs. Wigg, Brothers, and Steele, there has been this week de- posited a quantity of dry soil and clay, with a view of ascertaining what action the tide will have upon it. In fact, it is a kind of experimental start in the river opera- tions. Material daily accumulates on the wharves at the Old Quay, and is being prepared ready for use in the river.

div.head: THELWALL AND STATHAM.
div.p: THELWALL AND STATHAM.

The new German navvy which is being erected near Statham is not yet completed, but will probably be at I work in the early days of next week. The work has dur- ing the week been very vigorously carried on, and on Rixton Leys in particular great progress is being made, Near Thelwall the several steam navvies have brought the cutting to a considerable width, and operations are being extended with notable rapidity in the neighbour- hood of Morris Brook. The water of this brook will , doubtless be impounded after the canal is made, but at present temporary provision is being made for carrying the water over the workings. Excavating operations are now in full swing on the eastern part of the site of the intended Latchford locks, avid we understand that rock has here been struck upon, for the removal of which blasting operations will be necessary. ACCIDENT AT RIXTON.

A boy named Charles Whitfield, of Cadishead, met with an accident on Thursday night on the works at Rixton. While he was engaged greasing waggons the train started and crushed his legs. He was conveyed to the hospital erected on Skeer Rock, where his injuries were attended to. He is not expected to recover. BILL.
THE NEW

The Queen's consent has been signified to the Bill sanctioning the substituting plans for the construction of docks at Manchester in connection with the Ship Canal, and the Bill has been reported to the House of Lords from the Select Committee, with amendments. Early next week the Bill will be read a third time, and it will soon afterwards receive the Royal Assent.

LATEST NEWS.
Mr. W. J. Inghram, who formerly represented Boston, ha./ promised to contest the division of the county as a Liberal.

The inquest on Mr. Mandeville, at Mitchelstown, was temporarily adjourned on Friday, in consequence of the death of Dr. Ridley. Rev. Father imprisoned under the -Crimes Act, was released at Limerick on Friday. A crowd warmly cheered him.

Play'at Brighton, between the Sussex and Australian cricketers had ,to be abandoned yesterday afternoon owing to continued heavy rain. The inquest on the bodies of four women killed in the Hyde collision was resumed at Dukinfield yesterday. After evidence had been given it was adjourned till Tuesday:

Two -Baorgsas DROWNBD. - Early on Friday two brothers named Williams, sons of a farmer living at Llanrwrst, were drowned btthe capsizing of a boat in the river Conway. The bodies were recovered. The Association of Western Ironmasters has been dis- solved. Thirty-eight ums, employing about 25,000 hands, having signed the workers' scale of wages, the dispute between masters and men has ended in a vic- tory for the latter.

BRADLAUGH AND NORTHAMPTON. The Liberal and Radical Union of Northampton have convened a meeting of electors for Wednesday next, at which Mr. 1 Bradlaugh will attend, and will ask their formal decision on his conduct of the Oaths Bill. . Tam WIMBLEDON MEETING.—At Wimbledon,on Friday, it was announced that Private Wattleworth, 2nd Liver- pool, had wen £25, the first Olympic prize. Major Mc- Kerrill, Ist Ayr, won the £25 prize in the Dudley compe- tition. Mr. Stewart, Edinburgh, won the Any Rifle Association Cup. NEW MAGISTRATES FOR CHESTER.—At the Chester City Quarter Sessions, on Thursday morning, before the Re- corder, His Honour Judge Horatio Lloyd, Mr. John Cul- limore, solicitor, Dr. Watson and Mr. H. M. Bowers, 1 brick and tile merchant, qualified as Justices of the Peace for the city. OBTAINING GOLD WATCHES BY FEAXID.—On Friday, at the Mansion House, a respictable young man named Turner, who gave his address as Seely's Mount, Pendle- ton, Manchester, pleaded- guilty to defrauding Sir John Bennett of gold watches and chains of the value of 300 guineas by means of a forged letter. Prisoner was commit ed for trial.

_ SUICIDE OF A Docroity—A Fermoy correspondent tele- graphs that Dr. Ridley, of Tullamore gaol, committed suicide at the Royal Hotel, Fermoy, on Friday morning by cutting his throat. He was found in his bedroom'at nine o'clock quite dead, and from appearances he seemed to have committed the act before a mirror, and then got into bed and died.. Dr. Ridley attended the inquest on Mr. Mandeville, at Mitchelstown, on Thursday, .and would have been called subsequently to give evldence. Arm Enterer. MURDER AND SUICIDE. An attempt on the life of a woman named Ann Berry was made at Ply- mouth late on Thursday evening by a tailor named Chas. Vickers, who had for some months been living with her. Through his treatment she left him a few days ago, and on returning on Thursday evening for some articles he stabbed her three times with a table knife in the left breast. Vickers then cut his throat with the knife, but the wound was only superficial. The woman lies in a critical condition.

• SUND AY CLOSING IN IRELAND. The report of the Select Committee on the Sunday Closing Acts (Ireland) was issued on Friday. The following are the recom- mendations of the committee :—(1) That the Act of 1878 should be made perpetual and extended to the five cities now exempted from the lull operation of the Act:; (2) that the qualifying distance under the bona-fide provi- sion should be extended to six miles; and (3) that all houses for the sale of intoxicating liquors in Ireland should be closed at nine p.m. on Saturday.
