div.head: _,.._. MR. DIGGLE AT THE WORKMEN'S CLUB.
div.p: _,.._. MR. DIGGLE AT THE WORKMEN'S CLUB.

On Thursday night, at the Workmen's Club, Mr. William Diggle addressed a large and amused audience on the subject of the Sanitary Questions as connected with Longford Depot, etc. Punctually at the time appointed Mr. Diggle made his appear- ance on the platform, being greeted with a round of applause, after duly acknowledging which, he commenced—" Fellow ratepayers."—The meeting, however, had made up their minds to have the usual formality of a chairman, besides, part of the fun centred in the chairman, so there were cries of "Who's chairman, Diggle ?"—Mr. DIGGLE said, "Well, I leave that to you; everyone's so afraid of me, you see." This was what was desired, and it was proposed, seconded, and carried that Mr. Richard Siddle take the chair.

Mr. Sininn accordirrgl;-;Qtea—the platform, and, remarking that he should prefer some one else should occupy the position proceeded to say that the questions upon which they had met to deliberate were most im- portant ones. He expressed himself as tired of the exist- ing sanitary arrangements, and the steps taken by the Council with regard to them. He said he had been in- formed that there were members of the Council who pretended they could not experience these annoy- ances. (A voice: "They're fire-proof.") My friends, give Mr. Diggle a patient hearing.—Mr. DIGGLE : Bear in mind that I've got your twopences. (Applause.) Mr. Diggle then said that he was an injured man, and pro- ceeded to speak of some of the towns round about. He gave an account of the sanitary arrangements in vari- ous other towns, and was frequently interrupted by cries of "Have a drink Diggle," "Give us back our two- pences," until at last he gave vent to the exclamation that if he had known he would have brought some police and " chuckers-out." After further interruption Mr. Diggle spoke of the sanitary system, its increase, and upon the building of Longford depot. He then men- tioned the nuisance which was caused by the works. This nuisance he alleged had not been destroyed, but had simply been transferred from Longford and saddled upon some of the poorer people in the town. (Cries of hear, hear, and "shame.") He went on to state that what was, if rightly used, valuable manure, was given away to the farmers as waste, and a great loss was incurred. Mr. Diggle, amid some interruption, then read a report of a meeting of the Council, in which it was stated that Alderman Burgess indicated his intention to ask for a grant of some thousands of pounds in order to duplicate the machinery at Longford. Before that was granted he should like to see the profit and loss account that had been promised so long, but was net yet forthcoming. The lecturer remarked that he had not been surprised by the opposition he had received on the Ship Canal question, but he thought they would have received him better on the question then under discussion. After much badinage had taken place the Chairman vacated his positiOn, and the meeting, apparently acting in a spirit of mischief, adopted a vote of confidence in the Sanitary Committee, and a vote of censureon Mr. Diggle and the chairman of the meeting. The farce then ter- minated.

LYMIL. LICENSING CgANGE.—At the Altrincham Petty SESSiODS on Monday, an application for transferring the license of the Bull's Head, Lymm, from William Millyard to Charles Millyard was granted. BAPTIST CHAPEL LITTLE LEIGH. The anniversary services in connection with this place pf worship* took place on Sunday, when two sermons were preached by the Rev. J. B. Morgan, of Crewe. There were good congregations, and the collections amounted to £2.3 13s, ACCIDENT AT BROIDIIPATH.—On Monday afternoon, a boy named William Yearsley (15), whose father keeps the Navigation Hotel, Broadheath, met with an accident at the Atlantic Works, at Broadheath. While engaged at a circular saw, his right hand became entangled, and the whole of the fingers were cut off. A NARROW ESCAPE.—On Tuesday morning an engine- driver on the Ship Canal working in Statham, but who lives in Sandy-lane, left home for his work, having fast made a good fire. His child, about three years old, came downstairs in its nightdress, and was in the room by I itself, when its screams attracted the attention of its mother. She immediately rushed downstairs and found the nightdress of theichild ablaze, and had the presence of mind to wrap* in some clothing, which extinguished the flames. The child and mother are both burnt, but not very seriously. Goon TEMPLARY.—On Tuesday evening a projected open-air meeting, under the auspices of the "Tower of Refuges" was frustrated by the heavy fall of rain, and the meeting was held in the Congregational School- room. Mr. McGill ocupied the chair, supported by Mr: Wrathall (of Leeds), Mr. Dutton, and Mr. L. Ellison (Latchford.) After the singing of` a hymn and prayer Mr. McGill, in a short address, introduced the lecturer of the evening, Mr. WrathaJl, who gave an able address on "Thrift, citing many examples of it amongst the working-classes, with the happiest results to themselves and society, and earnestly impressing its value on his listeners. Votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close. ALTRINCHAM AND BOWDON FLOWER SHOW : SUCCESSFUL LYIIM Exrasyrons.—At the annual exhibition of the Altrincham and Bowdon Floral and Rose Society, held at Devisdale, Bowdon, on Friday and Saturday, the first prize in the competition for plants for dinner table decoration was awarded to Mrs. Grundy, West Leigh, Lymm, for a group formed of cratons, dracaenas, cocos, I pandanas Veitchii, and aralia Veitchii. Mrs. Battersby, also of Lymm, secured the second place in each of the following competitions :--Roses : amateurs and gentle- men's gardeners, 36 distinct varieties, single trusses ; eighteen distinct 'varieties, single trusses; and twelve distinct varieties, single trusses. It may -be mentioned that Mr. F. Simpson is gardener to Mrs. Battersby. In the fruit and vegetable competition Mrs. Grundy was also very successful, as she gained second prize for two bunches of white grapes, first prize for six peaches, and third prize for brace of cauliflowers: MrS. Battersby gained the second prize for the twelve stove and greenhouse cut blooms, distinct varieties.

MEETING OF FUSTIAN CtiTTEII9.—A meeting of fustian cutters was held on Monday night at the Millstone Inn clubroom to consider what action should be taken after the refusal of the masters to apt with the committee for ' the mutual benefit of each and the advantage of the I trade generally. Mr. Gatley occupied the chair. lie I said he was glad to be able to congratulate the commit- tee on the large increase which had taken place in the number of members who had joined the society during I the last week. It would appear that the publication of their proceedings did not meet with the approVal of the masters, but they (the working cutters) had nothing to hide in what they were doing, and they were only too glad that publicity was being given to their meetings. These reports, they were informed, were going to drive the trade out of Lymm, as the masters' attention had been called to the prices stated to be paid for the cutting, with the result that the price of

THE Hoawics TRAGEDY.—At Manchester Assizes, on Thursday, George Richard Walker, a striker, was,brought up to undergo a second trial on a charge of murdering Jane Hodgson, at llorwich, near Bolton, on the 14th April. The jury at the Liverpool Assizes failed to agree upon a verdict at the former trial, and on Thursday the Manchester jury expressed a desire to examine the scene of the alleged crime and left the court in charge of the Sub-Sheriff and a police-sergeant for that purpose. The theory of the prosecution was that the prisoner had thrown or dragged the woman down the dough. The prisoner denied all knowledge of the affair, and urged that the woman must have fallen down the dough. When the case for the prosecution was completed on Thursday, Mr. Justice Grantham directed the jury to re- turn a verdict of acquittal, aahe said it would not be safe to give any other verdict in such a case.

div.head: FIVE CHILDREN POISONED.
div.p: FIVE CHILDREN POISONED.

An extraordinary case of poisoning has occurred near HolYwell, five children of a widow named Hughes being the sufferers. Two of the children have died, and the others are in a very critical condition. No suspicion of foul play is entertained,ibut the manner in which the poison ,was taken remains a mystery. The coroner has ordered a post-mortem examination.

DESTRUCTIVE CLOUD-BURST IN AMERICA. LOSS OF TWENTY LIVES. A destructive cloud-burst occurred on Thursday at Wheeling, Virginia, causing the loss of twenty lives, and doing much damage to property. Many bridges,were demolished by the flood. PETROLEUM CARGO ON FIRE.

SIX MEN KILLED. A terrible catastrophe occurred at noon on Thursday at Rouen, in Prance. The steamer Astariano, with a cargo of 8,840 barrels of petroleum, took fire. The flames soon spread to the combustible fluid, and terrific explo- sions followed in rapid succession. Six men were killed. and two others, who were badly injured by burns, had to be conveyed to the hospital. The vessel was totally destroyed.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock.

ARGYLL AGAIN.—Lord BE-A-U-C-HARP moved that the names %f the Lords present in the House on Thursday, 12th July, and assenting to resolutions of confidence in Her Majesty's ministers passing nemine cost radieente, be printed and circulated with the thinutes. The carrying of the Duke of Argyll's motion without opposition must have been, he said; a matter of great satisfaction to the Govertment.—A long discussion ensued.—Lord GRAN= VILLE explained-that the Opposition were silent because the Duke of Argyll said nothing to affect ,the position in the country.—The DUKE of ARGYLL twitted noble lords on their base desertion of Lord Granville, and hoped the Opposition would gain courage.—Lord ROSZBERRY said the Duke never came down except to hold an assize, and condemn someone.—Lord SALISBURY had thought the Lords were silent because they had changed their views, but he now understood they had nothing to say. —The motion was agreed to on the words assenting to being left out —The House shortly afterwards ad- journed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock.

TME ALLEGATIONS BILL.—Mr. SMITH stated, in answer to Mr. A. O'Connor, that the usual provision wonld tie made for the expense of the Commission to be estab- lished in pursuance of the Allegations Bill., If it was necessary provision would be made for the discharge of the ordinary judicial duty of those employed in the Commission.—Mr. WALTER Itmes asked whether any correspondence had passed between the "Times " and the Government with reference to the Allegations Bill, and if so whether the docunfents would be laid before the Bouse.—Mr. Smrrir : There are no such documents of the kind.—Mr. SEXTON asked if there had been any oral COM. muni.cation.—Mr. &arm I decline to answer any such question. (Parnellite cheers.) LIBEL ON THE SPEAKER.—MR. CONYBEARE _ _ SUSPENDED.

_ Lord R. CHURCHILL asked Mr. Conybeare whether he was the author of a letter which appeared in the evening called "The Star," headed Mr. Conybeare and the Spea- ker 7—Mr. CoNTssikux said that as the noble lord had not read the letter he would not answer. Lord R. Click- affix said the hon. member might choose to look on it as a trifling matter. Having indicated, that the letter was in his view, a breach of privilege the Clerk at the table, at the order of the Speaker, read the letter, which reiterated Mr. Conybeare's statement that the applica- tion of the closure was a scandal, and stating though he thought it well to withdraw in order to avoid being named and suspended, he still adhered to the opinions he expressed. It further stated that the Government wan- ted to prevent discussion of the Drainage pill, and that the Speaker backed them up, and he hoped Mr. Speaker's constituency would be careful to mark his conduct. The letter was ' signed by Mr. Conybeare. Lord R. CHURCHILL again asked Mr. Conybeare if he wrote the letter.—Mr. CONYHEARE.— Yes. I Aid.— Lord R. CHURCHILL contended that the letter Was a breach, of privilege. He condelnned Mr. Conybea,re's ac- cusation of the Speaker's conduct as a public scandal, and said it was calculated to bring the House into disre- pute. It was an insult to the Speaker, whose action, he insisted, deserved the approval of the people of England. He concluded by moving that the letter was a gross libel on the Speaker, that it deserved severity of condemna- tion, and that Mr. Conybeare be suspended for the re- mainder of the session.-Mr. BIGGAR opposed the 'notion.— After observations from Mr. Lear and Mr. Redmond, the SPEAKER explained how the matter arose last night. He justified his conduct. The matter was now before the Hotue.—Mr. W. SMITH said the questioh now was whe- ther the Speaker has been libelled in the chair, and the House insulted in his person. The duty was to protect the chair, and he therefore supported the motion made.— Mr. GLADSTONE felt compelled to give his assent to the proposal, the necessity for which he lamented.—Mr. LABOUCHERE moved an amendknent to the motion sub- stituting the words breach of privilege for gross libel on the Speaker,—A long discussion ensued, in which it was contended that the letter was a breach of privilege and not a libel on thed'Speaker.—Mr. W. SMITH op- posed Mr. Labouchere's amendment.—Lord HALTING- me trusted that whatever the decision of the House might be it would be unanimous. The House divided on the amendment of Mr. Labou- there, when it•was rejected by 245 to 168.--The Speaker then put the first portion of Lord R. Churchill's motion from the chair, that the letter of Mr. Conybeare pub- lished in the " Star " newspaper was a gross libel on the Speaker of the House of Commons, and deserved the severest condemnation of the House. This was agreed to without division.—The Speaker then put the second por- tion of the motion, that the hon. member for Cambourne be suspended from the service of the Hefts° for the re- mainder of the session.—Mr. LABOUCHERE, as an amend- ment, moved the suspension be for one week'.—A discus- sion then arose as to whether the suspension in Lord R. Churchill's proposal was to be from the end of the sitting to the autumn sitting, or to the end of the session in December.—Lord R. CHURCHILL declined to give any definition of the term remainder of sassion..--Mr. Lewin- moue, as many members thought suspension for a week

was nnt sufficient, withdrew, by leave of the 110125f' amendment, and moved another, setting out that suspension should be for a fortnight.—Another cussion ensued as to the term of suspension.—x! Slum ultimately suggested that the suspension be for one month.--Dr. TANNER thought the best would be, as such diversity of opinion existed, t° time for deliberation. He therefore moved the 0 ment of the debate.—After a discussion that was negatived by 277 to 133, and then, after a. of controversy had continued nearly an hour, the divided on Mr. Labouchere's amendment that pension should be for a fortnight, which was rejeero 229 to 152.—Mr. W. Siam then moved the additio words to the motion that the suspension should be the reminder of the, session, or one calendar whichever should first terminate.—Sir W. HAI; , said the opposition adhered to the .protest they ha They believed the punishment exceeded the no7:', and thought it exceeded Parliamentry precedents subject.---Mr. SMITH'S proposal was then put fr°"'• chair, and a division was challenged. Before the was closed the members of the Opposition left the in a body, and when the Speaker again put the c that Mr. Conybeare's suspension should be for, mainder of the session or one calendar,montb, ever should first terminate, it was agreed to further objection. rvia SERVICE ESTIMATES.—The House then wept Committee of Supply on Civil Service Estimates. {LEFT SITTING.]

Two committment summonses were applied for by Messrs. John Walker and Co., printers, Warrington, and Messrs. Williams and Clay, masons, Warrington, against Mr. A. E. G. Robinson, veterinary surgeon of the same town. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the defendant. It transpired that there was a previous committal against the defendant which had not been put in force, in con- sequence of which the judge dismissed both applications. —An application for committment was made Isy Mr. H. J, Longton, solicitor, on behalf of Woodruff and Sons, against Michael Cryan, machinist, Warrington. As there was a previous committal which had not been enforced this application was also dismissed. Mr. Long- ton then applied on behalf of his client for costs, on the ground that the registrar, when he gave notice of his application for commitment should have in- formed him of the previous committal, thus saving- the expense. In support of this application he cited the case of Ball v. Blears heard that morning, in which a committal granted against Blears for 6s, to be paid in two months, from the 2nd of February last, by his Honour's ruling, barred the way against all subsequent applications for committal. The committal was never executed, and thus Blears was free to incur debts, being protected from his creditors by this previous committal. His Honour, however, dismissed the application.
